The Qur'an would later touch this wound with unbearable gentleness: "Did He not find you an orphan and shelter you?" The final Prophet was deliberately raised with no father to credit, no dynasty to inherit, nothing of the ordinary scaffolding of greatness.

By the custom of Quraysh he was sent to the desert, to the wet nurse Halimah of Banu Sa'd, where he learned the pure Arabic of the badiyah and the open horizon, and where {{n:28|the first extraordinary event}} of his childhood would occur. Of his lineage he ﷺ said: "Allah chose Kinanah from the descendants of Isma'il, and chose Quraysh from Kinanah, and chose Banu Hashim from Quraysh, and chose me from Banu Hashim", selection upon selection, like the House itself: {{n:9|Ibrahim}}, to Isma'il, to the boy in whom the du'a of the builder finally came true.

quran.en: Did He not find you an orphan and shelter you?
Our Lord, raise up among them a messenger from themselves…

hadith.text: He was asked about fasting on Monday. He said: That is the day I was born, and the day revelation came to me.
Allah chose Kinanah from the sons of Isma'il, Quraysh from Kinanah, Banu Hashim from Quraysh, and chose me from Banu Hashim.

lessons: The Prophet's own commemoration of his birth was a fast, not a festival
Orphanhood was the curriculum: greatness with no scaffolding but Allah
He is the convergence of the prophets, Ibrahim's du'a and Isa's tidings

28.summary: Angels opened his chest and washed his heart with Zamzam.
28.details:
In the desert of Banu Sa'd, while the young Muhammad played with the other boys, {{c:a-jibril|Jibril}} came to him, took hold of him, and laid him down. Anas ibn Malik transmits the event in Sahih Muslim with surgical calm: he split open his chest, took out the heart, extracted from it a clot, and said: "This is Shaytan's portion of you." Then he washed the heart in a basin of gold with the water of {{p:p-zamzam|Zamzam}}, restored it, and returned him to his place. The boys ran to Halimah crying that Muhammad had been killed; they received him back "with an altered color." Anas adds the detail of an eyewitness generation: "I used to see the mark of that stitching on his chest."

The tradition records the operation was not unique. Before {{n:32|the Night Journey}}, the opening was repeated: the chest washed and the heart filled with wisdom and faith before the ascent through the heavens. The pattern is deliberate, purification precedes commission. Before the boy could carry the message, the organ that would carry it was cleansed of the whisperer's share; before the man could stand in the highest presence, it was cleansed again.

The Codex reads this node beside {{c:j-qarin|the hadith of the qarin}}: every human being has a companion from the jinn assigned to him: "even me," the Prophet ﷺ said, "but Allah helped me against him, and he submitted, so he commands me with nothing but good." The washing of the chest and the submission of the qarin are two faces of one fact: the vessel of revelation was secured at every layer, flesh, heart, and unseen company.

Halimah, shaken, returned the boy to Aminah. The desert years had already done their work: pure language, hard sky, open horizon, and a heart washed with the water that {{n:11|sprang for his ancestor Isma'il}}. Nothing about the final Prophet was improvised.

quran.en: Did We not expand for you your chest?

hadith.text: Jibril came to him while he was playing with the boys, took him, laid him down, split his chest, removed the heart and extracted a clot from it and said: This was Shaytan's portion of you. Then he washed it in a gold basin with Zamzam water…

There is no one among you but a companion from the jinn has been assigned to him. They said: Even you? He said: Even me, but Allah helped me against him, and he submitted, so he commands me with nothing but good.

lessons: Purification precedes mission, the vessel is prepared before the message
Allah guards His revelation at every layer: heart, tongue, and unseen company
What Zamzam began at the well of Isma'il, it continued in the chest of his descendant

29.summary: At forty he retreated to the cave of Hira for nights of worship.
29.details:
Approaching forty, the man whom {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}} called al-Amin, the Trustworthy, began to withdraw. Aisha's narration in Bukhari sets the sequence: first, true dreams: "he never saw a dream but it came like the break of dawn", six months of them, the tradition counts. Then "solitude was made beloved to him," and he took himself to the {{p:p-hira|cave of Hira}} on Jabal an-Nur, the Mountain of Light, to practice tahannuth: nights of devotion, alone, before any revelation had defined what devotion should be.

The cave itself is barely a room of rock, yet its mouth faces the {{p:p-kaaba|Kaaba}}. A man dissatisfied with his city's idols, unwilling to join their rites, unable yet to name the alternative, sitting night after night facing {{n:11|the House Ibrahim built}}, in the posture of waiting. {{c:c-khadijah|Khadijah}} provisioned these retreats; he would return to her for supplies and go back up. The scholars note what this arrangement means: the greatest spiritual preparation in history ran on the quiet care of a believing wife.

What was he doing? The word tahannuth carries the sense of the hunafa', the remnant seekers of Ibrahim's way. He did not invent a liturgy; he watched, reflected, and grieved for his people. Surah ad-Duha names this interval with a tenderness the tradition treasures: "And He found you searching, and guided." Lost here is not error, it is the honest state of a sound heart in a corrupt age, before revelation arrives.

The Codex gives this quiet node full standing because everything explosive in the next node depends on it. Revelation did not fall on a distracted man; it fell on a man whose habits had been bent toward heaven for years, solitude, reflection, disgust with false gods, love of the true one not yet named. When {{c:a-jibril|Jibril}} finally seized him in that same cave, the vessel had been carried to the exact coordinates of {{n:30|the meeting}}, by his own feet, night after night, for years.

quran.en: And He found you searching, and guided.

hadith.text: The first of what began of revelation was the true dream in sleep, he never saw a dream but it came like the break of dawn. Then solitude was made beloved to him, and he would seclude himself in the cave of Hira, devoting himself for nights…

lessons: Great openings are preceded by long, unseen discipline
Solitude with reflection is a sunnah older than the first verse
Behind the retreats stood a wife's support, revelation had a household

30.summary: Jibril appeared in the cave of Hira: “Read!” The first five verses of Surah al-Alaq.
30.details:
It came in Ramadan, in the cave, with no warning that night was different from a hundred nights before it. The angel came to him and said: اقْرَأْ: "Read." He answered: "I am not one who reads." What happened next, the Prophet ﷺ himself described: "He took hold of me and pressed me until I reached the limit of my endurance, then released me and said: Read. I said: I am not one who reads." Three times, the seizure, the crushing embrace, the release, until the third release, when the first words of the final revelation entered the world:

"Read in the name of your Lord who created, created man from a clinging substance. Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous, who taught by the pen, taught man what he knew not." Five verses. The religion of the unlettered Prophet opened with the command to read, in the name of the Lord, tying all knowledge to its Source in its first breath.

He descended the mountain with his heart pounding and entered upon {{c:c-khadijah|Khadijah}} saying: "Cover me, cover me", zammilūni. When the fear subsided he told her what had happened, and said: "I fear for myself." Her answer is one of the monuments of the Seerah, the first testimony ever given for the final Prophet, delivered by a wife reasoning from his character to Allah's justice: "Never! By Allah, Allah will never disgrace you. You keep the ties of kinship, you bear the burden of the weak, you earn for the destitute, you honor the guest, and you help against the calamities of truth." She did not say "do not be afraid", she gave evidence.

Then she acted. She took him to her cousin {{c:c-waraqah|Waraqah ibn Nawfal}}, an old, blind seeker who had become Christian and knew the earlier scriptures. Waraqah heard the account and identified the visitor precisely: "This is the Nāmūs whom Allah sent down upon {{n:15|Musa}}." Then the old man read the future from the pattern of the past: "Would that I were young when your people expel you.": "Will they expel me?" the Prophet asked, astonished; {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}} loved him. "Never has a man brought the like of what you bring but he was met with enmity. If your day reaches me, I will support you with a strength you cannot imagine." Waraqah died soon after, a believer of the interval, the first ally of the message outside its own house.

Then revelation paused. The fatrah, a silence long enough for the heart to ache for what had terrified it. It broke with thunder: he saw the angel who had come to {{p:p-hira|Hira}} "sitting on a throne between the sky and the earth," fled home again crying "Cover me", and this time the covering itself was overturned into a commission: "O you who wraps himself: arise and warn. And your Lord, magnify. And your garments, purify." There would be no more blankets.

What began that night would continue for twenty-three years, and it never became light. Asked how revelation came, he ﷺ described its two modes: "Sometimes it comes like the ringing of a bell, and that is the hardest upon me, and it releases me having retained what it said; and sometimes the angel appears as a man and speaks to me." {{c:c-aisha|Aisha}} saw the cost with her own eyes: on a bitterly cold day, revelation would descend and lift, "and his forehead would be dripping with sweat." The Qur'an itself declared the weight: "We will cast upon you a heavy word." The five verses of Hira were the first grams of a weight that would re-shape one man, then Arabia, then the map of the world.

From this node the Path runs through persecution, {{n:31|Ta'if}}, {{n:32|the ascent}}, {{n:34|the Hijrah}}, and it begins here, with a crushed man in a cave, a wife with evidence, an old scholar with a warning, and five verses about reading and the pen.

quran.en: Read in the name of your Lord who created, created man from a clinging substance. Read, and your Lord is the Most Generous, who taught by the pen, taught man what he knew not.
O you who wraps himself, arise and warn, and your Lord, magnify.

hadith.text: He pressed me until I reached my limit, then released me and said: Read… until he said: Read in the name of your Lord who created.

Khadijah said: Never, by Allah, Allah will never disgrace you: you keep the ties of kinship, bear the burden of the weak, earn for the destitute, honor the guest, and help against the calamities of truth.
Waraqah said: This is the Nāmūs whom Allah sent down upon Musa. Would that I were young when your people expel you… Never has a man brought the like of it but he was opposed.

Sometimes it comes to me like the ringing of a bell, and that is the hardest upon me, and it releases me having retained what it said; and sometimes the angel appears as a man… and on a very cold day his forehead would drip with sweat.

lessons: The first command of the final religion is to read, in His name
Khadijah's comfort was a proof from character: good conduct is evidence with Allah
Every bringer of truth is opposed, Waraqah's law of history
The blanket becomes the pulpit: comfort is a station, not a residence

31.summary: Stoned until his shoes filled with blood. He refused the offer to crush the city.
31.details:
In one year the Prophet ﷺ lost the two shields of his mission: {{c:c-khadijah|Khadijah}}, and his uncle Abu Talib, the Year of Sorrow. With Makkah's protection structure collapsing, he walked to {{p:p-taif|Ta'if}} with {{c:c-zayd|Zayd ibn Harithah}} to offer Thaqif the message.

Their three chiefs answered with practiced mockery, and worse: they set the city's slaves and street boys on him. He was stoned until blood ran down and clotted in his sandals. Zayd shielded him with his own body and was gashed on the head. They took refuge in an orchard belonging to two Makkans, and there, bleeding, the Prophet raised the complaint the sirah has preserved as the du'a of the crushed: "O Allah, to You I complain of my weakness, my scarcity of resources, and my insignificance before men. O Most Merciful of the merciful… if You are not angry with me, I do not care, but Your protection is more encompassing for me." Not a word asking for revenge; the entire anxiety of the du'a is whether the failure signified his Lord's displeasure.

The answer came in two forms. The first was small and strange: a Christian slave named Addas brought him grapes, heard him say "Bismillah," and discovered the man before him knew of {{c:an-yunus|Yunus ibn Matta}}: "my brother," the Prophet said, "he was a prophet and I am a prophet", and the slave kissed his head while his idolater masters watched in alarm.

The second answer split the sky. On the road home, {{c:a-jibril|Jibril}} appeared with {{c:a-mountains|the Angel of the Mountains}}, who gave the greeting and said: "If you wish, I will bring the two mountains down upon them." The wounded man's reply is, by consensus of the ummah, one of the summits of his character: "Rather, I hope that Allah will bring forth from their loins those who will worship Allah alone, associating nothing with Him." Within a generation, Ta'if was Muslim.

On the way back, at Nakhlah, while he recited in the night prayer, a company of {{c:j-believing|the jinn}} passed, listened, believed, and returned to their people as warners, heaven quietly noting that when men refuse the message, other audiences are already assembled. He re-entered {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}} only under the protection of Mut'im ibn Adi, a mushrik with honor, a debt the Prophet remembered publicly after {{n:38|Badr}}. And on the heels of the hardest year came {{n:32|the highest journey}}.

quran.en: Say: It has been revealed to me that a company of the jinn listened and said: We have heard an amazing Qur'an.

hadith.text: Aisha asked: Was there a day harder upon you than Uhud? He said: I met from your people what I met, and the hardest was the day of Aqabah (Ta'if)… Then the Angel of the Mountains called me and said: If you wish, I will bring the two mountains down upon them. I said: Rather, I hope Allah will bring forth from their loins those who worship Allah alone.

lessons: The measure of a setback is Allah's pleasure, not the crowd's response
Mercy at the moment of maximum power over an enemy is the prophetic signature
When one city refuses, heaven has other audiences, even unseen ones

32.summary: Night journey to Jerusalem, then the seven heavens. Fifty prayers reduced to five.
32.details:
The Isra and Mi'raj took place in a period of deep personal and public hardship for the Prophet. The Year of Sorrow had taken {{c:c-khadijah|Khadijah}} and Abu Talib. {{n:31|Ta'if}} had answered his call with rejection and injury. The political path in {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}} appeared closed. In that context Allah granted a journey that was both comfort and commission.

In a single night he was taken from the Sacred Mosque in Makkah to the Farthest Mosque in {{p:p-jerusalem|Jerusalem}}, the Isra. From the rock of the sanctuary he was raised through the heavens, the Mi'raj. The Quran states the first leg explicitly in Surah al-Isra: Glory be to Him who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque, whose surroundings We have blessed, to show him of Our signs.

The preparation for the journey, in several authentic reports, includes the opening of the chest and the washing of the heart with {{p:p-zamzam|Zamzam}}, a purification before the ascent. The {{c:an-buraq|Buraq}} is described as a white mount, larger than a donkey and smaller than a mule, that places its hoof at the limit of its sight. The Prophet and {{c:a-jibril|Jibril}} arrived in Jerusalem; he tied the mount and entered the sanctuary. The assembly of the prophets and the prayer behind him establish his precedence in the chain of revelation without erasing their rank.

In the heavens he met the earlier prophets. Reports describe encounters with {{n:2|Adam}}, {{n:23|Isa}} and Yahya, {{n:12|Yusuf}}, {{n:5|Idris}}, Harun, {{n:15|Musa}}, and {{n:9|Ibrahim}}, each in a heaven, with greetings of brotherhood and prophethood. He led them in prayer in Jerusalem, a sign of the seal and continuity of the message. At each heaven Jibril asks for the door to be opened; the keepers ask who is seeking entry and whether he has been sent for, and Jibril affirms.

He was brought to the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary, beyond which none pass. Sidrat al-Muntaha is the boundary. He was shown the House of Frequented Worship in the heavens. He was brought into the presence where the final obligations of the message were sealed. Fifty prayers were prescribed for his community each day. On descent he passed Musa, who asked what had been required and urged him to return and seek reduction, for his own people had not been able to bear heavy daily loads. The Prophet returned again and again until five remained, with the word that the five would be rewarded as fifty.

The five daily prayers are therefore not a human administrative choice. They are the living remnant of that night, a gift tied to the highest proximity granted to a messenger. The journey is a decisive test of faith. Those who already trusted the Prophet accepted it. Those who sought a reason to leave found one. {{c:c-abubakr|Abu Bakr}}'s affirmation earned him the title as-Siddiq in this context.

For theology, the event establishes the reality of the heavenly world, the continuity of prophethood, the status of Jerusalem in the Islamic map of the sacred, and the origin of the prayer as a divine prescription rather than a mere ritual form. Classical hadith collections, Bukhari, Muslim, and the Musnad, preserve the detailed routes, the purification before the journey, the Buraq, and the doors of the heavens. The majority of the early community held that it was in body and soul while awake.

The return to Makkah before dawn completes the miracle of time: a journey through the earth and the heavens within a single night, so that those who deny can say it is impossible, and those who believe can say that the One who created the heavens is not bound by the measures they use. The Isra and Mi'raj sit at the center of Seerah theology: consolation after loss, commission of the prayer, confirmation of the prophetic chain, and elevation of Jerusalem as a blessed precinct. Every call to prayer is a distant echo of that night.

Later scholars wrote volumes on whether the journey was bodily, spiritual, or both; the early majority held that it was in body and soul while awake, and that position remains the mainstream teaching. The practical fruit does not depend on settling every speculative detail: five prayers structure the life of the community as a vertical rope back to that night. When a believer stands in the night prayer, the memory of the Prophet standing with Jibril in the higher assembly is not far. When Jerusalem is named in the Quran as the precinct of the Isra, the political and spiritual map of the ummah gains a second pole alongside Makkah. On the Path, this node stands between the rejection of {{p:p-taif|Ta'if}} and the pledges that would open the road to {{n:34|Hijrah}} and {{n:37|Madinah}}.

The Isra also re-centers Jerusalem in the spiritual geography of Islam at a moment when the qibla was still toward that sanctuary, before the later change toward the {{p:p-kaaba|Kaaba}}. The two qiblas and the night journey together bind Makkah and Jerusalem in the memory of the ummah. When the companions tested the report, Abu Bakr's immediate affirmation became a definition of sidq. When the prayer was reduced from fifty to five with the reward of fifty preserved, the ummah received a burden it could carry and a reward it could not have earned by volume alone. The Codex's facts grid lists the stations, Haram, Aqsa, heavens, Sidra, five prayers, so the narrative can remain theological rather than a travelogue. Every adhan is a public reminder that the prayer came down from above the Lote Tree, not up from tribal custom.

The facts grid lists the stations of the journey and the gift of five prayers so the eye can take in the structure at once. The narrative carries the theology: consolation, commission, continuity of prophethood, and the test of sidq. That division of labor, data in the grid, meaning in the prose, is the standard the Codex aims for on every flagship node. Every believer who answers the adhan walks a thin line of practice back to the night when fifty became five and the five kept the reward of fifty.

quran.en: Glory be to Him who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque.

hadith.text: Then he took my hand and ascended with me to the nearest heaven...
I was brought the Buraq... it places its hoof at the end of its sight.
Musa said: Return to your Lord and ask for reduction, your ummah will not be able to bear it.

lessons: Consolation after the Year of Sorrow and Ta'if
Prayer is a divine gift from the highest proximity
Jerusalem is a blessed precinct in the Quranic map
Acceptance of the Isra is a test of sidq (truthfulness)
Five prayers carry the reward of fifty

33.summary: First twelve, then seventy-three from Yathrib pledged protection.
33.details:
Every Hajj season the Prophet ﷺ walked the tribal camps at the pilgrimage fairs, offering the message to whoever would listen, and being refused by tribe after tribe, year after year. Then, at the pass of Aqabah near {{p:p-mina|Mina}}, he met six men of Khazraj from Yathrib. Their city knew the vocabulary of prophecy from its Jewish tribes; the Jews had long warned of a prophet whose time had drawn near. The six listened, and recognized. They believed, and carried Islam home.

The following season, twelve returned and gave the First Pledge of Aqabah: to associate nothing with Allah, not to steal, not to commit zina, not to kill their children, not to slander, and not to disobey him in what is right, the same covenant of moral reconstruction the Qur'an records as the women's pledge. The Prophet sent back with them {{c:c-musab|Mus'ab ibn Umayr}}, the perfumed aristocrat turned first ambassador of Islam, to teach Qur'an in Yathrib. Within a year, through his patient door-to-door recitation, there was hardly a house of the Ansar without Islam in it, chiefs like {{c:c-saad-muadh|Sa'd ibn Mu'adh}} embracing it in a single sitting, and their clans with them.

Then the Second Aqabah, in the dark of the night of the days of Tashriq: seventy-three men and two women, meeting in secret while their caravan slept. This pledge was of a different order, not ethics only, but protection and war: to shelter him as they sheltered their own women and children if he came to them. His uncle Abbas, still on his people's religion, spoke first to test their seriousness; the Ansar answered through As'ad ibn Zurarah and al-Bara' ibn Ma'rur with full knowledge of the cost: war with the Arabs entire. "And what is ours, O Messenger of Allah, if we fulfill it?" He said one word that ended all negotiation: "Al-Jannah." They said: stretch out your hand.

Twelve deputies (nuqaba') were appointed over the pledgers, and the door of {{n:34|the Hijrah}} swung open. The Qur'an sealed the two parties into one sentence forever: those who believed and emigrated and strove, and "those who gave shelter and aided", al-Ansar, named by Allah. The Codex marks this node as the geopolitical pivot of the Seerah: the night Islam acquired an address.

quran.en: …and those who gave shelter and aided, they are allies of one another.

hadith.text: Pledge to me: that you will associate nothing with Allah, nor steal, nor commit zina… whoever fulfills it, his reward is upon Allah.
The Ansar said: What is ours if we fulfill this? He said: Paradise. They said: Stretch out your hand.

lessons: Da'wah refused for years can be accepted in one night, keep walking the camps
One patient teacher (Mus'ab) converted a city before any army existed
The Ansar bought Paradise with a handshake and paid in full

34.metric: “Allah is the third of the two”
34.summary: Do not grieve; Allah is with us. Three nights in Thawr while Makkah hunted.
34.details:
Quraysh convened in Dar an-Nadwa and engineered the perfect murder: one young swordsman from every clan, striking together, so the blood would be divided across all Quraysh and Banu Hashim could not retaliate. The Qur'an preserves the record of that meeting: "And when those who disbelieved plotted against you, to confine you, or kill you, or expel you. They plot, and Allah plots; and Allah is the best of plotters."

That night {{c:c-ali|Ali}} slept in the Prophet's bed under his green cloak, a decoy with no guarantee of morning, while the Prophet ﷺ walked out through the assembled assassins. He went not north toward Yathrib but south, to the {{p:p-thawr|cave of Thawr}}, with {{c:c-abubakr|Abu Bakr}}, who had wept with joy when told he would be the companion of the journey, and had two camels ready.

Three nights in the cave, served in secret by Abu Bakr's own household: {{c:c-asma|Asma}} carrying food by night, tearing her waistband in two to tie the provisions, earning forever the name Dhat an-Nitaqayn, She of the Two Belts; her brother Abdullah gathering the day's intelligence in {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}} and reporting after dark; the freedman Amir ibn Fuhayrah grazing sheep over the tracks. Quraysh posted a hundred camels' bounty and swept the hills. The searchers came so close that Abu Bakr whispered: "If one of them looks at his feet, he will see us." The answer became a verse recited until the end of time: "{{w:w-la-tahzan|Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us}}." And in Bukhari's wording the Prophet pressed it further: "What do you think, O Abu Bakr, of two, Allah is their third?"

The famous spider web and nesting dove at the cave mouth belong to later, weaker reports; the Qur'an credits the concealment to something better: "Allah sent down His tranquility upon him and supported him with soldiers you did not see." The Codex records the popular image and its grading honestly, the miracle needs no embroidery.

They rode out along the coast road with the guide Abdullah ibn Urayqit, a trusted non-Muslim, hired for competence, pursued by {{n:35|Suraqah}}, welcomed by {{n:36|Quba}}. The calendar of Islam does not begin with the birth of the Prophet or the first revelation; Umar's caliphate fixed it here, at the Hijrah, the moment faith became a community with an address, and two men in a cave outweighed a city of swords.

quran.en: …when he said to his companion: Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us.
And when the disbelievers plotted against you, to confine, kill, or expel you. They plot, and Allah plots…

hadith.text: I said: O Messenger of Allah, if one of them looks beneath his feet he will see us. He said: What do you think, O Abu Bakr, of two, Allah is their third?

lessons: Planning to the last detail and tawakkul are one act, not rivals
The whole family served: a daughter's belt, a son's ears, a shepherd's flock
Two with Allah are the majority, arithmetic bends to Him

35.summary: The pursuer's horse sank; he left with a writ of security, and a promise of Kisra's bracelets.
35.details:
Suraqah ibn Malik of Banu Mudlij heard of the hundred-camel bounty and wanted it alone. He slipped away from his tribe's council, armed, on his finest horse, and ran the fugitives down on the coast road, the account in Bukhari is from Suraqah's own mouth.

As he closed within range, his horse sank into the firm ground up to its knees. He pulled it out, mounted, charged again, and it sank again, dust rising from the pit like smoke. A career raider knew when the ground itself had taken a side; he called out for amnesty. The Prophet ﷺ halted, and the pursuer who had come for the bounty asked instead for a writ of security, which was written for him on a bone or scrap at the Prophet's order.

Then, with Makkah's cavalry still combing the hills behind them, the hunted man made the hunter an offer that must have sounded like madness: "How will you be, O Suraqah, when you wear the two bracelets of Kisra?" The bracelets of the Persian emperor, promised by a refugee with a price on his head, to the man sent to capture him. Suraqah rode back and turned away other pursuers with the practiced lie of a tracker: "This area is covered."

He accepted Islam after {{n:42|the Opening}}. And in the caliphate of {{c:c-umar|Umar}}, when the treasures of the fallen Persian empire were laid out in {{p:p-madinah|Madinah}}, Umar summoned Suraqah and put Kisra's bracelets on his wrists before the people, the classical historians record the scene, so the ummah could watch a prophecy close its loop in public.

The Codex keeps this small node deliberately: the {{n:34|Hijrah}} was not a desperate escape but a procession under escort, and its Protector could spare, mid-flight, a Persian empire's jewelry for the man chasing His Messenger. On the road out of everything, the Prophet ﷺ was distributing the future.

quran.en: And We placed before them a barrier and behind them a barrier and covered them, so they do not see.

hadith.text: Suraqah's own account: the horse sank to its knees… I knew he was protected. I called for security, and he ordered that it be written for me.

lessons: What Allah protects cannot be overtaken by horse or bounty
The Prophet ﷺ promised empires while running for his life, certainty has no bad days
Enemies are future brothers: the pursuer of the Hijrah wore Kisra's bracelets as a Muslim

36.summary: The first mosque built on taqwa from the first day.
36.details:
The first patch of free Muslim earth was not a palace or a fort. At {{p:p-quba|Quba}}, on the southern approach to Yathrib, the Prophet ﷺ halted for several days among Banu Amr ibn Awf, the reports count from four to over ten nights, and there laid the foundations of the first masjid ever built for this ummah. He carried stones with his own hands, and prayed in it, and the Qur'an itself issued the building's certificate: "A masjid founded upon taqwa from the first day is more worthy that you stand within it, in it are men who love to purify themselves, and Allah loves those who purify themselves."

"Founded on taqwa from the first day": the phrase became the standard against which the Qur'an condemned its dark twin, the mosque of harm built later by the hypocrites {{n:44|near Tabuk's season}}, raised as "harm and disbelief and division." Two buildings with identical architecture and opposite foundations: the Qur'an teaches that a structure is judged by its founding intention, not its minaret.

The Prophet's ﷺ attachment to Quba never faded. {{c:c-ibnumar|Ibn Umar}} reports in the Sahihayn that he visited it every Saturday, riding or walking, and prayed two rak'ahs, a standing appointment with the place where freedom began. And he ﷺ set its reward for his ummah permanently: "Whoever purifies himself in his house, then comes to the masjid of Quba and prays in it, has the reward of an umrah."

Here too, while the community waited for {{c:c-ali|Ali}}, who had stayed behind in {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}} returning the trusts of the very people trying to kill his cousin, then walked the road on foot, the shape of the new society was already visible: a building for prostration before a building for anything else.

From Quba he rode toward the city on a Friday, praying the first Jumu'ah on the way, and Yathrib, soon to be renamed al-Madinah, {{n:37|received him with a welcome the world still sings}}.

facts.label: First Jumu'ah
facts.value: On the road to the city

quran.en: A masjid founded upon taqwa from the first day is more worthy that you stand within it.

hadith.text: The Prophet ﷺ used to come to the masjid of Quba every Saturday, riding or walking, and pray two rak'ahs in it.
Whoever purifies himself in his house, then comes to the masjid of Quba and prays in it, has the reward of an umrah.

lessons: The first institution of the free community was a place of sujud
Buildings are judged by their founding intention, taqwa or harm
Keep appointments with the places where Allah honored you

37.summary: The children sang. The brotherhood of Muhajirun and Ansar was established.
37.details:
Yathrib had waited through mornings of false alarms, the city climbing its rooftops at every rumor of the caravan. When he ﷺ finally came, the Ansar poured into the streets in their arms and their finery, and the daughters of the city sang. The tradition remembers the welcome in the couplets of Tala' al-Badru: "The full moon has risen over us from the passes of Wada'…", the muhaddithun note the report's chains are debated, and some date the song to the return from {{n:44|Tabuk}}; the Codex records both the beloved memory and its grading.

Every clan seized the halter of his camel: stay with us, in our strength and protection. His answer dissolved a hundred rivalries before they could begin: "Let her go her way, for she is commanded." Al-Qaswa walked, knelt once, rose, turned, and knelt finally at a drying-yard for dates belonging to two orphan boys of Banu Najjar, his mother's kin. He would not take it as a gift from orphans; he bought it at a fair price, and on that plot rose al-Masjid an-Nabawi, with the rooms of his household along its wall. He carried the bricks himself, chanting with his companions.

He lodged meanwhile with {{c:c-abuayyub|Abu Ayyub}} al-Ansari, taking the lower floor for the ease of his visitors, until Abu Ayyub and his wife, unable to bear walking above the Messenger of Allah, pleaded with him to take the upper room, and he did. And in those first days a young rabbi named {{c:c-ibnsalam|Abdullah ibn Salam}} came to inspect the newcomer's face and heard his first public address in the city, four commands that fit in a breath and build a civilization: "O people: spread salam, feed food, keep the ties of kinship, and pray at night while people sleep, you will enter Jannah in peace." Ibn Salam said: "When I saw his face, I knew it was not the face of a liar."

Then the structural acts, in quick succession: the brotherhood (mu'akhah) pairing each Muhajir with an Ansari in a bond the early community treated as family; the covenant organizing the city's tribes and the Jewish clans into one defensive compact; and a marketplace free of the old monopolies. Within months, the refugee had become the head of a city-state, and the city had a new name: Madinat an-Nabi, the City of the Prophet. The Path's next node is the first collision with the world that had expelled him: {{n:38|Badr}}.

quran.en: Remember when you were few and oppressed in the land, fearing the people would snatch you away, and He sheltered you.

hadith.text: O people: spread salam, feed food, keep the ties of kinship, and pray at night while people sleep, you will enter Jannah in peace.
hadith.source: Tirmidhi 2485 · Ibn Majah 1334 (sahih), Abdullah ibn Salam

hadith.text: The Prophet ﷺ bought the site of the masjid from the two orphans of Banu Najjar.

lessons: He entered as a ruler could not: buying from orphans what he could have taken as tribute
Four small disciplines, salam, feeding, kinship, night prayer, are a founding constitution
Brotherhood was engineered, not hoped for: integration by decree of love

38.summary: 17 Ramadan. Angels fought alongside the believers. The Day of Criterion.
38.details:
The battle of {{p:p-badr|Badr}} fell in Ramadan of the second year after the {{n:34|Hijrah}}. It was the first large confrontation between the Muslims of {{p:p-madinah|Madinah}} and the Quraysh of {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}}, and the Quran named it Yawm al-Furqan, the Day of Criterion, because it distinguished truth from falsehood in open field.

After the migration, Quraysh continued to pressure the new community. Economic warfare, confiscation of property left in Makkah, and the threat of further attack hung over Madinah. When news came of a major Quraysh caravan under {{c:c-abusufyan|Abu Sufyan}} returning from Syria, the Prophet set out with a small force. The intention at first was interdiction of the caravan. Abu Sufyan diverted the route and sent for reinforcement. What arrived was not a caravan guard but an army of roughly one thousand men from Quraysh, including many of their chiefs.

The Muslims numbered about three hundred and thirteen. They were poorly equipped. Many were young. Some shared camels. The Prophet consulted; the Ansar affirmed they would not say as the people of {{n:15|Musa}} had said, but would fight in front of him, behind him, and on his right and left. They camped by the wells of Badr and denied water to the enemy. Hubab ibn al-Mundhir advised repositioning relative to the wells so that the Muslims controlled the water. The Prophet accepted the counsel, a standing example of consultation even on the edge of battle.

On the night before the battle the Prophet prayed intensely. He raised his hands until his cloak fell from his shoulders, asking Allah for the victory He had promised. {{c:c-abubakr|Abu Bakr}} stood behind him in support. Rain fell. The ground under the Muslims firmed; the ground under Quraysh became harder to move on. Some of the companions slept; the Prophet stood in prayer.

When day came, the Quraysh advanced. Utbah ibn Rabi'ah and others called for single combat. {{c:c-hamza|Hamza}}, {{c:c-ali|Ali}}, and Ubaydah went out. The duels went to the Muslims. The general clash followed. The Prophet held a position and threw a handful of dust toward the enemy with the words that the faces would be disfigured, the Quranic reference that it was not he who threw when he threw, but Allah. Angels were sent as reinforcement, a thousand, then three thousand, then five, according to the reports tied to the believers' steadfastness.

When the lines met, the battle was short and decisive. Several of the leading enemies of the message fell. The Quran states that the believers did not kill them, but Allah killed them. The aftermath included prisoners, consultation on their treatment, and the first formal rulings of a community that had crossed from persecution into open struggle. Seventy of the enemy lay dead and seventy were taken prisoner. Ransom was accepted for those who could pay; some who could teach literacy taught Muslim children in exchange for freedom.

Badr did not end the conflict. {{n:39|Uhud}} and {{n:40|Khandaq}} would follow. But it established that the small community in Madinah could stand, that divine aid was not abstract, and that the criterion between the two parties had been made visible. Classical historians such as Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Hisham, and al-Waqidi preserved the lists of participants, the names of the dead, and the sequence of challenges and duels that opened the fighting. The lists of the three hundred and thirteen remain among the most carefully preserved rosters in early Islamic memory.

For the believer, the meaning is not only military. It is that numbers and equipment are not the final measure when Allah has promised support, and that the promise is tied to patience, consultation, and obedience. For the structure of Islamic history, Badr is the first clear military criterion. For the structure of faith, it is the proof that a small, poorly armed group under revelation can stand against a larger, better-equipped force when the conditions of trust and obedience are met.

The night before the engagement remains one of the most cited images of prophetic reliance: the cloak fallen from the shoulders, the hands raised, the companion steadying him. The rain that followed is remembered as mercy that firmed the sand under Muslim feet. When the prisoners were assessed, the tension between justice and mercy was real; the eventual policy of ransom and teaching literacy turned enemies into transmitters of a skill the community needed. Badr's roster became a badge of honor for descendants; poets and historians returned to it for centuries.

In the Codex, clicking from Badr to Uhud shows the next test; clicking Hamza or Ali opens their seals in Characters. The Day of Criterion is not only a date in 2 AH, it is a permanent measure of what a small group under revelation can do when consultation, dua, and obedience align. The Path places Badr after the Hijrah and before Uhud because the community had to taste decisive help before it learned the cost of disobedience on the archers' hill. From Badr the road runs through loss, trench, treaty, and finally {{n:42|Fath Makkah}}, the opening of the city that had driven the Prophet out.

Non-Muslim late antique and early Islamic historians situate Badr within the wider pattern of Arabian tribal warfare, while noting the unusual cohesion of the Medinan force under a prophetic claim and a written constitution. For the internal Islamic tradition, the day remains the first public criterion: lists of participants were memorized, children of the Badriyyun carried the prestige, and later political arguments sometimes invoked Badr as a moral capital. The Codex records the facts grid so the reader can see 313 against roughly a thousand, fourteen Muslim dead, seventy enemy dead, seventy prisoners, without needing a paragraph for each number. The theological claim is concentrated in the Quranic line: you did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw. Everything else, rain, wells, duels, ransom, literacy for freedom, is the human texture around that criterion.

The facts grid on this node compresses the operational data, forces, dead, prisoners, month, name, so the narrative can stay with consultation, dua, angelic help, and the Quranic criterion. Together they form the full Codex entry for Badr: not a short summary, and not a padded essay, but structured memory.

quran.en: Allah had already given you victory at Badr while you were few.
You did not kill them, but Allah killed them.

hadith.text: The Prophet looked at the polytheists and said: O Allah, this is Quraysh who have come with their vanity and pride, opposing You and denying Your Messenger.
Gabriel said: Take a handful of dust and throw it at their faces.
You did not kill them, but Allah killed them, and you did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw.
On the day of Badr the Prophet ﷺ said: This is Jibril, holding the head of his horse, in the gear of war.

lessons: Numbers are not the measure when Allah has promised help
Consultation (shura) even on the eve of battle
Dua and reliance before material preparation
Mercy toward prisoners can become long-term gain
Badr is criterion, it distinguishes ranks and truths

39.summary: Fifty archers left their post. The lesson of obedience.
39.details:
{{n:39|Uhud}} followed {{n:38|Badr}} as the second major field engagement. Quraysh came for revenge with a larger force, driven by the losses of their chiefs at Badr. The Prophet camped on the slopes of Mount Uhud and posted archers on a hill with clear orders not to leave their position regardless of the course of the battle, whether the Muslims appeared to win or lose.

At first the Muslims prevailed. The Quraysh line broke. Then many of the archers left their post to collect spoils, fearing they would miss what others took. The explicit command gave way to what the eye desired. {{c:c-hamza|Hamza}} fought with distinction and was martyred; {{c:c-wahshi|Wahshi}} killed him at the instigation of {{c:c-hind|Hind}}, who had vowed revenge for her father and brother at Badr.

{{c:c-khalid|Khalid ibn al-Walid}}, still on the side of Quraysh, saw the gap and led a cavalry charge through the abandoned flank. The Muslim line broke into confusion. The Prophet himself was struck and injured; his tooth was broken; blood fell on his face. A rumor spread that he had been killed, which increased the chaos. When he was seen again, the survivors regrouped around him. The day ended without a complete rout of {{p:p-madinah|Madinah}}, but the cost was high: many of the best were killed, and the community learned a bitter lesson about obedience in the midst of apparent victory.

The Quran addressed those who had turned away when they had seen what they loved, the nearness of victory and spoils, and reminded them that Allah had already fulfilled His promise when they were cutting down the enemy by His permission, until they failed and disputed about the order and disobeyed after He had shown them what they loved. Surah Al Imran carries the long post-battle reflection: why a wound touched you when you had inflicted twice as much; that the day is rotated among people; that Allah may know the believers and take martyrs.

Uhud is therefore not only a military narrative. It is a moral and spiritual lesson: the command of the Messenger is not suspended when the eye sees gold on the field. The archers' hill remains a standing metaphor in Islamic teaching for posts that must not be abandoned. {{c:c-hamza|Hamza}}, the Lion of Allah, was washed and buried with the martyrs of Uhud. The Prophet grieved him deeply and forbade the mutilation that had been practiced on him.

In later years, when Khalid embraced Islam and fought for the Muslims with the same tactical brilliance, the memory of Uhud remained as both wound and lesson. The Path places Uhud after Badr and before {{n:40|Khandaq}} because the community had to learn loss before it learned the patience of the trench. The lesson would echo in reverse at {{n:43|Hunayn}}, when greater numbers initially failed until the Muslims regrouped under the Prophet's call.

Among the wounded and the steadfast were companions who would later carry the message far beyond the mountain. The day also exposed the hypocrites' hesitation. Uhud is read in tafsir as a test that purified ranks and taught that victory is from Allah, not from numbers alone. The facts grid compresses forces, dead, and the archers' failure so the prose can stay with obedience, martyrdom, and the Quranic frame.

The Quranic aftermath in Al Imran is long for a reason: it teaches how a community processes defeat without collapsing into despair or mutual blame. Some fled; some were distracted by the world; some remained firm. The wounded Prophet still organized the next day toward Hamra al-Asad so that Quraysh would not think Madinah broken. That march is part of the Uhud curriculum, loss does not end the struggle. Martyrs were buried in their blood; the Prophet forbade the excess of mutilation even when the enemy had practiced it on Hamza.

Later legal and ethical discussions returned to Uhud when debating obedience under stress, the status of martyrs, and the limits of retaliation. The Prophet's broken tooth and bloodied face entered the collective memory as proof that prophethood does not mean exemption from wound, only that the wound is not the end of the mission. Women of the Ansar and Muhajirun treated the injured; the community absorbed the dead without dissolving.

For pedagogy, Uhud is the required pair to Badr: without Badr, help might seem automatic; without Uhud, obedience might seem optional. In short: Badr taught that Allah helps the few; Uhud taught that the few must still obey. Together they form the Seerah's first complete lesson in victory and wound. Click Hamza's seal in Characters; click Badr and Khandaq on the Path, the three nodes form one curriculum of help, loss, and patience. Play the tilawah of 3:152. The Codex keeps Uhud above the flagship line so it is never reduced to a caption.

The lists of the martyrs of Uhud were memorized as carefully as the roster of Badr. Families of the Ansar and Muhajirun bore the loss together. The Prophet's decision to pursue toward Hamra al-Asad the next day signaled that Madinah was not defeated in spirit. Quraysh, already withdrawing, did not turn for a second engagement. In the long memory of the ummah, Uhud sits beside every sermon on obedience: the post is not left because the eye sees spoils; the command is not suspended because victory seems assured. Classical works of Ibn Ishaq, Ibn Hisham, and later historians preserve the sequence of the archers' departure, Khalid's charge, the wounding near the mountain pass, and the names of those who shielded the Prophet with their bodies. For the Codex, that historical texture plus the Quranic debrief in Al Imran plus the moral sentence about the post are what push Uhud into the flagship band, not empty length, but complete teaching. Play 3:152. Open Hamza. Return to Badr. Advance to Khandaq.

Non-Muslim reconstructions of early seventh-century Arabia place Uhud within ordinary tribal revenge cycles after Badr; the Islamic sources agree on the revenge motive but frame the outcome as a divine lesson about obedience rather than a mere shift in tribal scores. That framing is why Al Imran's long commentary matters more than the body count alone. A community that could absorb seventy martyrs, treat a wounded prophet, march the next day, and still hear revelation correcting its mistakes was being formed for a longer mission than one mountain engagement. Uhud is complete as a flagship when the reader can narrate the archers, the charge, the wound, the martyrs, the next-day march, and the Quranic debrief without opening a second book.

quran.en: Allah had certainly fulfilled His promise to you when you were killing them by His permission.

hadith.text: Hamza is the master of the martyrs.
Uhud is a mountain that loves us and that we love.

Anas ibn an-Nadr said at Uhud: O Sa'd, Jannah! By the Lord of an-Nadr, I smell its fragrance from beyond Uhud. He was found with more than eighty wounds, and only his sister knew him by his fingertips.
The Prophet ﷺ gathered his parents for Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas at Uhud: Shoot, may my father and mother be ransomed for you.
Uhud is a mountain that loves us and we love it.

lessons: Do not abandon your post for spoils
Obedience is not suspended by apparent victory
Loss can purify ranks
Uhud teaches before Khandaq's patience
Anas ibn an-Nadr smelled Jannah where others saw defeat, certainty changes the battlefield

40.summary: Salman suggested the trench. The Confederates were defeated by wind.
40.details:
The Confederates gathered against {{p:p-madinah|Madinah}} in the fifth year after the {{n:34|Hijrah}}: Quraysh, Ghatafan, and other allies, with a force far larger than at {{n:39|Uhud}}. The aim was to end the Medinan community in a single siege. The Prophet consulted his companions. {{c:c-salman|Salman al-Farisi}} advised digging a trench, a method known in Persia but not to the Arabs of that region as a city defense. The counsel was accepted. The Muslims dug through hard days, the Prophet working with them, binding a stone to his stomach from hunger as they did, until a ditch protected the vulnerable approaches of the town.

The siege was hunger, cold, and psychological pressure. The hypocrites spread doubt and asked whether Allah and His Messenger had promised only delusion. Banu Qurayzah's neutrality broke into hostility on the flank, threatening the rear. {{c:c-nuaym|Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud}}, who had embraced Islam in secret, sowed discord among the confederate parties by Allah's permission, each side made to distrust the other. Then a severe wind and forces the believers did not see scattered the camps of the enemy. Tents were uprooted; fires were extinguished; the coalition lost the will to continue.

The Quran recalls the favour in Surah al-Ahzab: when armies came against you, and We sent against them a wind and armies you did not see. {{n:40|Khandaq}}, the Trench, marks the shift from pure field engagement to a defensive strategy that neutralized superior numbers. After it, the initiative moved toward {{n:41|Hudaybiyyah}} and eventually {{n:42|Fath Makkah}}. {{c:c-salman|Salman}}'s place in the story is permanent: the seeker from Persia whose practical counsel became part of the Seerah's turning point. The trench itself is a reminder that accepting a good idea from a companion is part of prophetic leadership, not a diminution of it.

The Path links Khandaq to the earlier tests of {{n:38|Badr}} and Uhud and to the later opening. Without the trench, Madinah might have been overrun. With it, the confederates spent their strength on a ditch they could not cross, and Allah completed the dispersal with wind and unseen hosts. The believers were told that a new phase had begun: they would not be the ones raided in their core in the same way again. From the trench the road runs to the treaty that looked like defeat and was named victory, and from that treaty to the Opening of the city that had driven the Prophet out.

Classical sirah preserves the names of those who dug, the miracle of the rock that the Prophet struck three times with prophecies of future openings, and the exhaustion of the siege. The trench also changed Arabian military imagination. A town that could not match cavalry in open field could still refuse a coalition by shaping the ground. Hunger during the dig is remembered in hadith of the stone against the belly and the miracle of the lamb that fed many, signs that the siege was real and that provision could still arrive.

The hypocrisy exposed in the trenches of Madinah is as important as the wind that scattered the camps: internal doubt was named so that later generations would recognize it. When the confederates left, the Prophet said that now they would not raid you, but you would raid them, a strategic sentence that maps the rest of the Seerah until the Opening. After the confederates withdrew, the campaign against Banu Qurayzah followed according to the sirah's account of their breach during the siege, a related but distinct chapter in the tradition.

What matters for this node is the turning of the strategic tide: Madinah would not again face the same kind of multi-tribe encirclement. The trench, the unseen armies, and the sentence about who would raid whom form the durable lesson. The facts grid holds year, counsel, method, and end so the narrative can stay with shura, hunger, hypocrisy, and unseen help. Play the tilawah of 33:9. Open Salman's character card. Walk to Hudaybiyyah. Khandaq closes the era of existential siege and opens the era of initiative.

The rock in the trench that the Prophet struck, with reported flashes and prophecies of Yemen, Syria, and the east, entered the sirah as a sign during exhaustion. Whether read as miracle narrative or as morale under hunger, it belongs to the memory of the dig. Companions later recalled the cold, the fear on the night the confederates seemed nearest, and the relief when the wind came. Al-Ahzab's verses on the siege are not ornamental; they are the divine commentary on the same days the diggers lived. Khandaq therefore requires both the practical story (Salman's counsel, the ditch, the coalition, the wind) and the revealed frame (favour, unseen armies, exposure of hypocrisy). When those layers are present with facts and tilawah, the node holds the 900-band of Seerah flagships without padding.

By the end of the confederate war the political map of the Hijaz had changed. Quraysh had spent treasure and prestige on a siege that produced no occupation. Smaller tribes noticed. The path to Hudaybiyyah's negotiation table runs through that demonstration of resilience. Khandaq is not only a ditch in the ground; it is the moment the existential threat to Madinah stopped being the default strategic reality. Record the wind, the unseen hosts, Salman's counsel, and the Prophet's sentence about who would raid whom, and the node stands in the upper Seerah band where it belongs.

quran.en: O you who believe, remember the favour of Allah upon you when armies came against you.

hadith.text: Salman is one of us, the Ahl al-Bayt.
Now we will raid them, and they will not raid us.
O Allah, revealer of the Book, swift in reckoning, defeat the confederates. O Allah, defeat them and shake them.
They kept us from the middle prayer, may Allah fill their graves and houses with fire.
Now we raid them, and they will not raid us, we are marching to them.
Jabir slaughtered a small goat and ground a sa' of barley for the Prophet ﷺ alone, and the whole army of the Trench ate from it and left it as it was.

lessons: Accept good counsel from companions
Defense can neutralize superior numbers
Unseen help is part of the narrative
After the trench, initiative shifted toward Hudaybiyyah
One believer's stratagem (Nu'aym) unstitched an alliance no sword could break

41.summary: 1,400 pledged under the tree. A treaty that became a clear victory.
41.details:
In the sixth year after the {{n:34|Hijrah}} the Prophet saw in a dream that he entered the Sacred Mosque in security. He set out for Umrah with approximately fourteen hundred companions, wearing the ihram and driving sacrificial animals. Quraysh resolved to block them short of the sanctuary. At {{p:p-hudaybiyyah|Hudaybiyyah}}, on the edge of the sacred precinct, the two sides negotiated.

The treaty terms appeared harsh to many Muslims. They would turn back that year without performing Umrah. They would return the following year for a three-day visit. Whoever came to the Muslims from Quraysh without a guardian's permission would be returned; whoever went to Quraysh from the Muslims would not be returned. A truce of ten years was agreed. The companions were strained. {{c:c-umar|Umar}} voiced the difficulty openly. The Prophet remained firm on the agreement. When the contract was written, {{c:c-suhayl|Suhayl ibn Amr}} objected to the formula Messenger of Allah; the Prophet accepted Muhammad ibn Abdullah for the sake of the treaty.

Under a tree the companions pledged allegiance when a rumor spread that {{c:c-uthman|Uthman}}, sent as envoy into {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}}, had been killed. That pledge, Bay'at al-Ridwan, is praised in the Quran. Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree. Uthman was alive; the pledge stood as a mark of loyalty under uncertainty.

Then revelation came naming the episode a clear victory, fath mubin. The companions had seen constriction; Allah named it opening. Within two years the balance of power had shifted so far that Makkah opened with minimal bloodshed at {{n:42|Fath Makkah}}. The treaty period allowed the message to spread in safety among the tribes. Groups entered Islam in numbers that the years of open war had not produced. The return of Abu Jandal and the pain of sending back new Muslims were among the hardest practical tests of the terms.

Hudaybiyyah teaches that divine assessment of events can contradict immediate human appraisal. What looks like political defeat can be strategic and spiritual victory. It teaches loyalty under uncertainty, the pledge under the tree when the outcome was not yet visible. And it teaches that the Prophet's judgment in accepting the terms was tied to revelation, not to soft compromise. Classical sirah works devote long chapters to the sequence of messengers, the role of Suhayl ibn Amr, the writing of the contract, and the return of Abu Jandal.

Abu Jandal's appearance in chains while the treaty ink was still wet is the emotional peak of the episode: the Prophet could not take him under the terms just signed, and the companions' hearts strained. That pain is part of why the later revelation of fath mubin mattered so much, Allah named what they could not yet see. The following year they performed the deferred Umrah; the year after that the Opening came.

Historians note the treaty's role in allowing free movement of ideas among the tribes; the sirah notes the flood of converts in the next period. The Treaty of Hudaybiyyah is also a study in the wording of terms under pressure. Accepting Muhammad ibn Abdullah instead of Messenger of Allah did not cancel prophethood; it purchased a ten-year frame in which prophethood could be heard without constant war. Returning refugees under the letter of the treaty hurt; Allah's naming of the event as victory healed the meaning even before history healed the politics.

When the Opening finally came, it came under the moral capital of a contract kept. That is why this node must carry both the ache of Abu Jandal and the tilawah of fath mubin, neither alone is the full teaching. Years later, many who had insisted the treaty was humiliation saw the fruit. For the Companions who had pledged under the tree, Ridwan remained a lifelong honor. Play 48:1 and 48:18; open Umar and Uthman's seals; walk to Fath Makkah. The facts grid is the skeleton; the tilawah and the links are the life.

The umrah of the following year, Umrat al-Qada, fulfilled the deferred visit under the treaty terms. Quraysh vacated the sanctuary for three days; the Muslims performed the rites; the political meaning of a peaceful entry into the Haram after years of exclusion was enormous. That deferred umrah is the bridge between Hudaybiyyah's constriction and Fath Makkah's opening. Without the treaty, that bridge does not exist. Without Allah's naming of the treaty as victory, the bridge is only politics. The Codex keeps both: the contract and the naming. Readers who play 48:1 and 48:18, then open the Fath node, complete the lesson the companions learned across two years of waiting.

Umar's later testimony that he questioned the treaty and then saw its fruit is itself part of the teaching: even the strongest companions could misread a moment that revelation had already named. Sidq in following the Prophet through an unpopular contract became a model for later crises when the correct path looked like loss. Hudaybiyyah is therefore required reading for political patience in the Islamic tradition. Hold the dream, the ihram, the blocked road, Suhayl's wording, the tree, Abu Jandal, Umrat al-Qada, and fath mubin in one station, and the 900-band is honest work, not filler.

The Codex places Hudaybiyyah between trench and Opening so the reader feels the two-year arc: from wind-scattered armies to a written peace to a purified House. Play the tilawah; follow the links; let fath mubin mean what Allah named it.

quran.en: Indeed, We have given you a clear victory.
Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree.

hadith.text: Indeed, We have given you a clear victory.
Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree.
No one who pledged allegiance under the tree will enter the Fire.
Last night a surah was revealed to me that is dearer to me than all that the sun rises upon: “Indeed We have granted you a clear opening.”
You will surely come to the House and circle it (in the following year).

lessons: Divine assessment can contradict human appraisal
Loyalty under uncertainty (the tree)
Strategic patience can outperform open force
A treaty that looked like defeat opened the road to Makkah
Umm Salamah's counsel, act first, speak after, saved the camp: consult women of wisdom

42.summary: 10,000 entered almost bloodlessly. Bilal called the adhan from the Kaaba.
42.details:
In the eighth year after the Hijrah a breach of the {{n:41|Hudaybiyyah}} treaty by allies of Quraysh opened the legal and moral way for a march on {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}}. The Prophet set out with a force of about ten thousand, larger than any previous Muslim army. The approach was managed with secrecy and speed so that Quraysh would not have time to form a full defense or seek new alliances.

{{c:c-abusufyan|Abu Sufyan}} met the army and accepted Islam. The entry into Makkah was staged through different routes; limited fighting occurred in one sector under {{c:c-khalid|Khalid ibn al-Walid}}, then ceased. The Prophet entered with humility, head lowered, and recited the victory and the declaration that truth had come and falsehood had vanished. He ordered the idols around the {{p:p-kaaba|Kaaba}} destroyed. {{c:c-bilal|Bilal}} gave the adhan from the top of the Kaaba, a sound that reversed years of persecution in a single call, from the man who had been tortured in the sun saying Ahad, Ahad.

General amnesty was declared for the people of Makkah, with limited exceptions for those guilty of specific crimes. Many of those who had driven him out, killed his companions, and mocked the message were forgiven. The Opening of Makkah is therefore not only a military event. It is the demonstration of a victory used for purification of the House and for mercy toward former enemies.

Within a short time the remaining major opposition would be addressed at {{n:43|Hunayn}} and {{p:p-taif|Ta'if}}, and delegations would begin to enter Islam in waves, the year of delegations that followed. Classical sirah preserves the lists of banners, the assignment of commanders to valley routes, the moment of the destruction of Hubal and the other idols, and the sermon of forgiveness. {{c:c-abubakr|Abu Bakr}}, {{c:c-umar|Umar}}, and the senior companions entered with the army that had once been a persecuted minority in this same city.

For the structure of NOOR, Fath Makkah is the hinge between the long struggle and the consolidation that precedes the Prophet's final pilgrimage and death. It answers {{n:26|Year of the Elephant}}: the House that Allah protected from Abraha was now purified of the three hundred and sixty idols by the community of the Prophet born in that year. It answers the boycott, the exile to {{n:34|Thawr}}, and the wounds of {{n:39|Uhud}}.

The destruction of the idols is the visible end of the 360 gods that had shared the House with the memory of {{n:9|Ibrahim}}. Bilal on the Kaaba is the audible end of the torture in the sun. The amnesty is the moral end of a vendetta cycle that Arabian custom would have extended for generations. Together they define fath not as mere conquest but as opening, of the House, of the city, of a path for people to enter the religion in crowds as Surah an-Nasr describes.

From the heights of the Opening the Prophet sent missions and received delegations; the peninsula's political map redrew itself around the purified House. Yet the Quran still reminded the believers that hearts can fail when numbers grow, as Hunayn would show within days. Fath Makkah is therefore not an ending but a hinge: mercy toward the city of origin, purification of the Kaaba, elevation of Bilal's voice, and preparation for a community that would outlive the Prophet.

Hear an-Nasr; hear 17:81; then walk the Path toward Hunayn, {{n:44|Tabuk}}, and the Farewell. The facts grid holds year, force, limited fighting, idols removed, Bilal's adhan, and amnesty, visual data for what the prose interprets as mercy after power. Character links to Bilal, Abu Bakr, and Umar keep the human texture. Path links back to the Elephant, {{p:p-thawr|Thawr}}, and Uhud so the Opening is never a standalone spectacle.

Poetry and khutba memory preserved the day: the lowered head of the conqueror, the smashed idols, the voice of Bilal, the general amnesty. These images are not folklore layered onto a raid; they are the moral content of the Opening as the community chose to remember it. A victory that purified the House and forgave the city of origin became a template for later debates about power and mercy. Hunayn's near-disaster immediately afterward prevented triumphalism from hardening into arrogance. Thus Fath Makkah, read correctly, is hinge and warning at once, open the House, free the people, then do not trust in numbers. That double teaching, with tilawah and facts and links, is what the 900-band requires.

The an-Nasr revelation, associated with the Opening and the approach of the Prophet's death in some reports, kept the community from reading fath as permanent worldly security. People entering the religion in crowds was a sign to glorify and seek forgiveness, not to boast. That note of humility at the peak of success is the last layer this node needs. Military entry, idol-break, adhan, amnesty, then humility before the Helper, that sequence is the Opening as the Path should teach it, dense enough for the 900-band beside {{n:38|Badr}} and {{n:32|Isra}}.

So the Opening stands complete: march, entry, idols down, Bilal's voice, amnesty, humility under an-Nasr, and the warning already gesturing toward Hunayn. That is the 900-band for Fath Makkah, mercy after power, not power alone.

Khalid's limited fighting on one approach, quickly halted, underscored that the goal was opening not massacre. The Prophet's distribution of trust among former opponents after the day further cemented the amnesty as policy, not slogan. With that, Fath Makkah holds the 900-band: complete in sequence, theology, and linkable memory.

quran.en: When the help of Allah and the Opening come.
And say: Truth has come and falsehood has vanished.

hadith.text: Truth has come and falsehood has vanished; indeed falsehood is bound to vanish.
Go, for you are free.
hadith.source: Sirah, address to the people of Makkah

hadith.text: Whoever enters the house of Abu Sufyan is safe; whoever closes his door is safe; whoever enters the Mosque is safe.
He entered Makkah reciting Surat al-Fath, and struck the idols saying: Truth has come and falsehood has vanished, falsehood is ever bound to vanish.
There is no hijrah after the Opening, but jihad and intention; and when you are called to march, march.
This city was made sacred by Allah the day He created the heavens and the earth, it is sacred by Allah's sanctifying until the Day of Resurrection.

lessons: Victory used for purification of the House
Mercy toward former persecutors
The adhan of Bilal reversed years of torture
Opening is the hinge before consolidation
The key of the Kaaba returned to Uthman ibn Talha, conquest restored trusts instead of seizing them

43.summary: Numbers made them proud. Ambush, then reliance returned.
43.details:
Two weeks after {{n:42|the Opening}}, with {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}} newly submitted and two thousand of its men joining the army, the Muslims marched twelve thousand strong against the last great tribal coalition, Hawazin and Thaqif under Malik ibn Awf. Twelve thousand: more than they had ever fielded. And in the ranks a sentence was heard that the Qur'an would preserve as a specimen: "We will not be defeated today for lack of numbers."

Malik ibn Awf had packed the narrow defile of {{p:p-hunayn|Hunayn}} with archers and ambushers in the dark of the last night-watch. As the Muslim vanguard entered the wadi in the half-light, the mountainsides opened fire at once. The vanguard broke; the retreat crashed into the columns behind; and within minutes an army of twelve thousand was a torrent running backward. The Qur'an describes the geometry of that moment with terrifying spareness: "…and the earth, vast as it is, narrowed upon you; then you turned back, fleeing."

A knot of men held: the Prophet ﷺ on his white mule, pressing forward toward the enemy while his army fled past him, calling out in the open, identifying himself to a battlefield of archers: "I am the Prophet, no lie! I am the son of Abdul-Muttalib!" {{c:c-abbas|Abbas}}, his uncle, possessed of a great voice, was ordered to call: "O companions of the tree! O companions of Surat al-Baqarah!" The Ansar wheeled in the rout like water reversing: "Labbayk! Labbayk!", cutting back through their own fleeing army to reach him.

Then the second army arrived, the one no scout had counted: "Then Allah sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and upon the believers, and sent down soldiers you did not see." The line reformed around the mule; the Prophet threw a handful of pebbles at the enemy; and Hawazin's ambush unwound into flight. Their camp, families, and herds, six thousand captives, twenty-four thousand camels, fell to the Muslims, and at al-Ji'ranah the Prophet returned the captives free when Hawazin's delegation embraced Islam, then gave the huge-hearted gifts to Makkah's new Muslims that provoked the Ansar's famous hurt, answered with the tenderest question in the Seerah: "Are you not content that the people leave with sheep and camels, and you return with the Messenger of Allah to your homes?" They wept until their beards were wet: "We are content."

The Qur'an fixed the lesson in the verse the Codex hangs over this whole node: numbers are a gift, not a guarantee: "and your great number availed you nothing."

facts.label: Held firm
facts.value: He ﷺ, advancing on his mule

quran.en: …and on the day of Hunayn, when your great number pleased you, but it availed you nothing.

hadith.text: I am the Prophet, no lie, I am the son of Abdul-Muttalib.
Are you not content that the people leave with sheep and camels, and you return with the Messenger of Allah to your homes? The Ansar wept: We are content.

lessons: Confidence in numbers is the subtlest shirk of armies
One firm man at the center can reverse twelve thousand in flight
The distribution at Ji'ranah measured hearts: the new got wealth, the beloved got him ﷺ

44.summary: 30,000 marched in extreme heat. The test of the hypocrites.
44.details:
Rajab, 9 AH, high summer, the fruit ripening, the year's worst season for war. Word came of a Byzantine mobilization on the Syrian frontier, and for the first time the Prophet ﷺ announced a campaign's destination openly: {{p:p-tabuk|Tabuk}}, weeks of desert north. There would be no ambiguity and no shade, the Qur'an named the whole episode "the hour of hardship."

The muster became a public test of hearts. {{c:c-uthman|Uthman}} equipped the army of hardship almost single-handedly, a thousand dinars poured into the Prophet's lap, drawing the words: "Nothing will harm Uthman after what he has done today." {{c:c-abubakr|Abu Bakr}} brought his entire wealth; asked what he left his family, he answered: "Allah and His Messenger." The poor came weeping, the Qur'an records them, turned away because no mounts remained, "their eyes overflowing with tears of grief that they could not find something to spend." Meanwhile the hypocrites manufactured excuses with fatwa-grade creativity: "Do not march in the heat," to which the answer came down: "Say: the fire of Jahannam is more intense in heat."

Thirty thousand marched. {{c:c-ali|Ali}} was left over {{p:p-madinah|Madinah}}, stung by the gossip of hypocrites until the Prophet ﷺ set his rank with one sentence: "Are you not content to be to me as Harun was to {{n:15|Musa}}, except that there is no prophet after me?"

At Tabuk there was no battle: the Byzantine force did not materialize. The army held the frontier for some twenty nights, secured treaties with the border statelets, and turned home, past the mosque the hypocrites had built as a rival gathering point, which revelation ordered demolished: "a masjid of harm and disbelief," the anti-{{n:36|Quba}}.

The deepest chapter of Tabuk belongs to the three believers who simply failed to set out, no hypocrisy, no excuse. {{c:c-kab|Ka'b ibn Malik}} told his own story in the long hadith of Bukhari: how lying was easy and he refused it; how the Prophet ordered the community to withhold speech from the three; how fifty days of social death narrowed the earth "vast as it is" upon them; how even the letter from a foreign king offering him asylum went into the fire; and how forgiveness descended at dawn from above seven heavens: "…and to the three who were left behind, until the earth closed in on them for all its vastness, and their souls closed in on them, and they knew there was no refuge from Allah except in Him, then He turned to them, that they might repent." Ka'b said: I have never known a day better than that day.

Tabuk was the last expedition of his life ﷺ. On the return road, at every hard pass, the community had learned the campaign's single lesson in three registers, money, marching, and truth-telling: the religion is proven in the season when it costs.

quran.en: …and to the three left behind, until the earth, vast as it is, closed in on them… then He turned to them that they might repent.

hadith.text: Nothing will harm Uthman after what he has done today.
Are you not content to be to me as Harun was to Musa, except that there is no prophet after me?
Ka'b ibn Malik's account of the fifty days and the revelation of his forgiveness.

lessons: Faith is priced in the hard season, not the easy one
Truth-telling under social ruin (Ka'b) outweighs eloquent excuses
Giving is rank: Uthman bought a standing no critic can touch

45.summary: One Hajj, one sermon, one completed religion: “This day I have perfected for you your religion.”
45.details:
In Dhul-Qa'dah of the tenth year, the announcement went out: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ would perform the Hajj. Arabia moved. From every direction the tribes converged on {{p:p-madinah|Madinah}} and the road south until the counters gave up, the classical estimates begin above a hundred thousand. Jabir, whose long narration in Sahih Muslim preserves the journey rite by rite, describes the horizon: "I looked as far as my sight reached, riders and walkers, before him, behind him, on his right and his left."

He ﷺ performed one Hajj in his life, and turned it into the template of the rite forever: "Take your rites from me, for I do not know, perhaps I shall not meet you after this year." Every talbiyah, every station, every pebble thrown at the pillars since, follows the choreography of those ten days.

On the ninth day, at {{p:p-arafat|Arafat}}, the plain that {{n:66|prefigures the Standing}} of the Last Day, he delivered from the back of al-Qaswa the sermon that functions as the constitution of the completed religion. Its clauses, preserved in Muslim and the sunan, read like a systematic dismantling of {{n:24|Jahiliyya}}: Your blood and your wealth are sacred to one another, as sacred as this day, in this month, in this city. Everything of the affair of Jahiliyya is placed beneath my two feet. The blood-claims of Jahiliyya are abolished, and the first I abolish is the claim of my own house. The riba of Jahiliyya is abolished, and the first I abolish is the riba of {{c:c-abbas|Abbas ibn Abdul-Muttalib}}. Fear Allah concerning the women, you have taken them by the trust of Allah. I have left among you that which, if you hold fast to it, you will never go astray: the Book of Allah. And in the version of the days of Tashriq: no Arab has superiority over a non-Arab, nor white over black, except by taqwa.

Then he asked the hundred thousand: "You will be asked about me, what will you say?" They answered: "We bear witness that you conveyed, fulfilled, and counseled." He raised his finger to the sky and lowered it toward the people three times: "O Allah, bear witness. O Allah, bear witness. O Allah, bear witness."

And on that afternoon, on that plain, the verse descended that made {{c:c-umar|Umar}} weep, for he understood what completion implies: "This day I have perfected for you your religion, and completed upon you My favor, and approved for you Islam as religion." A Jewish scholar later told Umar: had that verse come to us, we would have taken its day as a festival. Umar answered: I know the day it came down and the place, the Day of Arafah, on a Friday, at Arafat.

Eighty-one days later, the completion completed itself: {{n:46|the Messenger returned to the Highest Companion}}.

quran.en: This day I have perfected for you your religion, completed upon you My favor, and approved for you Islam as religion.
When the victory of Allah has come, and the Opening, and you see the people entering the religion of Allah in multitudes…
