"There is none of you but will arrive at it, a matter decreed upon your Lord, inevitable." The verse stunned the companions until the next verse exhaled: "Then We will save those who feared Him, and leave the wrongdoers therein on their knees." The arrival is universal; the crossing is not.

The bridge is laid across the back of Jahannam: "and I and my ummah," he ﷺ said, "will be the first to cross." The engineering specifications, from Sahih Muslim: "slippery, seizing; on it hooks like the thorns of as-Sa'dan", a desert thorn every Arab listener knew by the scar: "except that none knows their size but Allah; they snatch the people by their deeds." Abu Sa'id added the description the Codex sets in this tile's metric: "It has reached me that the bridge is thinner than a hair and sharper than a sword."

The crossing moves by a law this world never knew: speed measured by deeds. "The believer crosses like the blink of an eye, like lightning, like wind, like birds, like the finest horses and riders, one delivered safe, one scratched and released, one shoved down into the Fire." Under a bridge lit by nothing, each crosser is issued his own illumination: "their light running before them and on their right", and the hypocrites, who borrowed light in the world, watch it switched off mid-span: "Wait for us that we may borrow from your light. It will be said: go back and seek light." A wall is struck between, mercy on its inner face, punishment on its outer.

On the span, the only sound the tradition reports from its greatest voices is a two-word du'a. The prophets themselves, the same men who split seas and cooled fires, stand at the bridge saying: "{{w:w-sallim|Allahumma sallim, sallim}}", O Allah, bring them through, bring them through. Whoever wants to know what the Day does to confidence: it reduces the messengers to two words, repeated.

And the scene the Sahihayn add to the crossing, which the Codex refuses to trim: the Qantara. After the bridge, the saved are halted on an arch before {{n:71|the Garden}}, and retribution is settled between them for the injustices that remained among believers, "until, when they are refined and purified, they are given leave to enter." The Garden's law at its gate: no unresolved wrong walks through. Forgive your brother tonight, the tile suggests, or the arch will settle it later.

The last man across is the tradition's most tender comedy: dragged, scorched, crawling, and then bargaining with his Lord tree by tree, oath after broken oath, until he is asked what would satisfy him and laughed toward more than he dreamed. He is the floor of {{n:71|the next node}}: the least citizen of a kingdom {{n:71|ten times this world}}.

sequence.note: 19:71-72, universal arrival, selective salvation; Qantara after the span

timeline.label: He ﷺ and the ummah first

protection: Light on the bridge is earned now: “their light runs before them” · 57:12; wudu, salah, and Qur'an are its fuel
Settle wrongs before the Qantara settles them: forgive and seek forgiveness tonight
Constancy over heroics: the crossing speeds were set by ordinary daily deeds

quran.en: There is none of you but will arrive at it, a matter decreed. Then We save those who feared Him…
The Day you see the believing men and women, their light running before them…

hadith.text: The bridge is laid across Jahannam, and I and my ummah are the first to cross; and none speaks that day but the messengers, and the du'a of the messengers: O Allah, bring through, bring through.
On it are hooks like the thorns of Sa'dan, none knows their size but Allah, snatching the people by their deeds.
It has reached me that the bridge is thinner than a hair and sharper than a sword.
When the believers cross, they are halted on a qantara between Jannah and the Fire, and retribution is settled between them, until, refined, they are given leave to enter.

lessons: Your crossing speed is being set today, in traffic, at work, before dawn
Even prophets go monosyllabic at the Fire, take seriously what silences them
No grudge enters the Garden: the Qantara is the last customs check

71.titleEn: Jannah: What No Eye Has Seen
71.summary: Bricks of gold and silver, mortar of musk. The highest delight is the vision of Allah.
71.details:
The Codex ends where every sound heart was always pointed. "And those who feared their Lord will be driven to the Garden in companies, until, when they reach it, its gates are opened, and its keepers say: Peace be upon you; you have become pure; so enter it, abiding eternally." Eight gates, among them one the fasting alone may use: "In Jannah is a gate called ar-Rayyan; those who fasted enter through it, and when they have entered, it is closed." At the gates, on the record of the Sahihayn: "I will come to the gate of Jannah on the Day of Resurrection and ask for it to be opened. The keeper will say: Who are you? I will say: Muhammad. He will say: For you I was commanded, I open for no one before you."

What is inside was placed, by design, beyond the reach of preview: "I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has ever conceived." The Qur'an's descriptions, rivers of water, milk, honey, and wine that does not wound; gardens beneath which rivers flow; couches, brocade, pearls, pavilions, are, the scholars say, names borrowed from the world for realities that outgrow the names. The dimensions hint at the scale: a width like the heavens and the earth; a hundred levels between each of which is the distance of sky to earth: "so when you ask Allah, ask Him for al-Firdaws, for it is the middle of Jannah and the highest of it, and above it is the Throne of the Most Merciful, and from it the rivers spring." A tree in whose shade a rider travels a hundred years without crossing it. A market kept for every Jumu'ah, where a wind from the north lifts beauty onto the faces of a people already beautiful. The lowest citizen, {{n:70|the last man dragged across}}, receives ten times this entire world, and is made to feel he has been favored.

The residents arrive re-made: upon the form of their father {{n:2|Adam}}, sixty cubits, thirty-three years old, hearts like one heart, rancor extracted by decree, the disease of {{n:4|the first murder}} surgically removed at the door: "We remove whatever is in their breasts of resentment, brothers, on couches, facing one another." Families are reunited across the ranks: "We join their descendants to them, and We deprive them of nothing of their deeds", and {{c:a-ridwan|the keepers}} enter upon them from every gate: "Peace upon you for what you patiently endured, how excellent is the final home."

Then the tradition's two closing ceremonies, than which nothing higher exists. Death itself is brought "in the form of a fine ram" and slaughtered between the Garden and the Fire: "O people of Jannah, eternity, no death; O people of the Fire, eternity, no death." And the address from above: "Allah will say to the people of Jannah: O people of Jannah! They will say: At Your service, our Lord. He will say: Are you pleased? They will say: How could we not be pleased when You have given us what You gave no one of Your creation? He will say: Shall I not give you better than that? They will say: What could be better? He will say: I bestow upon you My pleasure, and I will never be angry with you after it, forever."

And above even the pleasure, the sight the whole Path has been walking toward, promised in the Qur'an's calmest sentence and confirmed in the Sahihayn's brightest hadith: "Faces that Day radiant, looking at their Lord.": "You will see your Lord as you see the full moon, without crowding." What {{n:20|Musa was denied at the mountain}} is granted to the least believer at home. The ziyada: "for those who do good: the best, and more", is, he ﷺ said, that the veil is lifted; "and they are given nothing more beloved to them than the look at His Face."

From the Throne over the water at {{n:1|the first node}} to the Throne above Firdaws at the last, from كن at the opening to سلام at the gates, the Codex closes its own circle here, and leaves the reader one working instruction, his ﷺ own: when you ask, ask for Firdaws.

sequence.note: Eight gates · 100 levels · Firdaws beneath the Throne

timeline.label: He ﷺ opens the first gate
The Vision
timeline.detail: “As you see the full moon” · Bukhari 554

quran.en: Faces that Day will be radiant, looking at their Lord.
No soul knows what delight of the eyes is hidden for them, a reward for what they used to do.
…and the angels enter upon them from every gate: Peace upon you for what you patiently endured, how excellent is the final home.

hadith.text: I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived.
When you ask Allah, ask Him for al-Firdaws, it is the middle of Jannah and its highest, above it is the Throne of the Most Merciful, and from it spring the rivers of Jannah.
Death is brought as a fine ram and slaughtered between Jannah and the Fire: O people of Jannah, eternity, no death.
I bestow upon you My pleasure, and I will never be angry with you after it, forever.
You will see your Lord as you see this full moon, you will not be wronged in seeing Him.

lessons: Ask specifically: Firdaws, beneath the Throne, he ﷺ told you the address
The Garden's peak is not a place but a Face, train the heart on 75:22-23 now
Rancor is removed at the door; whoever empties his heart early lives the Garden early
From Kun to Salam: the whole Path was one sentence of mercy completing itself

c-abubakr.role: As-Siddiq · First caliph · Companion of the cave
c-abubakr.summary: The first free man to believe, the second of two in the cave, and the hand that held the ummah together on its hardest morning.
c-abubakr.details:
Abu Bakr Abdullah ibn Abi Quhafah heard the message and did not negotiate with it. The Prophet ﷺ said of him: "I never invited anyone to Islam but he had some hesitation, except Abu Bakr." His belief pulled a generation behind him: {{c:c-uthman|Uthman}}, {{c:c-talha|Talha}}, {{c:c-zubayr|Zubayr}}, {{c:c-saad|Sa'd}}, and {{c:c-abdurrahman|Ibn Awf}} all entered Islam at his hands. When {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}} mocked {{n:32|the Night Journey}}, he answered with the sentence that earned his title: "If he said it, he has told the truth." From that day he was as-Siddiq.

He bought and freed the tortured, {{c:c-bilal|Bilal}} first among them. He was the companion of {{n:34|the cave}}, the second of two when Allah was the third. He led the prayer in the Prophet's final illness, and when {{n:46|the hardest morning}} came, he held the community upright with two sentences about the Living God. As caliph for two years he fought the riddah, sent Usama's army as commanded, and began gathering the Qur'an after Yamamah. The Prophet ﷺ said: "If I were to take an intimate friend other than my Lord, I would take Abu Bakr." He died asking to be buried beside his beloved, and he was.

quran.en: The second of two, when they were in the cave, when he said to his companion: do not grieve, indeed Allah is with us.

c-umar.summary: His Islam was a conquest, his justice a proverb, and shaytan took the other road when he walked.
c-umar.details:
Umar ibn al-Khattab set out one day to kill the Prophet ﷺ and arrived instead at his sister's house, where Surah Ta-Ha was being recited in the home of {{c:c-said-zayd|Sa'id ibn Zayd}}. He read, trembled, and walked to the house of al-Arqam to pledge. The Muslims prayed openly at the {{p:p-kaaba|Kaaba}} for the first time behind his shoulders. The Prophet named him al-Faruq, the one who splits truth from falsehood, and said: "By the One in whose hand is my soul, shaytan never meets you traveling on a road but he takes a road other than yours."

At {{n:45|the Farewell Hajj}} he understood the verse of completion and wept. After {{n:46|the Passing}} he drew his sword in grief, until steadied by {{c:c-abubakr|Abu Bakr}}, whom he served, then succeeded. His ten years opened {{p:p-jerusalem|al-Quds}}, Persia, {{p:p-egypt|Egypt}} and Sham; he took the title Amir al-Mu'minin, established the diwan and the Hijri calendar, patrolled {{p:p-madinah|Madinah}} at night carrying flour on his own back, and fixed {{n:34|the Hijrah}} as year one. He asked Allah for martyrdom in the Prophet's city and received both: struck at Fajr in his own mihrab, buried beside the two he loved.

facts.label: End
facts.value: Martyred at Fajr, buried with the two

c-uthman.summary: Married two daughters of the Prophet ﷺ, financed the hard hours, and gave the ummah one written Qur'an.
c-uthman.details:
Uthman ibn Affan was wealth wedded to shyness. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Shall I not feel shy before a man before whom the angels feel shy?" He married Ruqayyah, led an emigration to Abyssinia with her, and after her death married her sister Umm Kulthum: two lights, Dhun-Nurayn. His money moved the story at its hinges: he bought the well of Rumah and made it public water, and he equipped {{n:44|the army of hardship}} until the Prophet said nothing would harm him after that day. At {{n:41|Hudaybiyyah}} he was the envoy into {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}}, and the false report of his death triggered the Pledge under the tree; the Prophet pledged for him with his own left hand, calling it Uthman's hand.

As third caliph he expanded the two sanctuaries and, when recitation disputes spread with the conquests, commissioned the single written mushaf from the compilation kept since {{c:c-abubakr|Abu Bakr}}, sending copies to the garrison cities. Every printed Qur'an on earth descends from that decision. Besieged in his house in the first fitnah, he refused to shed Muslim blood in his defense and was killed while reciting; the tradition remembers his blood on the Book he unified.

facts.label: Hudaybiyyah
facts.value: The envoy; pledge made for him

c-ali.role: Fourth caliph · Gate of the city of knowledge
c-ali.summary: Raised in the Prophet's ﷺ house, slept in his bed on the night of the knives, carried the banner at Khaybar.
c-ali.details:
Ali ibn Abi Talib grew up in the household of the Prophet ﷺ and believed as a boy, among the very first. On the night of {{n:34|the Hijrah}} he lay in the Prophet's bed under the green cloak while the swordsmen watched the door, then stayed behind to return Makkah's deposits: the assassins' own valuables, held in trust by the man they wanted dead. He fought at {{n:38|Badr}} and {{n:39|Uhud}}, and at {{p:p-khaybar|Khaybar}} the Prophet said: "Tomorrow I will give the banner to a man who loves Allah and His Messenger, and whom Allah and His Messenger love," then gave it to Ali. At {{n:44|Tabuk}} he heard the words that fixed his rank: "You are to me as Harun was to {{n:15|Musa}}, except that there is no prophet after me."

He married {{c:c-fatimah|Fatimah}}; from them came {{c:c-hasan|al-Hasan}} and {{c:c-husayn|al-Husayn}}, the two masters of the youth of Jannah. His judgments made {{c:c-umar|Umar}} seek him; his sermons trained the Arabic tongue. As fourth caliph he carried the community through its bitterest years, and was struck by a Kharijite's blade at Fajr in Kufa. Sunni and Shi'i memory both orbit him; the Codex records the love and the rank on which all agree.

facts.label: First
facts.value: Among the first to believe, as a boy

c-khadijah.summary: She believed before anyone, spent everything, and received salam from her Lord and a house of qasab in Jannah.
c-khadijah.details:
Khadijah bint Khuwaylid ran her own caravans in a city that buried daughters. She hired the young Muhammad ﷺ for trade, read his character, and proposed. For twenty-five years she was his only wife and the mother of every child of his except {{n:9|Ibrahim}}. When he came down from {{n:30|Hira}} trembling, she wrapped him and argued from evidence: Allah would never disgrace a man who keeps ties, carries the weak, earns for the destitute, honors the guest, and helps bear the calamities that strike in the cause of truth. Then she took him to {{c:c-waraqah|Waraqah}}. She was the first human being to believe.

Her wealth absorbed the boycott years; her certainty absorbed the doubt. In {{n:31|the Year of Sorrow}} she died, and Makkah's roof over the message fell with her. Years later the Prophet ﷺ would still send gifts to her friends, and when her sister's voice reached him at the door his heart shook. {{c:a-jibril|Jibril}} came to him once with word from heaven: give Khadijah salam from her Lord, and give her glad tidings of a house in Jannah of qasab, in which there is no noise and no fatigue.

c-aisha.role: Umm al-Mu'minin · Jurist of the ummah
c-aisha.summary: The most knowledgeable woman of this ummah; a third of the household rulings of the religion reach us through her.
c-aisha.details:
Aisha bint Abi Bakr, daughter of {{c:c-abubakr|as-Siddiq}}, was the most beloved of the Prophet's ﷺ wives after Khadijah's era. Asked publicly who was dearest to him, he answered: "Aisha," and of men, "her father." Revelation came to him under no wife's blanket but hers, and he ﷺ said: "The superiority of Aisha over women is like the superiority of tharid over other food." When the slanderers attacked her honor in the affair of the ifk, heaven itself acquitted her: verses of Surah an-Nur recited until the Day of Judgment.

Her chamber was the classroom of the ummah. More than two thousand hadith reach us through her; the great companions returned to her for inheritance law, for the Prophet's night prayer, for the description of his character, which she summarized in four words: his character was the Qur'an. He ﷺ died with his head against her chest, in her turn, in {{n:46|her room}}, and was buried there. She lived on for decades as teacher and corrector of the ummah's memory, and her regret over the day of the Camel deepened her students' love. The Codex records her as the proof that the transmission of this religion stands on a woman's scholarship.

facts.label: His answer
facts.value: Dearest: Aisha; of men: her father

facts.label: His last hour
facts.value: Against her chest, in her room

c-hamza.summary: The Prophet's ﷺ uncle and shield, killed at Uhud; the Lion of Allah and of His Messenger.
c-hamza.details:
Hamza ibn Abd al-Muttalib, uncle of the Prophet ﷺ and his milk-brother, was Makkah's hunter and strongest arm. The day Abu Jahl abused the Prophet at Safa, Hamza came back from the hunt, struck Abu Jahl with his bow before the assembly, and declared himself on his nephew's religion; the persecutors recalculated that week. He fought at {{n:38|Badr}} with a distinction the enemy remembered by the ostrich feather he wore, and at {{n:39|Uhud}} he fell: {{c:c-wahshi|Wahshi's}} javelin, thrown for a bounty set by {{c:c-hind|Hind}}, whose men of Badr he had helped cut down.

What was done to his body after death grieved the Prophet ﷺ beyond any other loss of the day, and revelation and his own mercy sealed the response at {{n:42|the Opening}}: no revenge, and mutilation forbidden in this ummah forever. He was buried at Uhud with the martyrs, where his grave is greeted to this day. The Prophet called him Sayyid ash-Shuhada, the master of the martyrs, and the Lion of Allah. In the Codex he stands where courage and restraint meet: the man whose death taught the ummah how not to avenge.

facts.label: Islam
facts.value: Declared with a bowstrike at Safa

c-bilal.summary: Tortured under the rock saying Ahad, Ahad; his footsteps were heard in Jannah before he died.
c-bilal.details:
Bilal ibn Rabah, an Abyssinian slave, believed early and paid immediately. Umayyah ibn Khalaf staked him on the burning sand under a boulder, demanding he curse the Prophet ﷺ; the whole theology of Islam compressed into his two-word answer: Ahad, Ahad. One. One. {{c:c-abubakr|Abu Bakr}} bought him and freed him for Allah.

In {{p:p-madinah|Madinah}} the Prophet chose his voice for the first adhan, and for a decade Bilal called the ummah to prayer, stood at the Prophet's door, and carried his short spear before him at the Eids. On the day of {{n:42|the Opening}} the Prophet ordered him up onto the roof of the {{p:p-kaaba|Kaaba}} itself, and the freed slave gave the adhan over the heads of the aristocracy that had tortured him. The Prophet ﷺ asked him once: "Tell me the deed you hope in most, for I heard the sound of your footsteps ahead of me in Jannah." He answered: I never purify myself, night or day, except that I pray with that purification what was written for me. After {{n:46|the Passing}} the adhan broke him; he could not finish it, and left for Sham as a soldier, giving one last adhan in his life that made Madinah weep.

c-salman.role: The Seeker · Counsel of the Trench
c-salman.summary: Sold into slavery searching for one man; found him, freed himself by planting three hundred palms, and saved a city with a ditch.
c-salman.details:
Salman al-Farisi began as a Persian nobleman's son keeping the sacred fire, and left it for a church, then for teacher after teacher across Syria and Anatolia, each dying master pointing him onward, the last one telling him the signs: a prophet of the final religion, arising among the Arabs, who accepts the gift but not the charity, with the seal of prophethood between his shoulders. Kidnapped and sold into slavery in Yathrib, he was pruning palms when {{p:p-madinah|Madinah}} rang with the arrival of {{n:37|the emigrant}}. He tested the three signs one by one; at the third, he wept and embraced Islam. The Prophet ﷺ arranged his freedom: three hundred palm shoots, planted by the Prophet's own hands, and every one of them took root.

At {{n:40|the Trench}} his Persian engineering met Arabia's crisis: dig, he said, and the ummah dug. The Muhajirun and Ansar each claimed him, and the Prophet closed the auction with the sentence that ended ethnicity as rank: "Salman is from us, the People of the House." He governed al-Mada'in in Persia, the land of his birth, on a stipend he gave away, weaving palm leaves for his bread. The seeker's story is the Codex's proof that whoever walks toward the truth, the truth walks toward him.

facts.label: Journey
facts.value: Persia → churches of Sham → slavery → Madinah

c-zayd.role: The beloved · Only companion named in the Qur'an
c-zayd.summary: Chose slavery with the Prophet ﷺ over freedom with his father; heaven wrote his name into the Book forever.
c-zayd.details:
Zayd ibn Harithah was stolen as a boy, sold in {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}}, gifted to {{c:c-khadijah|Khadijah}}, and given by her to the Prophet ﷺ, who freed him. When Zayd's grieving father tracked him down with ransom, the Prophet offered Zayd the choice; Zayd chose the man who had never been anything but light to him: I have seen from this man what makes me choose him over everyone. The Prophet adopted him at the {{p:p-kaaba|Kaaba}}, and Makkah called him Zayd ibn Muhammad until revelation ended adoption's fictions and restored lineages: call them by their fathers. To compensate that loss with an honor no companion shares, Allah named him in the Qur'an itself: "when Zayd had concluded from her what he needed" (33:37).

He was the Prophet's most trusted commander, leading expedition after expedition, and the only man beside whose name love is recorded twice: the beloved, and son of the beloved, said of {{c:c-usama|Usama}} his son. He accompanied the Prophet to {{n:31|Ta'if}} and bled shielding him. At Mu'tah he held the banner first of the three, and fell first, a freed slave commanding the nobles of Quraysh by appointment of heaven's Messenger.

facts.label: The choice
facts.value: The Prophet over his own father

quran.en: So when Zayd had concluded from her what he needed, We married her to you.

c-zubayr.summary: First sword drawn for Islam; the Prophet ﷺ said every prophet has a disciple, and mine is az-Zubayr.
c-zubayr.details:
Az-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, son of the Prophet's ﷺ aunt Safiyyah and husband of {{c:c-asma|Asma}}, believed as a youth. When a rumor flew through {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}} that the Prophet had been seized, the boy came down the streets with a drawn blade, the first sword unsheathed for Islam. He emigrated to Abyssinia and then {{p:p-madinah|Madinah}}, fought at {{n:38|Badr}} in a yellow turban that the reports say the angels matched that day, and stood at {{n:40|the Trench}} where the Prophet said three times: "Every prophet has a disciple (hawari), and my disciple is az-Zubayr," after Zubayr alone volunteered thrice to scout Banu Qurayza.

One of the ten promised Paradise and one of the six of the shura, his body was a map of the battles; his son counted the scars. In the fitnah he marched toward the Camel, then withdrew from the field when {{c:c-ali|Ali}} reminded him of a word from the Prophet; he was murdered while praying by a man who thought he had done a service, and Ali told the killer to expect the Fire. His estate paid its debts and still overflowed: the trader of Paradise trusted with the trusts of Madinah.

facts.label: Family
facts.value: Husband of Asma, son of Safiyyah

c-saad.role: First arrow of Islam · Answered du'a
c-saad.summary: The Prophet ﷺ ransomed his parents for him at Uhud; Persia fell to his command at Qadisiyyah.
c-saad.details:
Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas believed at seventeen, third or fourth of all mankind, and shot the first arrow ever loosed in defense of this religion. His mother swore hunger to death to break his faith; he answered that were she to die a hundred deaths he would not leave it, and revelation enshrined the balance: obey parents in everything except shirk (31:15). At {{n:39|Uhud}} the Prophet ﷺ emptied his quiver for him with the words no other companion received: "Shoot, may my father and mother be ransomed for you."

The Prophet prayed: "O Allah, make his aim true and answer his supplication," and the ummah learned to fear Sa'd's du'a like a weapon. Under {{c:c-umar|Umar}} he commanded al-Qadisiyyah, the battle that broke the Sassanid empire, and founded Kufa. One of the ten promised Paradise and of the six of the shura, he withdrew from the fitnah entirely, saying: bring me a sword that knows the believer from the disbeliever. He was the last of the ten to die, on his farm outside {{p:p-madinah|Madinah}}, in the woolen cloak he had worn at {{n:38|Badr}}, kept for his shroud.

c-fatimah.role: Az-Zahra · Leader of the women of Jannah
c-fatimah.summary: A piece of the Prophet ﷺ; first of his house to follow him, mistress of the women of Paradise.
c-fatimah.details:
Fatimah bint Muhammad, youngest daughter of the Prophet ﷺ and {{c:c-khadijah|Khadijah}}, grew up inside the siege years of {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}}; as a girl she lifted the camel filth from her father's back at the {{p:p-kaaba|Kaaba}} while Quraysh laughed. He ﷺ said of her: "Fatimah is a piece of me; whoever angers her angers me." When she entered his room he would rise, take her hand, kiss her, and seat her in his place; the courtesy between them is its own chapter of the sunnah.

She married {{c:c-ali|Ali}} on a dowry of a shield, kept a house of handmill and waterskin, and asked her father for a servant; he taught her instead the tasbih of thirty-three that the ummah still recites at every bedtime. She bore {{c:c-hasan|al-Hasan}}, {{c:c-husayn|al-Husayn}}, Zaynab and Umm Kulthum: every descendant of the Prophet on earth passes through her. In his final illness he ﷺ whispered to her twice; she wept, then laughed. The secret, told later: he informed her he was dying, then that she would be the first of his house to follow him, and the leader of the women of the people of Jannah. She followed him within six months.

facts.label: Rank
facts.value: Leader of the women of Jannah

c-talha.role: The living martyr · Ten promised Paradise
c-talha.summary: Shielded the Prophet ﷺ at Uhud with his own hand until it was paralyzed.
c-talha.details: At {{n:39|Uhud}}, when the lines broke, Talha stood between the Prophet ﷺ and the arrows and took them with his body; his hand was struck defending the Prophet's face and remained paralyzed for life. The Prophet said: "Whoever wishes to look at a martyr walking upon the earth, let him look at Talha ibn Ubaydillah." Among the earliest converts through {{c:c-abubakr|Abu Bakr}}, tortured for Islam, and one of the ten promised Paradise. Of him and his day at Uhud, Abu Bakr used to say: "That day belonged entirely to Talha." He fell at the Battle of the Camel, an old man still in the saddle.

c-musab.role: First envoy of Islam · Banner of Uhud
c-musab.summary: Makkah's perfumed aristocrat who traded everything, taught Madinah, and died holding the flag.
c-musab.details: The most pampered youth of {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}}, his mother's wealth dressed him in the finest cloth, until Islam cost him all of it. Sent after {{n:33|the First Aqabah}} as the first teacher-ambassador to Yathrib, his gentle recitation opened house after house, and chiefs like {{c:c-saad-muadh|Sa'd ibn Mu'adh}} entered Islam at his hands, a city converted by one man's adab before any army existed. He carried the banner at {{n:38|Badr}} and at {{n:39|Uhud}}, where both his arms were cut holding it before he fell. At his burial there was only one small cloak: cover the head and it left the feet bare; cover the feet and it left the head bare; so the Prophet ﷺ ordered his head covered and grass laid upon his feet.

c-saad-muadh.role: Chief of Aws · The Throne shook
c-saad-muadh.summary: Believed in one sitting, led his clan to Islam by nightfall, and died of the Khandaq wound.
c-saad-muadh.details: Chief of the Aws in {{p:p-madinah|Madinah}}, he came to scold {{c:c-musab|Mus'ab}} and sat down to listen; by evening he told his clan: your speech to me is forbidden until you believe, and Banu Abd al-Ashhal entered Islam in a night. At {{n:38|Badr}} he spoke the Ansar's loyalty into history: "Proceed, O Messenger of Allah, for by Allah, if you plunged into this sea we would plunge with you." At {{n:40|the Khandaq}} an arrow cut his arm-vein; he asked Allah to keep him alive only until he saw judgment upon Banu Qurayza; named their judge, he gave it in accordance with Allah's ruling from above the seven heavens, as the Prophet ﷺ said, and died of the reopened wound. The Prophet said: "The Throne of the Most Merciful shook at the death of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh."

c-hudhayfah.role: Keeper of the Secret · Scout of the Trench
c-hudhayfah.summary: The Prophet's confidant on the hypocrites, and the lone scout of the Confederates' camp.
c-hudhayfah.details: The Prophet ﷺ entrusted Hudhayfah alone with the names of the hypocrites, {{c:c-umar|Umar}} himself would ask him whether he was on the list. On the freezing night of {{n:40|the Khandaq}}, when the Prophet asked who would bring news of the enemy and the hunger-worn camp fell silent, he named Hudhayfah, who slipped among the Confederates as the storm tore their pots and tents, heard {{c:c-abusufyan|Abu Sufyan}} order the retreat, and returned with the news of the siege's collapse. He asked the Prophet about the evil that follows good and about the callers at the gates of Jahannam: one companion keeping watch ahead for the whole ummah. He supervised Uthman's unification of the mushaf.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: Asked about evil, to avoid it

c-nuaym.role: The one-man stratagem of the Trench
c-nuaym.summary: Converted in secret mid-siege and unstitched the Confederate alliance with words alone.
c-nuaym.details: A man of Ghatafan trusted by every faction, Nu'aym came to the Prophet ﷺ secretly during {{n:40|the Khandaq}}: my people do not know of my Islam, command me. The Prophet said: "You are among us one man; so divert from us what you can, for war is deception." Nu'aym went to Banu Qurayza and counseled them to demand hostages from Quraysh; then to Quraysh and Ghatafan, warning that Qurayza would hand them hostages to redeem their pact. When Quraysh tested Qurayza on the Sabbath and the hostage demand surfaced exactly as scripted, each side read betrayal, and the alliance came apart. Then Allah sent the wind. One believer's precision was worth ten thousand men.

c-umm-salamah.role: Mother of the Believers · Counsel of Hudaybiyyah
c-umm-salamah.summary: Her one sentence at Hudaybiyyah saved the camp from the brink.
c-umm-salamah.details: Hind bint Abi Umayyah, among the first emigrants to Abyssinia and then {{p:p-madinah|Madinah}}, widowed by the wounds of {{n:39|Uhud}}, then honored as a Mother of the Believers. Her fiqh entered history at {{n:41|Hudaybiyyah}}: when the companions, crushed by the treaty's terms, did not rise to the Prophet's ﷺ command to sacrifice and shave, he entered upon her in grief, and she counseled: go out, speak to no one, slaughter your own sacrifice and call your barber. He did; the camp leapt to follow; the crisis dissolved without a word of rebuke. Scholars count her counsel among the finest political judgments in the Seerah. She narrated hundreds of hadith and outlived nearly all the wives.

facts.label: Hudaybiyyah
facts.value: The counsel that saved the camp

c-khalid.role: Sayfullah, the Drawn Sword of Allah
c-khalid.summary: Broke the Muslims at Uhud; then never lost a battle for Islam.
c-khalid.details: The cavalry mind who saw the abandoned hill at {{n:39|Uhud}} and turned the day, against the Muslims. After {{n:41|Hudaybiyyah}} he weighed the road ahead and rode to {{p:p-madinah|Madinah}}; the Prophet ﷺ received him: "Praise be to Allah who has guided you, I always saw in you an intellect that I hoped would deliver you to good." He led a column at {{n:42|the Opening}}, took command at Mu'tah when three commanders fell, earning the name Sayfullah, the Drawn Sword of Allah, and later broke the ridda and opened Iraq and Sham at Yarmuk. Removed from command at his peak by {{c:c-umar|Umar}}, he obeyed without a murmur, proof the sword had no ego. He died in his bed, grieving that a man of his scars should not die in battle: "There is no rest for the Sword of Allah but Jannah."

c-abbas.role: Uncle of the Prophet · The voice of Hunayn
c-abbas.summary: Guardian of Zamzam, secret ally before Fath, and the rally-cry that reversed a rout.
c-abbas.details: Uncle of the Prophet ﷺ and custodian of the pilgrims' water, Abbas attended {{n:33|the Second Aqabah}} as his nephew's guarantor before his own Islam, and served the believers from inside {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}} until he emigrated just before {{n:42|the Opening}}, where he escorted {{c:c-abusufyan|Abu Sufyan}} to safety and Islam. At {{n:43|Hunayn}}, when the army broke in the defile, the Prophet ordered Abbas, a man of mighty voice, to call: "O companions of the tree! O companions of Surat al-Baqarah!" and the Ansar wheeled back through their own rout: labbayk, labbayk. In the famine year, {{c:c-umar|Umar}} sought rain by his du'a: "O Allah, we used to seek rain by Your Prophet, and we seek it by his uncle." The riba of Jahiliyya was abolished at {{n:45|the Farewell Hajj}} beginning with his own claims.

c-abusufyan.role: Commander of the enemy · then companion
c-abusufyan.summary: Led Quraysh at Uhud and the Trench, and entered Islam the night before the Opening.
c-abusufyan.details: For two decades the manager of Makkah's war: the caravan that triggered {{n:38|Badr}}, command at {{n:39|Uhud}}, the grand alliance of {{n:40|the Khandaq}}. Yet his answers to Heraclius, recorded in Bukhari, testified to the Prophet's ﷺ truthfulness even while he fought him: "We have never known him to lie." On the eve of {{n:42|the Opening}}, brought in by {{c:c-abbas|Abbas}}, he submitted; and the Prophet honored the old chief's pride into safety: "Whoever enters the house of Abu Sufyan is safe." At {{n:43|Hunayn}} he stood firm holding the Prophet's stirrup, and at {{p:p-taif|Ta'if}} and Yarmuk he gave his eyes in Allah's cause, the last chapters rewriting the first.

c-uthman-talha.summary: The key was taken from him at the Opening, and returned to him forever.
c-uthman-talha.details: His house of Banu Abd ad-Dar held the hijabah, custody of the Kaaba's key, from the age of Qusayy. In Jahiliyya he once refused the Prophet ﷺ entry; the Prophet said: "O {{c:c-uthman|Uthman}}, perhaps you will one day see this key in my hand, to place it where I will." At {{n:42|the Opening}}, the Prophet took the key, entered, prayed, and as {{c:c-abbas|Abbas}} and {{c:c-ali|Ali}} each hoped the custody would pass to their house, the verse descended: "Allah commands you to render trusts to their owners" (4:58). He called Uthman back: "Take it, O Banu Talha, eternally, none shall take it from you except an oppressor." The key remains in that family's hands to this day: conquest, in Islam, restores trusts.

c-suhayl.role: Negotiator of Hudaybiyyah · Orator of steadfastness
c-suhayl.summary: Struck out “Rasulullah” from the treaty, then held Makkah firm for Islam at the ridda.
c-suhayl.details: Quraysh's finest orator, sent to negotiate {{n:41|Hudaybiyyah}}, where he refused the words "Messenger of Allah" on the document and pressed every hard clause, including the return of his own son Abu Jandal, dragged back in chains. {{c:c-umar|Umar}}, enraged that day, would later say: I kept giving charity and fasting for fear of that speech of mine. Suhayl accepted Islam at {{n:42|the Opening}}, and when the Prophet ﷺ died and {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}} swayed toward apostasy, the old negotiator stood at the {{p:p-kaaba|Kaaba}} and held the city with a speech in the spirit of {{c:c-abubakr|as-Siddiq's}} in {{p:p-madinah|Madinah}}: whoever worshipped Muhammad, Muhammad has died; whoever worships Allah, Allah is Living. The tongue once hired against Islam became its anchor, exactly as the Prophet had foretold to Umar: "Perhaps he will stand a station that will please you."

c-jafar.summary: Defended the muhajirin before the Negus, and traded two arms for two wings at Mu'tah.
c-jafar.details: Elder brother of {{c:c-ali|Ali}} and the Prophet's ﷺ look-alike in face and character: "you resemble my form and my manners." Before the Negus of Abyssinia he delivered the emigrants' defense: we were a people of ignorance, idols, dead flesh, the strong devouring the weak, until Allah sent us a messenger whose lineage and truthfulness we know… and he recited Maryam until the king wept into his beard. He returned the day {{p:p-khaybar|Khaybar}} fell: "I do not know which delights me more, the conquest of Khaybar or the coming of Ja'far." At Mu'tah he held the banner until both arms were cut, and fell; the Prophet said Allah exchanged his arms for two wings, with which he flies in Jannah wherever he wills, Ja'far at-Tayyar.

c-ammar.role: Son of the first martyrs · Filled with faith
c-ammar.summary: Tortured beside his parents; the Prophet promised his family Paradise.
c-ammar.details: Son of Yasir and {{c:c-sumayyah|Sumayyah}}, the household on whom {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}} tested its cruelty. The Prophet ﷺ would pass their torture and say: "Patience, family of Yasir, your appointed place is Paradise." Under torment that no flesh sustains, Ammar spoke words of relief with a heart at rest in faith, and revelation excused his very case: "except one who is compelled while his heart is secure in iman" (16:106). He dug {{n:40|the Trench}} with a double share of dust, and the Prophet said of him: "Ammar is filled with faith to his collarbones." The word he ﷺ gave him: "you will be killed by the transgressing party", settled at Siffin, where the old man fell asking for milk, remembering his Prophet's sign.

c-sumayyah.summary: An enslaved old woman, the first soul to die for La ilaha illallah.
c-sumayyah.details: An elderly enslaved woman of {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}} with no clan to avenge her, which is precisely why Abu Jahl chose her family for public torture, and precisely why her stand mattered most. She refused to renounce, under the sun and the stones, and Abu Jahl killed her with a spear: the first person in the history of this ummah to die for the testimony of faith. The religion whose final ranks include kings was opened, in blood, by a woman society priced at nothing. Her husband Yasir died under the same torment; her son {{c:c-ammar|Ammar}} carried their banner for sixty more years. "Patience, family of Yasir, your appointed place is Paradise."

c-anas-nadr.summary: Missed Badr, vowed Allah would see what he would do, and was found with eighty wounds.
c-anas-nadr.details: He missed {{n:38|Badr}} and it burned him: "If Allah grants me a battle with His Messenger, Allah will see what I do." At {{n:39|Uhud}}, when the lines collapsed and men sat down in despair, he walked forward past them: "O Sa'd, Jannah! By the Lord of an-Nadr, I smell its fragrance from beyond Uhud", and fought until they found him with more than eighty wounds of sword, spear, and arrow, his body known only to his sister by his fingertips. The companions held that the verse descended about him and his like: "Among the believers are men true to what they pledged to Allah" (33:23). Uncle of Anas ibn Malik, and the standing definition of making up a missed opportunity.

c-hanzala.summary: Ran from his wedding night to Uhud, and the angels performed his ghusl.
c-hanzala.details: Married the night before {{n:39|Uhud}}, he heard the call at dawn and left before the ritual bath, plunging into the battle until he was killed. The Prophet ﷺ told the companions: "I saw the angels washing Hanzala between the sky and the earth with the water of the clouds in vessels of silver." They asked his wife, who told of the night, and the ummah gave him his eternal name: Ghasil al-Mala'ikah, the one washed by the angels. Son of Madinah's chief enemy monk, he chose his own line. The report is carried in the classical sirah and graded sound by its collectors (Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim). No image of martyrdom in the Seerah is more tender: heaven completing the sunnah the groom had no time for.

c-abdullah-jubayr.summary: Held the hill at Uhud with ten men after forty left, and died at his post.
c-abdullah-jubayr.details: The Prophet ﷺ set him over the fifty archers on the hill at {{n:39|Uhud}} with the order that decided the day: "Do not leave your position even if you see the birds snatching us." When victory glittered and forty of his men descended for the spoils, Abdullah ibn Jubayr stood in the gap quoting his orders, and held the ridge with ten, against {{c:c-khalid|Khalid's}} wheeling cavalry, until every one of them fell. He obeyed the letter of a command whose wisdom the disobedient learned within the hour. In the Codex he stands for every guardian of an unglamorous post: the reward of the hill is not measured by the crowd that left it.

c-wahshi.role: Killer of Hamza · then of Musaylimah
c-wahshi.summary: The spear that killed the best of men later killed the worst.
c-wahshi.details: An Abyssinian slave promised freedom for one throw: at {{n:39|Uhud}} his javelin killed {{c:c-hamza|Hamza}}, and he watched {{c:c-hind|Hind}} mutilate the fallen lion. After {{n:42|the Opening}} he fled until the door of tawbah found him; he came to the Prophet ﷺ, testified, and was accepted, though the Prophet, in his humanity, asked him to keep his face from him, and Wahshi complied with a debtor's humility. At Yamamah he took his old spear hunting a new target and killed Musaylimah the arch-liar. His own summary survives in Bukhari's narration: "I killed the best of people in my ignorance and the worst of people in my Islam, and I hope one cancels the other." The Codex keeps him as tawbah's hardest test case, passed.

c-hind.role: Avenger of Badr · then believer of Fath
c-hind.summary: From mutilating Hamza to pledging allegiance, the fiercest reversal in the Seerah.
c-hind.details: Daughter of Utbah; her father, uncle, and brother all fell at {{n:38|Badr}}, a grief she converted into the vengeance of {{n:39|Uhud}}, hiring {{c:c-wahshi|Wahshi}} against {{c:c-hamza|Hamza}} and mutilating the martyr. At {{n:42|the Opening}} she came veiled among the pledging women, and answered the Prophet's ﷺ terms with the sharp tongue that never left her: does a free woman commit zina?, and on theft, her husband {{c:c-abusufyan|Abu Sufyan}} pardoned in advance. Accepted, she said: "O Messenger of Allah, no household on earth was more hateful to me than yours, and now no household is more beloved." At Yarmuk she stood in the women's line breaking the retreat. Islam's door, the Codex notes, was wide enough for the woman of Uhud.

c-abdurrahman.summary: Refused half a fortune as a gift: “show me the market”, and gave caravans away.
c-abdurrahman.details: Paired at the mu'akhah with Sa'd ibn ar-Rabi', who offered him half of everything; his answer founded Muslim commercial ethics: "May Allah bless your family and wealth for you, show me the market." From a borrowed nothing he rebuilt a fortune, then spent it in convoys: seven hundred camels' cargo given in a day. One of the ten promised Paradise, one of the six of Umar's shura, and the man behind whom the Prophet ﷺ himself prayed a raka'ah at {{n:44|Tabuk}}, the only such honor. He wept over abundance: "{{c:c-musab|Mus'ab}} was better than me and was shrouded in one cloak… I fear our reward was hastened to us here." Wealth in his hand, never in his heart.

c-abu-ubaydah.summary: “Every nation has its trustworthy one, and ours is Abu Ubaydah.”
c-abu-ubaydah.details: Early convert, emigrant to both hijrahs, veteran of {{n:38|Badr}} and every field after, at {{n:39|Uhud}} he drew the two helmet-rings from the Prophet's ﷺ cheek with his front teeth, losing them and gaining the most honorable gap in history. The Prophet fixed his title in the Sahihayn: "Every nation has its amin, and the amin of this ummah is Abu Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah," and sent him when Najran asked for "a trustworthy man, truly trustworthy." One of the ten promised Paradise; commander of the armies of Sham; and when the plague of Amwas took its toll, he refused to flee his post: "shall we flee from the decree of Allah? To the decree of Allah", and was buried with his soldiers.

c-said-zayd.role: Son of the hanif · Ten promised Paradise
c-said-zayd.summary: His father sought Ibrahim's religion before revelation; the son found it in full.
c-said-zayd.details: Son of Zayd ibn Amr ibn Nufayl, the hanif of {{n:24|Jahiliyya}} who refused idols and searched for the religion of {{n:9|Ibrahim}}, of whom the Prophet ﷺ said he would be raised "a nation by himself." Sa'id and his wife {{c:c-fatimah|Fatimah}} bint al-Khattab believed early; it was in their house that {{c:c-umar|Umar}} heard Surah Ta-Ha and turned from executioner to brother. Among the ten promised Paradise, present at every field after {{n:38|Badr}}'s season, and famously feared in du'a: when Arwa accused him falsely over land, he prayed, O Allah, if she is lying, blind her eye and kill her in her land, and {{p:p-madinah|Madinah}} watched it happen. Piety with teeth.

c-asma.role: Dhat an-Nitaqayn, She of the Two Belts
c-asma.summary: Fed the Hijrah from her own waistband, and taught her son to die free.
c-asma.details: When the two men hid in {{n:34|Thawr}}, the supply line was a young pregnant woman climbing a mountain by night. Lacking a rope for the provisions, she tore her waistband in two, and the Prophet ﷺ named her forever Dhat an-Nitaqayn, She of the Two Belts. She faced Abu Jahl's slap without surrendering the route, raised her son Abdullah ibn {{c:c-zubayr|az-Zubayr}}, the first child born to the muhajirin in {{p:p-madinah|Madinah}}, and, nearly a century old and blind, delivered the Seerah's fiercest last counsel when he feared mutilation after death: "Does the flayed sheep feel the skinning? A clean death by the sword." Daughter of {{c:c-abubakr|as-Siddiq}}, sister of {{c:c-aisha|Aisha}}, the household that carried the Hijrah on its back.

c-kab.role: Poet of the Prophet · The truthful of Tabuk
c-kab.summary: Fifty days of silence bought him a verse of forgiveness read until the end of time.
c-kab.details: One of the Prophet's ﷺ three poets, present at {{n:33|Aqabah}} and every field except {{n:38|Badr}} and one more, {{n:44|Tabuk}}, which he missed with no excuse and refused to invent one: "By Allah, if I sit before anyone other than you I could escape his anger with an argument, but I know if I lie to you today, Allah will soon anger you against me." The boycott followed: fifty days, the earth narrowing "for all its vastness," the letter from Ghassan's king burned unread, his wife sent away, until forgiveness descended from above seven heavens (9:118) and the mosque rose to congratulate him. His own verdict: "Allah never blessed me after Islam with anything greater than my truthfulness that day." The Codex sets him beside every easy excuse never made.

c-waraqah.summary: The first outside witness of the revelation: “this is the Namus of Musa.”
c-waraqah.details: Cousin of {{c:c-khadijah|Khadijah}}, one of the hunafa' of {{n:24|Jahiliyya}} who had refused the idols, become Christian, and learned the earlier scriptures until age took his sight. When Khadijah brought her trembling husband after {{n:30|Hira}}, the old scholar listened and identified the visitor from the books he knew: "This is the Namus whom Allah sent down upon {{n:15|Musa}}." He read the road ahead, expulsion, enmity, war, from the pattern of every prophet before, and pledged the support he would never live to give: "If your day reaches me, I will help you with a strength unimaginable." He died within days. The Prophet ﷺ saw him in a dream in white garments, a believer of the interval, first ally of the final revelation.

c-abuhurayrah.summary: Four years of companionship, a spread cloak, and the largest memory in the history of the sunnah.
c-abuhurayrah.details:
Abd ar-Rahman ibn Sakhr ad-Dawsi came to {{p:p-madinah|Madinah}} around {{p:p-khaybar|Khaybar}}, poor, unmarried, and unencumbered, and made a decision that shaped the religion: while others traded and farmed, he attached himself to the mosque and to the Prophet's ﷺ heels on a full stomach or an empty one. He complained once of forgetting; the Prophet told him to spread his cloak, made a motion into it, and said gather it to yourself. "I never forgot anything after it." More than five thousand narrations reach the ummah through him; the daily architecture of a Muslim's worship, dhikr, and manners leans on his memory everywhere.

He mothered his mother in da'wah, weeping to the Prophet when she insulted the message, returning with the du'a "O Allah, guide the mother of Abu Hurayrah" to find her behind the door saying the shahadah. The cat-father nickname came from a kitten he carried; the scholars' title came later: the imam of the huffaz. Under {{c:c-umar|Umar}} he governed Bahrain, under the ummah's need he governed nothing but the transmission, teaching in {{p:p-madinah-masjid|the Prophet's mosque}} until his death near sixty years after the {{n:34|Hijrah}}.

c-anas.summary: His mother gave him to the Prophet ﷺ as a gift; ten years of service, and never once the word 'uff'.
c-anas.details:
When {{n:37|the Prophet ﷺ entered Madinah}}, Umm Sulaym brought her ten-year-old son and said: O Messenger of Allah, Anas will serve you. For ten years he did, and his testimony is the finest character reference ever recorded: "He never said to me about anything I did, why did you do it, nor about anything I left, why did you not do it. And he never once said to me: uff." He carried the Prophet's water, his secrets, and his sandals, and grew up inside the household of revelation.

The Prophet ﷺ prayed for him: "O Allah, increase his wealth and his children, and bless what You give him, and admit him to Jannah." Anas lived to bury, by his own count, over a hundred of his descendants, his orchards fruited twice a year, and he died past a hundred years old in Basra, the last companion to die there, still narrating: over two thousand hadith, the childhood memories of the ummah. His nephew asked him about the fourth part of the du'a; Anas said: I have seen three, and I await the fourth.

c-muadh.role: The scholar of halal and haram
c-muadh.summary: Sent to Yemen with the method of the ummah's law in three answers; will walk ahead of the scholars on the Day of Rising.
c-muadh.details:
Mu'adh ibn Jabal of the Ansar pledged at {{n:33|Aqabah}} as a teenager and became the young man the Prophet ﷺ seated behind him on the mount to teach tawhid: do you know the right of Allah upon His servants? He ﷺ said: "The most knowledgeable of my ummah in halal and haram is Mu'adh ibn Jabal," and told him plainly: "O Mu'adh, by Allah I love you; do not leave off saying after every prayer: O Allah, help me to remember You, to thank You, and to worship You well." The ummah still says it.

Sent as judge and teacher to Yemen, he received at his departure the methodology of Islamic law in three questions: by what will you judge? The Book of Allah. If you do not find it? The Sunnah. If you do not find it? I will strive with my own reasoning, and the Prophet struck his chest with approval. On the road the Prophet gave him the summary of the whole path: the head of the matter is Islam, its pillar is the prayer, and its peak is jihad; then he held his tongue: restrain this. Mu'adh died young in the plague of Amwas in Sham, asking his Lord for his family's share of the epidemic like a bride's gift.

facts.label: Expertise
facts.value: Halal & haram, by his ﷺ word

c-abudharr.summary: Believed before the mosque existed, shouted tawhid at the Kaaba, and died alone as promised.
c-abudharr.details:
Jundub ibn Junadah of Ghifar, a highway tribe, was a monotheist before he ever heard of the message. When rumor of a prophet reached him he sent his brother, then came himself, sleeping in the mosque precinct until {{c:c-ali|Ali}} smuggled him to the Prophet ﷺ. He believed on the spot, and refused the counsel of secrecy: he stood at the {{p:p-kaaba|Kaaba}} and shouted the shahadah into the faces of Quraysh, was beaten to the ground twice, and went home to convert half his tribe.

The Prophet ﷺ said: "The sky has not shaded, nor the earth carried, anyone more truthful of tongue than Abu Dharr." That tongue cost him dearly. His asceticism hardened after {{n:46|the Passing}} into public rebuke of hoarded wealth, quoting the verse of the treasurers of gold; the friction ended with his withdrawal to the desert of ar-Rabadhah, where he died with no one beside him but his family, exactly as the Prophet had foretold at {{n:44|Tabuk}}: "May Allah have mercy on Abu Dharr; he walks alone, dies alone, and will be raised alone." A caravan of Iraq, {{c:c-ibnmasud|Ibn Mas'ud}} at its head, buried him weeping.

c-ibnmasud.role: First public reciter · The two thin shins
c-ibnmasud.summary: A shepherd boy who became the ummah's Qur'an; heavier on the Scale than Uhud.
c-ibnmasud.details:
A slight shepherd of Makkah's outskirts, Ibn Mas'ud met two fugitives asking for milk and watched a dry udder fill at the Prophet's ﷺ touch; he asked to be taught, and became the sixth person in Islam. He was the first man after the Prophet to recite the Qur'an publicly at the {{p:p-kaaba|Kaaba}}, taking the beating that followed and offering to do it again tomorrow. The Prophet told the ummah: "Whoever wishes to recite the Qur'an fresh as it was revealed, let him recite it upon the reading of Ibn Umm Abd," and counted him among the four from whom the Qur'an should be taken.

He carried the Prophet's sandals, siwak, and secrets, walked with him, and absorbed his manner until visitors mistook the household resemblance. When the wind lifted his garment from his thin shins and the companions laughed, the Prophet said: "By the One in whose hand is my soul, they are heavier on the Scale than {{n:39|Uhud}}." He taught Kufa its Qur'an and its fiqh; the school that became Iraq's jurisprudence begins in his mosque circle. He asked to recite for the Prophet once and moved him to tears at "how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness, and bring you over these as a witness."

c-ubayy.summary: Allah named him from above seven heavens to hear Surah al-Bayyinah, and he wept.
c-ubayy.details:
Ubayy ibn Ka'b of the Ansar, a scribe of revelation and one of the four collectors of the Qur'an in the Prophet's ﷺ lifetime, holds an honor that staggered him for the rest of his life. The Prophet said: "Allah has commanded me to recite to you: 'Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book...'" Ubayy asked: did He name me? "He named you." And Ubayy wept. The Lord of the worlds had specified one listener in {{p:p-madinah|Madinah}} by name.

The Prophet called him Abu al-Mundhir and tested him: which verse of the Book of Allah is greatest? Ayat al-Kursi, he answered, and the Prophet struck his chest: "May knowledge be pleasant to you, Abu al-Mundhir." He ﷺ ranked him aloud: "The best reciter of my ummah is Ubayy ibn Ka'b." Under {{c:c-umar|Umar}}, who called him the master of the Muslims, he led the first congregational tarawih of Ramadan; every Ramadan night prayer on earth since stands in a line he started. His mushaf readings remain a resource of tafsir; his fear of the fitnah of position remains a resource of sincerity: he asked Allah to be forgotten, and Allah preserved his name in every science of the Qur'an instead.

c-zaydthabit.role: Scribe of revelation · Collector of the Qur'an
c-zaydthabit.summary: Too young for Badr, chosen at twenty-one to gather the Book between two covers.
c-zaydthabit.details:
Turned away from {{n:38|Badr}} and {{n:39|Uhud}} for his age, Zayd ibn Thabit conquered by intellect instead: he arrived in {{p:p-madinah|Madinah}} with seventeen surahs memorized, and the Prophet ﷺ ordered him to learn the script of the Jews, which he mastered in half a month, becoming the Prophet's translator and foremost scribe of revelation. When the ayah of the mujahidin descended while his shoulder bore the Prophet's writing board, he felt the weight of revelation nearly crush his thigh; he wrote "not equal are the sitters" and then the exemption came for the excused in that same breath, under his pen.

After Yamamah killed hundreds of reciters, {{c:c-abubakr|Abu Bakr}} and {{c:c-umar|Umar}} summoned him for the task he described as heavier than moving a mountain: collect the Qur'an. "You are a young man, intelligent, and beyond suspicion, and you used to write the revelation for the Messenger of Allah." He verified every verse against memory and written witness together, and years later chaired {{c:c-uthman|Uthman's}} committee that copied the single mushaf for the ummah. The judge and inheritance-jurist of Madinah for a generation, he is the quiet proof that the Book reached us through discipline, not accident.

c-ibnabbas.summary: The Prophet ﷺ pressed him to his chest and asked Allah to teach him ta'wil; tafsir begins with him.
c-ibnabbas.details:
Son of {{c:c-abbas|al-Abbas}}, born in the boycott years, Ibn Abbas was about thirteen at {{n:46|the Passing}}, and yet no name stands taller in the interpretation of the Book. The reason is a du'a: the Prophet ﷺ embraced him and said, "O Allah, teach him the Book," and in the narration of the ablution night, "O Allah, give him understanding in the religion and teach him the interpretation." The boy who set out water for the Prophet's wudu received in exchange the keys of tafsir.

His method built the science: he chased the companions door to door with a pillow under his arm, waiting at thresholds while they napped, answering when asked why the cousin of the Prophet begged knowledge at doors: knowledge is not attained with the body at rest. {{c:c-umar|Umar}} seated the youth with the elders of {{n:38|Badr}} and proved his rank with the tafsir of Surah an-Nasr: the announcement of the Messenger's approaching death, which only Ibn Abbas saw. Hibr al-ummah, the learned of the nation, and its tarjuman al-Qur'an, he taught at {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}} until blindness, and died at {{p:p-taif|Ta'if}} with the community's knowledge multiplied through his students for every century after.

facts.label: Method
facts.value: A pillow at the doors of the elders

facts.label: Proof
facts.value: The tafsir of an-Nasr before Umar

c-ibnumar.summary: “What a good man Abdullah would be, if he prayed at night.” He never left the night prayer again.
c-ibnumar.details:
Son of {{c:c-umar|al-Faruq}}, Ibn Umar was rejected at {{n:38|Badr}} and {{n:39|Uhud}} for youth and accepted at {{n:40|the Trench}} at fifteen. As a young man he dreamed of two angels showing him the Fire and a rescuer saying you will not be harmed; his sister {{c:c-hafsah|Hafsah}} relayed it, and the Prophet ﷺ answered with the sentence that governed the rest of his life: "What a good man Abdullah is, if only he prayed at night." From that day he barely slept the last third.

He became the ummah's specialist in following: he prayed where the Prophet prayed, halted his mount where the Prophet's halted, and transmitted the pilgrim's rites step for step. In the fitnah he sheathed his sword entirely and became the reference both armies trusted; offered the caliphate more than once, he refused it unless every Muslim agreed, which is to say he refused it. He gave away fortunes of Umar's estate while patching his own garment, freed slaves by the thousand, and narrated with a terror of misquoting the Prophet that made his precision proverbial. He died in {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}} past eighty, the last of the elder school, having fulfilled one sentence for sixty years.

c-usama.role: The beloved, son of the beloved
c-usama.summary: Commander at eighteen over the elders of Badr; the Prophet's ﷺ last army marched under him.
c-usama.details:
Son of {{c:c-zayd|Zayd}} and of {{c:c-ummayman|Umm Ayman}} the Prophet's ﷺ nurse, Usama grew up on the Prophet's knee, paired there with {{c:c-hasan|al-Hasan}}: "O Allah, love them both, for I love them." Makkah's measure of him is the intercession story: when a noblewoman's theft case sought a favorite to soften the law, they chose Usama, the beloved, son of the beloved, and his request drew the Prophet's most famous statement of equality: peoples before you were destroyed because they excused the noble and punished the weak; by Allah, if {{c:c-fatimah|Fatimah}} the daughter of Muhammad stole, I would cut off her hand.

In his final days the Prophet ﷺ tied the banner of the Sham expedition for Usama, eighteen years old, with {{c:c-umar|Umar}} in his ranks; the murmurs about his youth were answered from the minbar: he is worthy of command, as his father was. {{c:c-abubakr|Abu Bakr's}} first act as caliph was to dispatch that army unchanged, walking beside the mounted teenager he refused to outrank. Usama had one scar he carried from a battlefield misjudgment, a shahadah spoken under his raised sword that he did not accept as sincere; the Prophet's rebuke, did you split open his heart, made Usama wish he had entered Islam only that day, and fixed forever how this ummah receives the professed word of faith.

facts.label: Loved
facts.value: With al-Hasan, on his ﷺ knee

c-abuayyub.summary: The camel knelt at his door; he died a soldier under the walls of Constantinople.
c-abuayyub.details:
{{c:c-khalid|Khalid}} ibn Zayd of Banu Najjar won the lottery every house in {{p:p-madinah|Madinah}} wanted: when {{n:37|al-Qaswa knelt}}, it was at his door, and the Prophet ﷺ lodged with him seven months while the mosque rose. The householder's adab became legend: he and his wife could not bear walking on the floor above the Messenger of Allah, cornering themselves at the room's edge by night, until the Prophet moved upstairs for his hosts' peace. When a dish returned untouched because it carried garlic, Abu Ayyub asked in alarm if it was haram; no, said the Prophet, but I converse with One you do not converse with.

He fought at {{n:38|Badr}}, {{n:39|Uhud}}, and every field, and refused to retire: an old man jihad-bound every fighting season under whichever banner marched. Past eighty he joined the first campaign against Constantinople, fell ill under its walls, and asked for the most forward grave in the army's reach: carry me as far as you can into their land. There he lies to this day, the host of Madinah buried at the edge of Byzantium, teaching the Codex's readers that hospitality and striving were one temperament, not two.

c-ibnsalam.summary: Looked once at his face and knew it was not the face of a liar; promised Jannah by name.
c-ibnsalam.details:
Al-Husayn ibn Salam was the rabbi of Banu Qaynuqa, a man who knew the awaited prophet's description the way he knew his own son. When {{n:37|the Messenger entered Madinah}} he went to look, and his verdict entered the sunan: "When I saw his face, I knew it was not the face of a liar." He tested him with questions whose answers only a prophet would know: the first sign of the Hour, the first meal of the people of Jannah, the resemblance of the child. Then he asked the Prophet ﷺ to conceal him and summon the Jewish leaders; they praised Abdullah as their best and their master, until he stepped out with the shahadah, and became in one minute their worst and the son of their worst. His shelter came in the verdict of revelation: "a witness from the Children of Israel testified to its like" (46:10), a verse read as his.

The Prophet renamed him Abdullah; the sunnah records for him what it records for barely anyone: a promise of Jannah by name while walking the earth, and a dream of a firm handhold interpreted by the Prophet as his dying upon the rope of Islam. He did, decades later, having spent his knowledge translating the two scriptures for the ummah of the last one.

c-amr.summary: Came to Islam between Khalid and Uthman ibn Talha in one caravan; Egypt entered Islam through him.
c-amr.details:
Quraysh's sharpest diplomat, sent to Abyssinia to drag the emigrants home, Amr watched {{c:c-jafar|Ja'far's}} defense defeat him in front of the Negus and carried the splinter of that day for years. After {{n:41|Hudaybiyyah}} the calculation completed itself: he rode north and met {{c:c-khalid|Khalid}} and {{c:c-uthman-talha|Uthman ibn Talha}} on the same errand. At his pledge he demanded a clause, that his past be forgiven, and learned the rule the ummah recites to every convert since: "Do you not know that Islam demolishes what was before it?"

The Prophet ﷺ used the new instrument immediately: command of Dhat as-Salasil, with {{c:c-abubakr|Abu Bakr}} and {{c:c-umar|Umar}} under his flag, and the young general asked the question every ambitious heart asks, who is most beloved to you, expecting his own name; the answer, {{c:c-aisha|Aisha}}, and of men her father, taught him where love actually ranked. Under Umar he opened {{p:p-egypt|Egypt}} with four thousand men and founded Fustat with its mosque, first in Africa; his deathbed scene in Sahih Muslim, weeping through the three chapters of his life, ends with the tawhid of hope: none but the Most Merciful for what remains.

c-ikrimah.role: Son of this ummah's Pharaoh, martyr of Yarmuk
c-ikrimah.summary: He fled the Opening by sea; the storm's tawhid brought him back to the gate of mercy.
c-ikrimah.details:
Son of Abu Jahl, raised at the furnace of his father's hatred, Ikrimah commanded a flank against the Muslims at {{n:39|Uhud}} and fought on at {{n:42|the Opening}} after resistance collapsed. Excluded from the amnesty, he fled for Abyssinia by sea, and in the storm heard the sailors say: nothing avails here but calling on Allah alone. He said to himself: if none avails at sea but Him, none avails on land but Him, and turned around on the strength of a wave's theology. His wife Umm Hakim had already taken his pardon from the Prophet ﷺ, who received him with joy and forbade the Muslims to curse his dead father, for cursing the dead wounds the living.

He spent himself like a man paying arrears: Qur'an pressed to his face, saying the Book of my Lord, the Book of my Lord. At Yarmuk he dismounted with the pledge-unto-death band and fell covered in wounds; the tradition sets his death among the wounded brothers passing the water cup down the line, each refusing it for the next, all dying before it returned. From the first enemy's son to that cup is the full width of Islam's door.

facts.label: Etiquette
facts.value: His dead father not to be cursed

c-ummayman.summary: She carried him ﷺ as an orphan and wept after him for the revelation that had ceased.
c-ummayman.details:
Barakah al-Habashiyyah belonged to the Prophet's ﷺ father and was the young widow Aminah's companion on the journey where she died; the six-year-old rode back to {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}} in Barakah's arms, and she never left him. He freed her, called her "my mother after my mother," and married her to {{c:c-zayd|Zayd}}; their son was {{c:c-usama|Usama}}, the beloved son of the beloved. She made both hijrahs, Abyssinia and {{p:p-madinah|Madinah}}, on foot and fasting until, the reports say, heaven sent down a bucket to her thirst.

She appears at the seams of the story: bandaging at {{n:39|Uhud}}, carrying water, scolding the routed at {{n:43|Hunayn}} with her accented Arabic the Prophet gently corrected. After {{n:46|the Passing}}, {{c:c-abubakr|Abu Bakr}} and {{c:c-umar|Umar}} visited her as he used to, and found her weeping. Do you not know that what is with Allah is better for His Messenger? I know, she said: I weep because revelation from heaven has ceased. Her tears defined the loss for the whole ummah, and the two caliphs wept with her. Every prophet's story hides a woman who carried it before it could walk; the Codex names this one.

facts.label: Family
facts.value: Wife of Zayd, mother of Usama

c-hafsah.role: Umm al-Mu'minin · Keeper of the mushaf
c-hafsah.summary: The fasting, praying wife to whom the ummah entrusted the only master copy of the Qur'an.
c-hafsah.details:
Daughter of {{c:c-umar|Umar}}, widowed young after {{n:38|Badr}}, Hafsah was offered by her anxious father to {{c:c-abubakr|Abu Bakr}} and Uthman before heaven resolved the matter better: the Prophet ﷺ married her, and {{c:a-jibril|Jibril}} himself testified for her when a divorce nearly proceeded: "Take Hafsah back, for she is given to much fasting and much prayer, and she is your wife in Jannah."

Her rank in the ummah's history is custodial and immense. When the first collection of the Qur'an was completed under her father's counsel, the sheets passed from Abu Bakr to Umar, and from Umar not to a caliph but to Hafsah: the master copy of the Book of Allah lived in a wife's room. Years later {{c:c-uthman|Uthman}} borrowed those sheets to copy the unified mushaf and returned them to her hand. She fasted the day she died, as Jibril had described her. Between her keeping and {{c:c-aisha|Aisha's}} narrating, the two young widows of the Prophet's house held the Book and the Sunnah for the generations, and no shelf in Islam is more honored than the chest where her sheets lay.

facts.label: Jibril's word
facts.value: Fasting, praying, his wife in Jannah

facts.label: Custody
facts.value: The master sheets of the Qur'an

c-safiyyah.role: Umm al-Mu'minin · Daughter of Harun's line
c-safiyyah.summary: “My father is Harun and my uncle is Musa.” The Prophet ﷺ taught her the answer that silenced every taunt.
c-safiyyah.details:
Daughter of Huyayy ibn Akhtab, chief of Banu Nadir of the line of Harun, Safiyyah dreamed before {{p:p-khaybar|Khaybar}} of a moon falling into her lap, and carried the slap-mark her husband gave her for it into the day the dream landed. Widowed at Khaybar, she was freed by the Prophet ﷺ, who made her emancipation her dowry and married her, seating her on his own mount with his knee for her step.

Madinah's tongues tested the newcomer's lineage; one day she came to the Prophet weeping from a taunt of Jewish daughterhood. His reply armed her forever: "Why did you not say: my father is Harun, my uncle is {{n:15|Musa}}, and my husband is Muhammad?" In his final illness she said before the wives: I wish it were I in your place, and when some smiled he ﷺ defended her sincerity: by Allah, she is truthful. She lived into the fitnah lowering food by rope to besieged {{c:c-uthman|Uthman}}, and died in {{p:p-madinah|Madinah}}, a bridge of the two covenants in one woman: prophet's daughter by blood, prophet's wife by choice, buried in al-Baqi among the mothers of the believers.

c-zaynab.summary: “Allah married me from above seven heavens.” The longest hand in charity among the wives.
c-zaynab.details:
Cousin of the Prophet ﷺ, first married to {{c:c-zayd|Zayd}} in a match arranged to demolish class pride, then divorced, Zaynab became the center of the verse that ended adoption's marriage fictions: "We married her to you" (33:37). Her wedding contract was dictated by revelation, and she knew what she held: to the other wives she would say, your families gave you in marriage; Allah married me from above seven heavens.

{{c:c-aisha|Aisha}}, her rival in rank, gave her the testimony that settles her portrait: "I have never seen a woman better in religion than Zaynab, more fearing of Allah, more truthful in speech, more attentive to kinship, greater in sadaqah." She worked leather with her own hands and gave the earnings away. When the wives asked which of them would follow him ﷺ first, he answered: the one with the longest hand. They measured wrists against the wall until the meaning arrived with her death: the longest hand was the most giving one. Zaynab followed him first, in Umar's caliphate, leaving nothing behind: she had already sent it ahead.

c-hasan.role: Master of the youth of Jannah · The reconciler
c-hasan.summary: “This son of mine is a sayyid; through him Allah will reconcile two great parties of the Muslims.”
c-hasan.details:
Firstborn of {{c:c-ali|Ali}} and {{c:c-fatimah|Fatimah}}, named by the Prophet ﷺ himself, al-Hasan rode his grandfather's back in sujud and his shoulder in the streets, and carried his face: the most resembling of the household. From the minbar the Prophet issued the prophecy that became this man's biography: "This son of mine is a sayyid, and perhaps Allah will reconcile through him two great parties of the Muslims."

Forty years later he held the caliphate of Iraq with an army at his back and every incentive of blood and title to use it. He weighed the ummah against the throne and handed power to Mu'awiyah on terms, in the Year of the Jamaa, retiring to {{p:p-madinah|Madinah}} as the man who proved the Prophet's word by giving up what men kill for. With his brother {{c:c-husayn|al-Husayn}} he holds the shared title: the two masters of the youth of the people of Jannah. He was generous past accounting, twice splitting his entire wealth with the poor, and died in Madinah, asking burial beside his grandfather if it caused no conflict, and al-Baqi when it would have: peacemaking even in the grave.

c-husayn.role: Master of the youth of Jannah · Martyr of Karbala
c-husayn.summary: “Husayn is from me and I am from Husayn.” The grandson whose stand defined the price of principle.
c-husayn.details:
Second son of {{c:c-ali|Ali}} and {{c:c-fatimah|Fatimah}}, al-Husayn was the other half of the pair the Prophet ﷺ called "my two sweet basils of this world," lengthening his sujud rather than hurry a grandson off his back, praying: "O Allah, I love them, so love them." Of him specifically he said: "Husayn is from me and I am from Husayn; Allah loves whoever loves Husayn."

He grew in his brother's counsel and outlived him into the hour when kingship asked the Prophet's grandson for its stamp. He refused the pledge he judged an injustice, answered Kufa's letters, and was intercepted at Karbala with his family: some seventy against thousands, cut off from the river. On Ashura of 61 AH he fell with his infant in his arms and his household around him, and the head of the man whom the Messenger of Allah kissed on the mouth was carried to a palace. The ummah's grief is not sectarian property; the Sunni canon itself carries his rank, and the Codex records both the love and the warning: whoever makes power absolute will meet the family of the Prophet at his reckoning.

a-jibril.summary: Six hundred wings, the horizon filled twice; every verse of every scripture passed through his trust.
a-jibril.details:
Jibril is the channel of revelation itself: "he brought it down upon your heart by permission of Allah" (2:97). The Qur'an gives him titles of rank and inviolability: the Trusted Spirit, "possessed of power, secure with the Owner of the Throne, obeyed there, trustworthy" (81:20-21). The Prophet ﷺ saw him in his true form twice: once at the horizon after {{n:30|Hira}}, six hundred wings blocking the sky, and once at the Lote Tree of the furthest limit during {{n:32|the Mi'raj}} (53:13-14).

Usually he came as a man: as Dihyah al-Kalbi, or as the traveler in white of the famous hadith of Jibril, who sat knee to knee with the Prophet and questioned him on islam, iman, and ihsan so the ummah would inherit its own syllabus, "that was Jibril, who came to teach you your religion." He pressed the first word of the Book into the Prophet at {{n:30|Iqra}}, reviewed the whole Qur'an with him every Ramadan and twice in the final year, led him through the heavens, and stood at {{n:38|Badr}} in the gear of war. {{n:15|Musa}} called him his companion at every calamity; this ummah recites his name in its creed among the angels believed in by name.

quran.en: The Trusted Spirit brought it down upon your heart, that you may be of the warners.

a-mikail.summary: Named beside Jibril in the Qur'an; steward of the rain and the measures of sustenance.
a-mikail.details:
Mika'il is one of only two angels the Qur'an names in a single breath, sealing the matter of anyone who would love one envoy of Allah and hate another: "Whoever is an enemy to Allah, His angels, His messengers, and Jibril and Mikal, then indeed Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers" (2:98). The verse descended when a party of the People of the Book claimed Jibril as their enemy and Mika'il as their friend; heaven refused the sorting.

The tradition assigns him the treasuries of mercy in their most material form: the rain, the wind that carries it, and the growth that follows, measures weighed and dispatched, not weather at random. In the Prophet's ﷺ opening du'a of the night prayer he is invoked by name: "O Allah, Lord of Jibril, Mika'il, and {{c:a-israfil|Israfil}}, Originator of the heavens and the earth." A report in the Musnad adds a portrait of his gravity: the Prophet asked {{c:a-jibril|Jibril}} why he never saw Mika'il laugh, and was told he had not laughed since the Fire was created. The angel who waters the world does not find it a light responsibility.

facts.label: Gravity
facts.value: Has not laughed since the Fire (Ahmad)

quran.en: Whoever is an enemy to Allah, His angels, His messengers, and Jibril and Mikal, then Allah is an enemy to the disbelievers.

a-israfil.summary: Forehead inclined, ear turned, waiting since creation for one command.
a-israfil.details:
Israfil is the angel of the single deferred act: the blast. The Prophet ﷺ described his readiness in the hadith that reframes every calm afternoon: "How can I be at ease, when the bearer of the Horn has put the Horn to his mouth, inclined his forehead, and turned his ear, waiting for the command to blow?" The companions asked what to say in the face of that image; he gave them the words of {{n:9|Ibrahim}}: hasbunallahu wa ni'mal-wakil.

He is invoked by name with {{c:a-jibril|Jibril}} and {{c:a-mikail|Mika'il}} in the Prophet's night-prayer opening, a trio the scholars read as the angels of life: revelation that gives hearts life, rain that gives earth life, and the blast that gives the dead their rising. His two blows are fixed in {{n:64|the Trumpet node}}: the stun that retires the universe and the rising that fills {{n:66|the plain}}.
