Between them, a wait of forty, whose unit the narration deliberately withholds. Every node of this Codex from the first tile onward has taken place inside the interval of his held breath; the Codex places him where he stands, at the hinge of existence.

a-malik.summary: The people of the Fire will beg him for annihilation; his answer takes a thousand years of silence to say.
a-malik.details:
Malik commands the Fire and its nineteen wardens, "over it are angels, stern and severe; they do not disobey Allah in what He commands them" (66:6). The Qur'an records the one conversation the Fire's people will have with him: "They will call: O Malik, let your Lord finish us. He will say: You are staying" (43:77). Classical tafsir adds that the answer comes after an interval that mocks the request; the mercy of quick death is not his to give.

The Prophet ﷺ met him: on {{n:32|the Night Journey}} Malik was the one angel who did not smile at him, and {{c:a-jibril|Jibril}} explained that he has never smiled at anyone since he was created; were he to smile for any, it would have been for you. In the dream-vision of Bukhari the Prophet saw him kindling, and identified him plainly: this is Malik, the keeper of the Fire. The Codex sets him beside {{c:a-ridwan|the keeper of the Garden}} deliberately: both abodes have their appointed keepers, and their gates stand beyond all human bargaining. The door out of his jurisdiction is open only on this side of death.

quran.en: They will call: O Malik, let your Lord put an end to us. He will say: indeed, you are staying.

a-munkar-nakir.role: The two questioners of the grave
a-munkar-nakir.summary: Three questions in the first night of the afterlife; the answers were written by how a life was lived.
a-munkar-nakir.details:
The grave is the first station of the Hereafter, and the sound tradition fills in its examination. Two angels come to the buried soul, sit him up, and ask: Who is your Lord? What is your religion? Who is this man who was sent among you? The believer answers with firmness, for "Allah keeps firm those who believe with the firm word in this life and in the Hereafter" (14:27), which the Prophet ﷺ said descended precisely about the questioning of the grave. His grave is widened, furnished from Jannah, and opened to its breeze. The hypocrite answers with history's most honest confession of secondhand religion: "Ah, ah, I do not know; I heard the people saying a thing, so I said it," and his grave closes on him.

The names Munkar and Nakir appear in Tirmidhi's narration; the questioning itself is in Bukhari and Muslim. The Prophet taught the living their part: stand at the fresh grave and ask firmness for your brother, "for right now he is being questioned," and seek refuge from the grave's punishment in the last sitting of every prayer. The Codex records the mercy inside the test: the exam's answers are not memorized; they are the residue of a life.

a-ridwan.summary: The Garden has keepers who greet with salam; tradition names their chief Ridwan.
a-ridwan.details:
The Qur'an shows the office in action: the God-conscious are driven to the Garden in companies "until, when they reach it, its gates are opened and its keepers say: peace be upon you, you have done well, so enter it to abide" (39:73). Angels of welcome, entering upon the residents from every gate with salam for their patience (13:23-24). The name Ridwan for their chief comes from the tradition and the scholars rather than from a verse or rigorously sound hadith, and the Codex marks that grading honestly, as it does for {{c:a-malakalmawt|the Angel of Death's}} popular name.

What is beyond doubt is the doorman scene of the Sahihayn: the Prophet ﷺ said, "I will come to the gate of Jannah on the Day of Rising and ask for it to be opened. The keeper will say: who are you? I will say: Muhammad. He will say: for you I was commanded; I open for no one before you." The first door ever opened in the eternal world swings for him ﷺ. Whoever wants the keeper's greeting rehearses it now: the people of salam in this world are met by salam at that door.

quran.en: Its keepers will say: peace be upon you; you have done well; enter it, abiding eternally.

a-harut-marut.role: The two angels of Babylon, a test
a-harut-marut.summary: They taught nothing until they had warned: we are only a trial, so do not disbelieve.
a-harut-marut.details:
In {{p:p-babylon|Babylon}}, in the generations after {{n:22|Sulayman}}, the shayatin marketed sorcery under a prophet's name, claiming his kingdom had run on it. Revelation demolished the libel: "Sulayman did not disbelieve, but the shayatin disbelieved, teaching people magic" (2:102), and the same verse sets down the strangest entry in the angelic record: what was sent down upon the two angels at Babylon, Harut and Marut. They taught no one until they had delivered the disclaimer that separates a test from a temptation: "We are only a fitnah, so do not disbelieve."

People learned anyway, the verse continues, what separates a man from his wife, harming none except by Allah's permission, learning what hurt them and did not profit them, having purchased it with their share of the Hereafter. The Codex keeps this seal for the discipline it teaches: knowledge itself can be a trial; a warning delivered does not excuse the one who ignores it; and the transaction the verse describes, trading the akhirah for a technique, remains available in every century under newer names. The later storyteller embellishments about the two angels' sins are not in the Qur'an and carry no sound chain; the Codex leaves them where the muhaddithun left them.

quran.en: They taught no one until they said: we are only a trial, so do not disbelieve.

a-malakalmawt.summary: “Say: the angel of death, who has been entrusted with you, will take you.”
a-malakalmawt.details: The Qur'an names his office, not his name: "Say: the angel of death, entrusted with you, will take you in full, then to your Lord you are returned" (32:11). The name "Azra'il," widespread in later books, does not occur in the Qur'an or the authentic Sunnah, the Codex records the office as revelation records it. He commands hosts: the angels of mercy who draw out the fragrant soul of the believer gently "as a drop from the waterskin's mouth," and the angels of punishment for the other extraction, both scenes detailed in the sound hadith of al-Bara'. And he obeys limits: sent to {{n:20|Musa}}, he was struck by the prophet who did not wish to die, returned to his Lord, and came back with a bargain of years measured in the hairs of a bull's hide · Bukhari and Muslim carry the account. At {{n:64|the first blast}}, his office completes itself and closes.

quran.en: Say: the angel of death, who has been entrusted with you, will take you, then to your Lord you will be returned.

a-kiraman.role: Recorders on the right and left
a-kiraman.summary: “Not a word does he utter but with him is an observer ready.”
a-kiraman.details: Two on every human: "When the two receivers receive, seated on the right and on the left, not a word does he utter but with him is an observer ready" (50:17-18). The right records the good; the left, the tradition reports, is instructed toward patience, held back while the servant is given time to repent. Deeds are lifted in shifts: "angels of the night and angels of the day succeed one another among you, meeting at Fajr and Asr", and the ascending shift is questioned about how they left His servants: praying, they answer, and praying we found them. The Codex sets them beside {{n:69|the Hisab}}: the ledgers opened on the Day are being written in this sentence, by readers of it. "And indeed, over you are keepers, noble, writing, they know whatever you do" (82:10-12).

quran.en: Indeed, over you are keepers, noble, writing, they know whatever you do.

a-hamalat.titleEn: Hamalat al-Arsh, Bearers of the Throne
a-hamalat.summary: They carry the Throne, glorify their Lord, and pray for the believers below.
a-hamalat.details: Above every rank of angel stand the bearers of the {{n:1|Throne}}. Their scale defies the page: the Prophet ﷺ was given leave to speak of one of them: "between his earlobe and his shoulder is the journey of seven hundred years" (Abu {{n:21|Dawud}}, sahih). On the Day, "eight will bear the Throne of your Lord above them" (69:17). But the Qur'an's longest look at them is not at their size, it is at their occupation: "Those who carry the Throne and those around it glorify the praise of their Lord, believe in Him, and seek forgiveness for those who believe: Our Lord, You encompass all things in mercy and knowledge, so forgive those who repent and follow Your way, and spare them the punishment of Hellfire" (40:7). The mightiest creatures in existence spend their strength making du'a for the weakest believers on earth. The Codex records them as the Path's highest comfort: you are being prayed for, from directly beneath the Throne.

quran.en: Those who carry the Throne and those around it glorify the praise of their Lord and seek forgiveness for those who believe.

a-mountains.role: Offered to crush Ta'if, and was declined
a-mountains.summary: “If you wish, I will bring the two mountains down upon them.”
a-mountains.details: He appears once in the record, on the worst day of the Seerah. After {{n:31|Ta'if's}} stones, {{c:a-jibril|Jibril}} called to the Prophet ﷺ: "Allah has heard what your people said to you, and He has sent you the Angel of the Mountains, to command as you will." The angel gave his greeting and made history's most terrifying offer with a servant's courtesy: "If you wish, I will bring the two Akhshabayn down upon them." The bleeding Prophet's answer defines the mission the Codex documents: "Rather, I hope that Allah will bring forth from their loins those who will worship Allah alone, associating nothing with Him." The angel of demolition met the prophet of mercy, and mercy commanded. Ta'if's grandchildren filled the mosques.

a-badr.summary: The only battlefield where the unseen ranks were named, counted, and remembered by the survivors.
a-badr.details:
At {{n:38|Badr}} the du'a of a desperate few was answered with a troop movement from the unseen: "I will reinforce you with a thousand of the angels, following one another" (8:9). Their rules of engagement came from the same verses: "I am with you, so strengthen those who believe; I will cast terror into the hearts of those who disbelieve, so strike above the necks" (8:12). {{c:a-jibril|Jibril}} himself attended; the Prophet ﷺ said: "This is Jibril, holding the head of his horse, in the gear of war" (Bukhari 3995).

The survivors carried unexplainable memories: heads falling before swords arrived, a lash-mark like a green whip on prisoners' faces, a voice urging forward, aqdim Hayzum, from riders no one could place. And heaven's own ranking descended through Jibril's question in Bukhari 3992: what do you count the people of Badr among you? The best of the Muslims, they said. He said: and likewise the angels who attended Badr. An aristocracy exists among the angels, and its patent of nobility is the same as the believers': having stood at the hard place on the hard day.

quran.en: I will reinforce you with a thousand of the angels, following one another.

j-iblis.role: The refuser · Enemy of the line of Adam
j-iblis.summary: One act of pride, one request for respite, and a war declared on every child of the one he envied.
j-iblis.details:
Iblis was of the jinn, worshipping among the angels, when the command came to prostrate to {{n:2|Adam}}; "he refused and was arrogant" (2:34). His argument was history's first racism of substance: "I am better than him; You created me from fire and created him from clay" (7:12). Expelled, he did not repent; he asked one thing, respite until the Day they are raised, and declared his strategy: "I will surely sit for them on Your straight path, then come at them from before them and behind them, from their right and their left" (7:16-17). Note the geometry the scholars noted: no approach from above, where du'a travels, nor from below, where sujud lands.

His methods are whisper and false promise: "he promises them nothing but delusion" (17:64), and his own closing speech on the Day is the tradition's most honest confession: "Allah promised you the promise of truth, and I promised you and betrayed you… so do not blame me; blame yourselves" (14:22). Against him the Book prescribes not fear but contempt: "the plot of shaytan is ever weak" (4:76). He bested no one by force; every victory of his is a signature the victim provided.

quran.en: I will surely sit for them on Your straight path, then come at them from before them and behind them…

j-believing.role: The delegation that heard and returned as warners
j-believing.summary: Seven or so of the unseen stood at Nakhlah, heard the Qur'an once, and re-founded their nation's religion overnight.
j-believing.details:
On the road back from {{n:31|Ta'if}}, at Nakhlah, the Prophet ﷺ recited in the night prayer, and an audience he could not see stopped mid-journey: "a company of the jinn listened and said: we have heard an amazing Qur'an; it guides to right conduct, so we have believed in it, and we will never associate anyone with our Lord" (72:1-2). Surah al-Jinn preserves their entire internal debate: their astonishment, their confession that among them are the righteous and otherwise, their discovery that the heaven's listening posts were now guarded with flames, and their theology, sounder after one recitation than centuries of their elders': "exalted is the majesty of our Lord; He has taken neither wife nor son."

Surah al-Ahqaf shows their method on returning: "O our people, respond to the caller of Allah" (46:31), da'wah copied precisely from the man they had listened to. The Prophet later read to a delegation of them by night, and showed {{c:c-ibnmasud|Ibn Mas'ud}} their traces at dawn. The Codex keeps them as the rebuke of every excuse: no book in their hands, no prophet of their kind, one hearing, total reform.

facts.label: Their creed
facts.value: No wife, no son, no shirk

quran.en: Say: it has been revealed to me that a company of the jinn listened and said: we have heard an amazing Qur'an.

j-ifrit.summary: Offered to carry a throne across kingdoms before the council rose; outbid by knowledge in a blink.
j-ifrit.details:
When {{n:22|Sulayman}} asked his assembly who would bring him the throne of Bilqis before her delegation arrived in submission, the first bid came from raw power: "an ifrit of the jinn said: I will bring it to you before you rise from your place, and I am strong and trustworthy for it" (27:39). A cross-kingdom heist inside a council session: the outer limit of what muscle can promise.

The counter-bid reset the scale of the possible: "the one who had knowledge of the Book said: I will bring it to you before your glance returns to you" (27:40), and the throne stood before them. The Qur'an does not name the scholar; it names what he had. Sulayman's response modeled the believer's reaction to capability: "this is from the bounty of my Lord, to test me whether I am grateful or ungrateful." The Codex keeps the ifrit as the honest measure of jinn power, real, large, and second place: creatures who build, dive, and haul thrones (34:12-13), and still stood in a court where one verse-bearer outran them. Strength serves in this story; it does not preside.

facts.label: Lesson
facts.value: Power serves; it does not preside

quran.en: An ifrit of the jinn said: I will bring it to you before you rise from your place.

j-qarin.role: The whisperer attached to every human
j-qarin.summary: “Even me,” he ﷺ said: “but Allah helped me against him, and he submitted.”
j-qarin.details: "There is no one among you but a companion from the jinn has been assigned to him." They said: Even you, O Messenger of Allah? He said: "Even me, but Allah helped me against him, and he aslama (submitted / I am safe from him), so he commands me with nothing but good" (Muslim 2814). The qarin is the whisperer posted closest of all: on the Day he disowns his man: "Our Lord, I did not make him transgress; he was himself in far error" (50:27), and the two arrive together, companion turned accuser: "his qarin will say: this is what is ready with me" (50:23). The defense the Prophet ﷺ prescribed is not exorcism but dhikr: the whisperer "shrinks when Allah is remembered." The Codex sets this seal beside {{c:j-iblis|Iblis}}: the general has a soldier stationed on every heart, and the heart holds the high ground with two words of remembrance.

quran.en: His companion will say: Our Lord, I did not make him transgress, he was himself in far error.

j-khinzab.summary: The one shaytan whose name and neutralization the Prophet ﷺ issued together.
j-khinzab.details:
{{c:c-uthman|Uthman}} ibn Abi al-As came to the Prophet ﷺ with the complaint of every praying human since: shaytan comes between me and my prayer and my recitation, confusing it for me. The answer named the operative and issued the countermeasure in one breath: "That is a shaytan called Khinzab. When you sense him, seek refuge in Allah from him, and spit dryly to your left three times." Uthman said: I did that, and Allah removed him from me (Muslim 2203).

The Codex keeps this small seal for what it proves about the war's granularity: the whispering enemy is not an abstraction or a mood; the assault on concentration in salah is a named assignment with a named agent, and the defense is neither talent nor willpower but a prescription: recognition, isti'adhah, and contempt. The scholars drew the wider rule: the qarin whispers through the day, Khinzab besets the meeting of prayer itself, precisely because that is where the servant stands closest. Sabotage concentrates where the treasure is. Whoever finds his mind scattered at the takbir may take strange comfort in knowing his enemy is named: he is being interfered with because he is somewhere worth interfering with.

an-salih.role: The she-camel of Allah · Sign for Thamud
an-salih.summary: She came out of the rock with her drinking day appointed by heaven; her hamstringing cost a civilization everything.
an-salih.details:
Thamud, the rock-carvers of al-Hijr, demanded a sign on their own terms, and received one with a title no other creature carries: "this is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you" (7:73). The tradition describes her emerging from the mountain itself, vast, drinking a whole day's water; revelation set the timetable: "she has a drinking day, and you have a drinking day, appointed" (26:155), and a single prohibition: touch her not with harm.

The test was pure restraint, and it failed by committee: they called their most wretched (91:12), a red-faced man the Prophet ﷺ identified in a sermon as the match of history's killers, and he hamstrung her while the town assented. Three days' warning, then the cry seized them kneeling in their homes. Surah ash-Shams prices the deed in nine short verses ending with the coldest clause in the Book: "and He does not fear its consequence" (91:15). Passing al-Hijr at {{n:44|Tabuk}}, the Prophet covered his face and hastened, forbidding entry to the punished valley except weeping. Her seal stands in the Codex for every shared trust given to a community: the sign need not be harmed by the many; it is enough that the many permit the one.

quran.en: The messenger of Allah said to them: the she-camel of Allah and her drink. But they denied him and hamstrung her.

an-kahf.summary: Stretched his forelegs at the cave mouth for three centuries and entered the Qur'an with the friends of God.
an-kahf.details:
When the young monotheists of {{n:23|the generations after Isa}} fled a city that punished tawhid, a dog followed them to the cave. The Qur'an paints him into the miracle with a guard's posture: "and their dog stretching his forelegs at the threshold" (18:18), keeping the door of a sleep that lasted three hundred years and nine. The same verses describe the staging around him: the sun bending off the cave's mouth, the sleepers turned right and left, an aura of dread that would have filled any intruder with flight.

The scholars drew from his presence a chain of quiet lessons the Codex loves: the companion of the righteous is preserved with them, even a dog; loyalty at a threshold outweighs pedigree; and the Book that records kings forgetting God found room for an animal who stayed. When the town's descendants later argued over the sleepers' number, the Qur'an dismissed the arithmetic and kept the dog in every count they proposed: three and the fourth their dog, five and the sixth their dog, seven and the eighth their dog (18:22). Whatever the census, the dog is in it. Guard something sacred long enough, the tile suggests, and you become part of its story permanently.

quran.en: …and their dog stretching his forelegs at the threshold.

an-hoopoe.role: Scout of Saba · The bird with a case
an-hoopoe.summary: Absent without leave, back with intelligence two empires lacked, and a theology sounder than a kingdom's.
an-hoopoe.details:
{{n:22|Sulayman}} inspected the birds and found a gap in the ranks: "why do I not see the hudhud, or is he among the absent?" (27:20). The threat was execution-grade discipline; the defense, when the bird landed, is the Qur'an's most confident opening statement by a subordinate: "I have encompassed what you have not encompassed, and I bring you from Saba certain news" (27:22). A queen, a great throne, a prosperous people, and the flaw his small eye diagnosed at once: "I found her and her people prostrating to the sun instead of Allah" (27:24), when prostration belongs to "Allah, who brings forth the hidden in the heavens and the earth" (27:25).

Sulayman tested the report with a letter, carried by the same bird: drop it upon them, then withdraw and watch. The chain that ended with {{p:p-saba|an empire's}} conversion began with one absence justified by reconnaissance. The Codex keeps the hudhud as the patron of every small observer with great news: rank did not see what he saw; and his instinct, on discovering a wrong qiblah, was neither idle gazing nor silence, but to report to the one who could act.

quran.en: I have encompassed what you have not encompassed, and I bring you from Saba certain news.

an-ant.role: The ant who moved a colony
an-ant.summary: One warning cry for her people made an emperor smile, and gave a surah its name.
an-ant.details:
As {{n:22|Sulayman's}} columns crossed the valley of the ants, one ant issued the Qur'an's finest example of leadership at the smallest scale: "O ants, enter your dwellings, lest Sulayman and his soldiers crush you while they do not perceive" (27:18). Every clause is jurisprudence: she warned her own, named the threat precisely, prescribed the action, and excused the powerful of intent, "while they do not perceive," guarding her colony's hearts from grudge along with their bodies.

Sulayman, granted the speech of birds and more, heard her from the head of an army and did not ride on. "He smiled, laughing at her speech, and said: My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your favor" (27:19). An emperor was halted by an ant and moved to gratitude: the sound tradition adds a matching account, the prophet of old who, stung by an ant, burned the colony and was corrected by revelation for punishing "a nation among the nations that glorify." The surah of the great throne-heist and the hudhud's mission is named, in the end, an-Naml: the Ants. Heaven's index gives the smallest voice the title page.

quran.en: An ant said: O ants, enter your dwellings… and he smiled, laughing at her speech.

an-yunus.summary: “So the whale swallowed him, and he was blameworthy”: a prison with one exit, built of a sentence.
an-yunus.details:
When {{n:23|Yunus}} left his city in anger before permission, boarded a ship, and lost the lot three times, the sea's discipline was already commissioned: "the whale swallowed him, and he was blameworthy" (37:142). The Qur'an is exact about the exit: had he not been of those who glorify, "he would have remained in its belly until the Day they are raised" (37:143-144). The cell was escape-proof to everything except dhikr.

In the layered darknesses, of the night, the sea, and the belly, he called with the call the Prophet ﷺ certified as universal: "None has the right to be worshipped but You; glory be to You; I have been of the wrongdoers" (21:87). "No Muslim ever supplicates with it for anything except that Allah answers him" (Tirmidhi). The whale delivered its passenger to the shore alive, mission renewed, a gourd vine grown over him for his healing, and a hundred thousand of his people believed: the only city in the Qur'an whose iman, once the punishment loomed, availed it (10:98). The Codex counts the whale among the signs as the gentlest jailer in scripture: commissioned to hold a prophet exactly as long as it took him to say three clauses truthfully.

quran.en: None has the right to be worshipped but You; glory be to You; indeed I have been of the wrongdoers.

an-fil.role: Mahmud and the birds of Ababil
an-fil.summary: An elephant that knelt facing Makkah, and flocks that dismantled an army: the year the calendar started counting.
an-fil.details:
Two animals share this tile because heaven used them as a pair. The first was Abraha's great elephant, Mahmud by the sirah's naming: at the edge of the sanctuary it knelt and would not rise toward {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}}, though they beat it and turned it, and it would run willingly toward Yemen. Creation refusing an order the whole army obeyed. The second came from the sea's direction in flocks, ababil, each bird with stones of baked clay; "He made them like eaten straw" (105:5).

The Prophet ﷺ ratified the event's legal weight at {{n:42|the Opening}}: "Allah held back the elephant from Makkah, and gave His Messenger and the believers authority over it," and at {{n:41|Hudaybiyyah}}, when al-Qaswa knelt, he read his own camel through that older kneeling: "the One who held back the elephant has held her back." Arabia dated its years from the event, and in that year {{n:27|Muhammad ﷺ was born}}. The Codex pairs the two signs as one sentence: the largest land animal refused to break the House, and the smallest airborne ones sufficed to defend it.

quran.en: He sent against them birds in flocks, striking them with stones of hard clay, and made them like eaten straw.

an-wolf.summary: Yusuf's brothers convicted an innocent animal; the shirt they brought was torn by no teeth.
an-wolf.details:
The wolf enters {{n:12|Yusuf's story}} twice, and never once in the flesh. First as the father's fear: "I fear that a wolf will eat him while you are heedless of him" (12:13), the pretext Ya'qub handed his sons unwittingly. Then as the sons' alibi: "O father, we went racing and left Yusuf with our things, and a wolf ate him" (12:17), delivered at night, with weeping, and with the evidence that refuted itself: a shirt dipped in false blood, uncut, untorn, as if the wolf had been a careful launderer of garments.

Classical tafsir preserves the wit the moment deserved: a wolf remarkably merciful, that devoured the boy without tearing his shirt. Ya'qub read the forensics and the hearts behind them: "rather, your souls have enticed you to a matter; so patience is beautiful" (12:18). The Codex keeps this seal for every innocent blamed to cover the guilty: nature accused, evidence fabricated, and a slow providence that let the lie stand for decades, then unwound it in a palace with the liars bowing. The wolf never touched the boy; the brothers never escaped the shirt.

facts.label: Appears
facts.value: Only in speech, never in flesh

quran.en: They brought his shirt with false blood. He said: rather, your souls have enticed you to a matter; so patience is beautiful.

an-cow.summary: One simple command, inflated by questions into a rare golden specimen; the surah of the whole Shari'ah bears her name.
an-cow.details:
A man of Bani Israel was murdered for an inheritance, and the town traded accusations. The command through {{n:20|Musa}} was one line: "Allah commands you to slaughter a cow" (2:67). Any cow. Instead of obedience came questions: what is she? what color? they all look alike to us. Each question narrowed the specification, until the open command had become a scavenger hunt for a golden heifer, unyoked, unblemished, pleasing to beholders, which they purchased, the tafsir records, for a fortune, "and they almost did not do it" (2:71).

Then the point: strike the dead man with part of it, "thus Allah gives life to the dead and shows you His signs" (2:73). The victim rose, named his killer, and the case closed with resurrection entered into evidence. The Prophet's ﷺ standing rule reads like this story's summary: "what I have forbidden you, avoid; what I have commanded you, do as much as you can; those before you were destroyed by their many questions." The longest surah of the Qur'an, the surah of law itself, is named al-Baqarah after the cow that taught the first rule of law: the command you question into complexity was simple when it arrived.

quran.en: We said: strike him with part of it. Thus Allah gives life to the dead.

an-fish-khidr.titleEn: The Fish of Musa and the Servant
an-fish-khidr.role: The fish that marked the meeting place
an-fish-khidr.summary: A dead fish revived in a basket and swam out through a tunnel of sea: the only compass heaven ever gave.
an-fish-khidr.details:
{{n:20|Musa}} was assigned a teacher he could find only by coordinates no map carries: the junction of the two seas, marked by a sign that would perform itself. Take a fish in a basket, he was told; where you lose it, there he is. At the rock, while {{n:15|Musa}} slept, the salted fish stirred, slid to the water, "and took its way into the sea, tunneling" (18:61), the Qur'an describing the water holding a dry corridor around its path, sarabah, like an arch.

The young companion, Yusha per the tradition, saw it and forgot to report it until a day's hunger later: "did you see, when we took shelter at the rock? I forgot the fish, and none made me forget it but Shaytan; and it took its way into the sea, amazingly" (18:63). Musa's answer is the traveler's cry of recognition: "that is what we were seeking" (18:64), and they retraced their footsteps to find al-Khidr at the rock. The Codex places the fish where the story places it: revelation sometimes marks its meeting places not with addresses but with small resurrections, and the servant's part is to notice where the miracle happened and walk back to it.

facts.label: The exit
facts.value: A tunnel held in the sea

quran.en: They forgot their fish, and it took its way into the sea, tunneling.

an-buraq.summary: White, beyond the donkey and below the mule, its stride lands at the edge of its sight.
an-buraq.details: "I was brought al-Buraq, a white beast, taller than the donkey and shorter than the mule, whose stride lands at the farthest point of its sight" (Muslim 162). On its back the Prophet ﷺ crossed from {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}} to {{p:p-aqsa|al-Aqsa}} in a night, {{n:32|the Isra}}, where he tethered it at the ring, the reports say, where the prophets tethered before him: revelation's own relay animal, serving the caravan of prophethood across the ages. {{c:a-jibril|Jibril}} accompanied; at al-Aqsa the prophets assembled behind their final brother in prayer; then the ascent went up beyond any mount's road. The Codex keeps al-Buraq among the animals of the signs as the tradition keeps it: a creature of light-speed obedience, proof that every scale of creation, beast, angel, heaven, was staged for the journey of one rider.

an-ram.summary: “And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice”, the animal that ended human sacrifice.
an-ram.details: At the instant {{n:10|Ibrahim's}} knife had nothing left to prove, heaven substituted a ram: "And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice" (37:107). The Qur'an calls the animal azim, great, because of what it carried: the abolition, inside the very story that seemed to demand it, of offering human beings to God. Every Eid al-Adha since is that morning re-enacted; the Prophet ﷺ sacrificed two horned, black-and-white rams with his own hand, saying the takbir and setting his foot on their sides (Bukhari 5565). The Codex places the ram where the tradition places it: the most consequential animal in the history of worship, one creature standing in, forever, for every child of {{n:2|Adam}} laid on every altar of false devotion.

quran.en: And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice.

an-staff.summary: A shepherd's tool by day, a devourer of illusions before Pharaoh.
an-staff.details: "What is that in your right hand, O {{n:15|Musa}}?", a staff: I lean on it, I bring down leaves for my sheep. "Throw it down." And it became a rushing serpent, {{n:17|at Tuwa}} a training in fearlessness ("take it and do not fear; We will return it to its former state"), and before Pharaoh "a manifest serpent" (7:107) that swallowed the ropes and rods of the magicians' theater. The professionals fell in prostration first, they alone knew the difference between trick and creation. The Codex lists the serpent among the sign-creatures with a jurist's note: the animal existed at Allah's command inside a tool, the way every "solid" thing in the Path exists, {{n:9|fire that cools}}, {{n:18|sea that stands}}, matter awaiting instructions.

an-wolf-speaking.summary: A wolf argued jurisprudence with a shepherd and preached the Prophet's ﷺ mission; two men in Madinah believed it instantly.
an-wolf-speaking.details:
A herdsman was among his sheep when a wolf seized one; he chased it and tore his sheep back. The wolf sat up on its tail and delivered the rebuke the sunnah preserved: do you not fear Allah, taking from me a provision Allah drove to me? The stunned man said what every era says at a miracle: a wolf, speaking the speech of men? The wolf's reply aimed higher than its meal: shall I not tell you of something more wondrous? The Messenger of Allah, in {{p:p-madinah|Madinah}} between the two harrahs, informing people of the news of what has passed and what is to come.

The herdsman drove his flock to the city, verified, and the Prophet ﷺ ordered him to tell the people, then sealed it from the minbar: "He has spoken truly. By the One in whose hand is my soul, the Hour will not rise until beasts speak to men…" And when the account was first told, he ﷺ said: "I believe in it, and {{c:c-abubakr|Abu Bakr}} and {{c:c-umar|Umar}}," though the two were not present. The Codex keeps the talking wolf beside {{c:an-wolf|Yusuf's silent one}}: the animal falsely accused in one story testifies in another, and the fastest believers are those whose hearts had already stopped requiring convenience of their miracles.

facts.label: Instant iman
facts.value: Abu Bakr and Umar, in absentia

an-birds-ibrahim.summary: Cut, scattered on the hilltops, and summoned: they came to the Friend of Allah at a run.
an-birds-ibrahim.details:
{{n:9|Ibrahim}} asked his Lord the question of every honest heart: "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead." The reply tested his faith first: "Do you not believe?" He said: "Yes, but so my heart may be at rest" (2:260). Heaven granted the laboratory: take four birds, draw them to yourself, then place a portion of them on every hill, then call them; "they will come to you in haste. And know that Allah is Mighty and Wise."

He did as commanded, the parts distributed across the hilltops, and at his call the pieces rose, assembled, and flew to him running. The tafsir tradition names the species variously and the Codex declines the details the Book withheld; what the verse fixes is the protocol: the Friend of Allah was permitted to hold the experiment of the {{n:65|Ba'ath}} in his own hands, one call standing in for the Trumpet. The scholars treasured the verse's mercy for the rest of us: itmi'nan, the heart's rest, is a legitimate request; asking to see is not doubt when it comes from love. The birds' seal closes with the phrase the resurrection itself will close with: they came in haste.

facts.label: The request
facts.value: “So my heart may be at rest”

quran.en: Then call them; they will come to you in haste. And know that Allah is Mighty and Wise.

an-sabbath-fish.summary: They surfaced only on the forbidden day, shining and abundant, and a town invented the first legal loophole.
an-sabbath-fish.details:
The town by the sea, al-Ayka of the tafsir maps or Aylah on the gulf, was tested with a schedule: fishing forbidden on the Sabbath they themselves had demanded as sacred. The fish obeyed the decree: "their fish came to them on their Sabbath day, appearing openly, and on the day they kept no Sabbath, they did not come; thus We tested them for their defiance" (7:163). Shoals surfacing shamelessly on the one closed day, gone every open one: temptation engineered with a timestamp.

The response founded a genre: the loophole. Nets set Friday, hauled Sunday; ponds dug so the Saturday tide would strand the fish for a lawful Sunday harvest. The town split three ways: the schemers, the preachers, and the shrugging third who asked the preachers why they bothered, and received the Qur'an's charter of speaking truth regardless: "as an excuse before your Lord, and that perhaps they may fear Him" (7:164). The verdict fell on the schemers alone, "be apes, despised" (7:166), while those who forbade evil were saved. The fish keep their seal in the Codex as the shiniest bait in scripture, and the town keeps its lesson: a law evaded by cunning is a law broken all the same.

facts.label: The trap
facts.value: Surfacing on the closed day only

quran.en: Their fish came to them openly on their Sabbath day, and on the day they kept no Sabbath they did not come.

an-uzayr-donkey.titleEn: The Donkey of the Hundred Years
an-uzayr-donkey.summary: Its rider slept a century; his food stayed fresh and his mount was rebuilt bone by bone as he watched.
an-uzayr-donkey.details:
A man, Uzayr in the dominant tafsir reading, passed a town fallen in on its roofs and asked the scholar's version of despair: "How will Allah give life to this after its death?" (2:259). The answer was a demonstration with himself as the specimen: "So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him." The questioning on waking is the Qur'an's gentlest irony: how long did you remain? A day, or part of a day. "Rather, you remained a hundred years."

Then the evidence, split with a scientist's care into a control and an experiment: "look at your food and your drink, they have not spoiled; and look at your donkey." The perishables were preserved; the durable skeleton had gone to scattered bone. "And look at the bones, how We raise them, then clothe them with flesh." Before the rider's eyes his mount was reassembled, joint by joint, hide and breath returned: the {{n:65|Ba'ath}} performed on one beast for an audience of one. "So when it became clear to him, he said: I know that Allah is over all things competent." The donkey's seal stands for the verse's method: heaven does not always argue with doubt; sometimes it schedules a demonstration.

quran.en: And look at the bones, how We raise them, then clothe them with flesh.

e-dajjal.summary: One-eyed, marked kafir, forty distorted days, and a paradise that is a fire: the final exam of appearances.
e-dajjal.details:
The full account stands at {{n:55|its Path chapter}}; this seal keeps the marks by which he is known. A young man, ruddy and thick-set, hair in tight curls, blind in his right eye like a floating grape, and between his eyes the letters kaf-fa-ra, read by every believer, literate or not. "There is no trial between the creation of {{n:2|Adam}} and the rising of the Hour greater than the Dajjal" (Muslim 2946). Every prophet warned of him; ours ﷺ alone mapped him: emergence from the east through the gap between Sham and Iraq, forty days with the first like a year, rain and ruin at his command, a paradise and fire inverted, the youth he kills and revives who then out-argues him.

He is barred from {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}} and {{p:p-madinah|Madinah}} by ranks of angels; Madinah will quake three times and shake its hypocrites out to him. He is already chained: {{c:e-jassasa|al-Jassasah's}} island interview (Muslim 2942) records him asking about the palms of Baysan and the lake of {{p:p-tiberias|Tiberias}}, counting down his own leash. His end has an address, {{p:p-ludd|the gate of Ludd}}, and an executioner, {{c:e-isa-return|the son of Maryam}}. The Shield is prescribed at the Path node: Kahf's opening verses, the fourfold refuge, distance, and the creed that your Lord is not one-eyed.

e-dabba.summary: When the word falls, the earth itself produces the announcer; after her speech no one is undecided.
e-dabba.details:
Her verse is explicit and singular: "When the word falls upon them, We will bring forth for them a creature from the earth speaking to them, that mankind was not certain of Our signs" (27:82). A land creature, from the earth, with intelligible speech, dispatched at the moment persuasion's era is formally closed. Muslim 2941 welds her timing to {{n:58|the western sunrise}}: whichever of the two comes first, the other follows close behind, and Muslim 158 counts her among the three signs after which a soul's new faith no longer avails it.

The sunan reports add the marking: the believer's face brightened, the denier's nose stamped, so that in the marketplace each would be called by what he is, O believer, O disbeliever. Those chains sit below the Sahihayn and the Codex says so, while noting that their meaning only restates the verse's function: after the Dabba, ambiguity is over for good. Her anatomy is deliberately withheld by revelation, and the Codex declines to invent what the Book concealed. Her full sequence stands at {{n:59|its Path chapter}}; her lesson stands at every mirror: the mark she stamps is the externalization of one being written now, choice by choice.

quran.en: We will bring forth for them a creature from the earth, speaking to them.

e-yajuj.summary: Sealed by Dhul-Qarnayn's iron and copper, released in Isa's era, ended by worms in a single night.
e-yajuj.details:
Two nations of the children of {{n:2|Adam}}, corrupters on the earth of old, walled off by {{n:57|Dhul-Qarnayn}} behind iron sheets fused with molten copper between the two mountains (18:94-96), with the builder's disclaimer stamped on the work: "this is a mercy from my Lord; when the promise of my Lord comes, He will level it" (18:98). The Prophet ﷺ saw the first breach in his own era and woke red-faced: "woe to the Arabs from an evil that has drawn near; today a gap has been opened like this," ringing his thumb and finger (Bukhari 3346).

Their release is fixed in Muslim 2937, in the era of {{c:e-isa-return|Isa}} after the {{c:e-dajjal|Dajjal}}: "from every height they swarm" (21:96), the vanguard drinking {{p:p-tiberias|Tiberias}} dry, the rearguard finding mud, their arrows returning from the sky stained as they announce victory over heaven. No army engages them; revelation directs {{n:23|Isa}} to shelter the believers at {{p:p-tur|at-Tur}} while Allah ends the unfightable with naghaf worms in their necks, all of them "dead as the death of one soul." Birds like camels carry the corpses; a rain washes the earth to a mirror. Their multitude supplies the greater part of the Fire's people in Bukhari 3348. The full sequence stands at {{n:57|its Path chapter}}.

facts.label: The breach
facts.value: Shown to him ﷺ, a finger-ring

quran.en: Until, when Yajuj and Majuj are opened, and they swarm from every height.

e-isa-return.role: The Descent · The true Masih ends the false one
e-isa-return.summary: Down the wings of two angels at Fajr in Damascus: the story left open in Surah an-Nisa closes at Ludd.
e-isa-return.details:
He was not killed and not crucified; "Allah raised him to Himself" (4:157-158), and the story so suspended resumes at the appointed minute: Fajr, {{p:p-damascus-minaret|the white minaret east of Damascus}}, iqamah already called. He descends in two saffron garments, hands on the wings of two angels; when he lowers his head it drips, when he raises it, pearls fall (Muslim 2937). He declines {{c:e-mahdi|the Mahdi's}} mihrab with the sentence that honors this ummah forever: your imam is from among you.

His agenda is the dismantling of his own deification and the deceiver who borrowed his name: he breaks the cross, ends the swine, abolishes the jizyah, and hunts the {{c:e-dajjal|Dajjal}} to {{p:p-ludd|the gate of Ludd}}, where the false masih dissolves like salt in water and dies on a true spear. Then the earth's sabbath: security so complete the lion lies with the camel; a pomegranate shading a company; rancor lifted. {{n:57|Yajuj and Majuj}} interrupt; he shelters the believers and heaven ends the hordes. He remains forty years, performs Hajj at the ancient House, marries, dies, and the Muslims pray over him: the ultimate janazah of tawhid. His full node stands at {{n:56|the Descent}}; his instruction for whoever lives to see him is on record: give him my salam ﷺ.

quran.en: Indeed, he is a sign of the Hour, so do not doubt it.

e-mahdi.role: The rightly-guided ruler of the last days
e-mahdi.summary: Of Fatimah's line, name matching the Prophet's, seven years of justice before the end.
e-mahdi.details: A man of the Prophet's ﷺ house: "of the sons of {{c:c-fatimah|Fatimah}}," his name matching the Prophet's name, whom Allah rectifies in a night and sends when the earth is full of wrong: "he will fill it with fairness and justice as it was filled with oppression and wrong, and rule seven years" (Abu {{n:21|Dawud}}). Wealth in his days is given without counting. He is not named "Mahdi" in Bukhari and Muslim, the Codex says so plainly, but he stands described there: the imam of the believers behind whom {{c:e-isa-return|Isa ibn Maryam}} prays at Fajr in Damascus, and the man at the House against whom an army marches and is swallowed at al-Bayda (Muslim 2882). His full account stands at Path node {{n:54|Al-Mahdi}}. His counterfeits, thirty dajjals claiming his cloak across history, are themselves one of the signs he was promised.

e-jassasa.summary: “I am al-Jassasah, go to that monastery, for a man there longs for your news.”
e-jassasa.details: The strangest witness statement in the canon, told by Tamim ad-Dari, a Christian sailor who became Muslim, and then retold by the Prophet ﷺ from the minbar because it confirmed what he had been teaching (Muslim 2942). Storm-driven for a month, Tamim's crew landed on an island where "a beast of abundant hair, they knew not front from back" met them: "I am al-Jassasah", the gatherer of news, and it directed them to the monastery, where a shackled giant interrogated them: do the palms of Baysan still fruit? does the lake of {{p:p-tiberias|Tiberias}} still hold water? has the prophet of the unlettered emerged? Then the declaration: "I am {{c:e-dajjal|al-Masih (ad-Dajjal)}}, and I am about to be given leave to emerge." The Codex keeps the Jassasah as the canon's eeriest testimony: the last fitnah already exists, already chained, already asking about the water levels.

facts.label: Function
facts.value: Gathers news for the chained one

e-suwayqatayn.summary: After the last believer is taken, a thin-legged man from Abyssinia dismantles the House stone by stone.
e-suwayqatayn.details:
The House that {{n:11|Ibrahim raised}}, that {{n:26|the birds defended}}, that {{n:42|the Opening purified}}, has one hour still written for it, and the sound tradition does not soften it: "Dhul-Suwayqatayn, the man of two thin legs, from Abyssinia, will demolish the {{p:p-kaaba|Kaaba}}" (Bukhari 1591, Muslim 2909). The Prophet ﷺ described the scene with terrible precision: "as if I am looking at him: black, bandy-legged, dismantling it stone by stone" (Bukhari 1595).

The sequencing is the theology. This does not happen while one worshipper remains: it follows {{n:62|the gentle wind}} that harvests every believing soul, in the age when no one on earth says Allah, Allah. The hadith corpus adds what closes around it: the Hajj and Umrah will have been performed to the end of their appointed era, and in the hour of the worst of people the protection held over the House since the Elephant is allowed to end, because a sanctuary's sanctity lived in the ummah that honored it. The Codex keeps this darkest seal deliberately: buildings, even that building, were never the point; the direction of prayer was a means, and when no one prays, stones return to being stones. The believer reading this will never see it; that is precisely the mercy of the sequence.

facts.label: Timing
facts.value: After the wind; no believers remain

facts.label: Seen by him ﷺ
facts.value: “As if I am looking at him”

p-kaaba.role: The First House · Qiblah of mankind
p-kaaba.summary: Raised by Ibrahim and Isma'il, ringed by idols, purified at the Opening: the axis every prayer on earth turns toward.
p-kaaba.details:
"The first House established for mankind was that at Bakkah, blessed, and a guidance for the worlds" (3:96). {{n:11|Ibrahim and Isma'il raised its foundations}} begging acceptance; forty centuries of pilgrims have answered {{n:11|the proclamation}} made from its hill. One prayer within the surrounding mosque outweighs a hundred thousand elsewhere (Ibn Majah 1406, sahih).

Its biography is the Path in miniature: ringed with {{n:24|360 idols}} in the long forgetting, defended by {{n:26|birds}} when no believer could defend it, circled secretly by the persecuted, set as {{n:37|the qiblah}} in the second year of the {{n:34|Hijrah}}, purified by {{n:42|the Opening}} while {{c:c-bilal|Bilal}} stood on its roof, and destined, after the last believer is taken, for {{c:e-suwayqatayn|the thin-legged demolisher}}. Its key rests with {{c:c-uthman-talha|Banu Talha}} by the verse of trusts. The Black Stone at its corner descended, the Prophet ﷺ said, whiter than milk, and the sins of the children of {{n:2|Adam}} darkened it (Tirmidhi 877, hasan). Whoever cannot reach it turns toward it: five times daily, the planet quietly agrees on one point.

quran.en: The first House established for mankind was that at Bakkah, blessed, and a guidance for the worlds.

hadith.text: One prayer in this mosque of mine is better than a thousand prayers elsewhere, except al-Masjid al-Haram.

p-madinah-masjid.role: His mosque ﷺ · A garden of Paradise
p-madinah-masjid.summary: Built by his own hands on the orphans' lot; between his house and his minbar lies a garden of Jannah.
p-madinah-masjid.details:
When {{n:37|al-Qaswa knelt}}, the Prophet ﷺ bought the drying-yard of two orphans at a fair price and built, with his own hands in the brick-line, the headquarters of the religion: mosque, school, court, shelter for the poor of as-Suffah, and along its wall the rooms of his household. One prayer in it is better than a thousand elsewhere, except {{p:p-kaaba|the Sacred Mosque}} (Bukhari 1190).

Inside it lies the most precisely bounded ground in the tradition: "between my house and my minbar is a garden from the gardens of Jannah" (Bukhari 1195, Muslim 1390), the Rawdah, where the ummah still crowds shoulder to shoulder to stand momentarily on ground heaven has claimed for its own. Here {{n:45|the pilgrims' rites were taught}}, here {{c:c-abubakr|Abu Bakr}} led the prayer of the final illness, and here, in {{c:c-aisha|Aisha's}} room on its edge, {{n:46|the Prophet was buried}} where he died. Visiting greetings are given to him and his two companions to this day. The mosque of the emigrant grew into the ummah's second sanctuary; its minbar, he said, stands over his Basin.

facts.label: Holds
facts.value: His grave ﷺ, Abu Bakr, Umar

hadith.text: Between my house and my minbar is a garden from the gardens of Jannah, and my minbar is upon my Basin.

p-aqsa.role: First qiblah · Station of the Isra
p-aqsa.summary: Second mosque ever placed on earth, terminus of the Night Journey, prayer-hall of all the prophets for one night.
p-aqsa.details:
{{c:c-abudharr|Abu Dharr}} asked which mosque was placed on earth first; the Prophet ﷺ answered al-Masjid al-Haram, then al-Aqsa, "and between them forty years" (Bukhari 3366, Muslim 520). The Qur'an's single most concentrated sentence of geography binds the two forever: "Glory to Him who took His servant by night from al-Masjid al-Haram to al-Masjid al-Aqsa, whose surroundings We have blessed" (17:1).

On {{n:32|the night of the Isra}}, {{c:an-buraq|al-Buraq}} was tethered at its ring and the prophets assembled behind their final brother in prayer: the transfer of the imamate of mankind, performed in the building's own liturgy. It was the first qiblah of this ummah, faced for sixteen or seventeen months in {{p:p-madinah|Madinah}} until {{n:37|the verse of turning}}. It is one of only three mosques to which journeys may be set out (Bukhari 1189), and its opening to the ummah came bloodlessly under {{c:c-umar|Umar}}, who cleaned its rock with his own cloak. The end of time returns here too: the road of {{n:57|the hordes}} and the era of {{n:56|Isa's justice}} run through this land, "whose surroundings We have blessed."

facts.label: Isra
facts.value: All prophets prayed behind him ﷺ

quran.en: Glory to Him who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Furthest Mosque, whose surroundings We have blessed.

p-quba.role: Founded on taqwa from the first day
p-quba.summary: The first mosque this ummah ever built; a Saturday habit of the Prophet ﷺ, and an umrah's reward for two rak'ahs.
p-quba.details:
On the southern approach to {{p:p-madinah|Madinah}}, {{n:36|the first free Muslim building}} rose before the city itself was reached: the Prophet ﷺ halted among Banu Amr ibn Awf, laid stones with his own hands, and prayed in the mosque whose praise came down from heaven: "a mosque founded on taqwa from the first day is more worthy that you stand within it; in it are men who love to purify themselves" (9:108).

The attachment never faded: "the Prophet ﷺ used to come to Quba every Saturday, riding or walking, and pray two rak'ahs" (Bukhari 1193, Muslim 1399), and he priced the visit for the rest of history: "whoever purifies himself in his house, then comes to the mosque of Quba and prays in it, has the reward of an umrah" (Ibn Majah 1412, sahih). The Qur'an contrasted it explicitly with the mosque of harm built {{n:44|near Tabuk's season}} to divide the believers: identical architecture, opposite foundations. Quba stands in the Codex as the standing proof that a building is judged by its founding intention, and that the cheapest umrah on earth is two rak'ahs and a short ride away for the people of one city.

quran.en: A mosque founded on taqwa from the first day is more worthy that you stand within it.

p-hira.summary: A rock cell above Makkah, facing the Kaaba, where five verses re-aimed history.
p-hira.details:
The Mountain of Light earns its name from one small hollow near its summit: a cell of rock barely a man's length, its mouth aimed at {{p:p-kaaba|the Kaaba}}. Here the man {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}} called al-Amin practiced {{n:29|tahannuth}}, provisioned by {{c:c-khadijah|Khadijah}}, climbing away from a city of idols night after night for years.

In Ramadan of his fortieth year the visitor came. {{c:a-jibril|Jibril}} filled the cell, pressed him three times to the limit of endurance, and released into the world the first words of the final Book: {{n:30|Iqra}}. "Read, in the name of your Lord who created" (96:1). The mountain held the weight of that night once more in the tradition's memory: Hira trembled beneath the Prophet ﷺ and his companions years later, and he stilled it: "be firm, Hira, for upon you are none but a prophet, a siddiq, and martyrs" (Muslim 2417). No shrine stands there and none is prescribed; the summit's honor is textual, not ritual. The Codex maps it as the exact coordinates where heaven resumed contact with the earth.

hadith.text: Be firm, Hira: upon you are none but a prophet, a siddiq, and martyrs.

p-thawr.role: Shelter of the second of two
p-thawr.summary: Three nights, two men, and a verse that made a rock cavity part of the creed.
p-thawr.details:
South of {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}}, opposite the road anyone would watch, the mountain of Thawr hides the cavity where {{n:34|the Hijrah}} held its breath for three nights. Inside: the Prophet ﷺ and {{c:c-abubakr|Abu Bakr}}, whose fear was not for himself; outside: a hundred-camel bounty and search parties close enough to be seen by their feet.

The exchange inside entered the Qur'an and the creed together. Abu Bakr whispered that a glance downward would discover them; the answer became {{w:w-la-tahzan|a permanent sentence of the religion}}: "do not grieve, indeed Allah is with us" (9:40), and in Bukhari's wording: "what do you think, O Abu Bakr, of two, Allah is their third?" The provisioning was a family's quiet heroism: {{c:c-asma|Asma}} climbing with food by night, her brother carrying the city's gossip, a freedman's flock erasing footprints. The popular spider and dove at the entrance rest on weak chains, and the Codex says so plainly; the Qur'an credits the concealment to "soldiers you did not see." Thawr's teaching stands opposite {{p:p-hira|Hira's}}: one cave received revelation, the other proved reliance on it.

facts.label: Supply line
facts.value: Asma, She of the Two Belts

quran.en: When he said to his companion: do not grieve, indeed Allah is with us.

p-uhud-mount.summary: Red granite over Madinah's north: battlefield, graveyard of seventy martyrs, and the only mountain with a certified friendship.
p-uhud-mount.details:
Uhud walls Madinah's north in red granite, and carries a testimonial no other landform holds: "this is a mountain that loves us, and we love it" (Bukhari 4083, Muslim 1365). The Prophet ﷺ said it returning from campaign, when the sight of Uhud meant home.

At its feet the ummah took {{n:39|its bitterest early lesson}}: the archers' hill abandoned, {{c:c-hamza|Hamza}} and seventy martyrs buried where they fell, in the graves the city still visits with salam. On its slopes the Prophet bled, and his tooth broke, and {{c:c-talha|Talha's}} hand took the arrows meant for his face. Once, the mountain itself shook beneath the four it carried, and was told: "be firm, Uhud, for upon you are a prophet, a siddiq, and two martyrs" (Bukhari 3675), a sentence that quietly foretold how {{c:c-umar|Umar}} and {{c:c-uthman|Uthman}} would die. The Prophet fixed its size as the ummah's unit of moral measure: gold equal to Uhud would not settle what a companion's handful of deeds weighs, and {{c:c-ibnmasud|Ibn Mas'ud's}} two shins outweigh it on the Scale.

hadith.text: This is a mountain that loves us, and we love it.

p-tur.summary: Site of the burning tree, the forty nights, and the manifestation that turned rock to dust.
p-tur.details:
Only a handful of created things receive the honor of a divine oath; this mountain opens a surah with one: "By at-Tur" (52:1), and stands inside another: "by the fig and the olive, and Mount Sinin" (95:1-2). At its side {{n:17|Musa saw the fire}} and heard, in the valley of {{p:p-tuwa|Tuwa}}, the address every muwahhid memorizes: "indeed, I am Allah; there is no god but Me" (20:14).

Here he returned for {{n:20|the forty nights}}, received the Tablets "in whose inscription is guidance and mercy," and made the request that measured all requests: show me. "You will not see Me; but look at the mountain." The manifestation came to the summit and leveled it, and {{n:15|Musa}} fell unconscious (7:143). The mount kept later appointments too: raised over Bani Israel as a canopy for the covenant (2:63), and appointed in Muslim 2937 as the refuge where {{n:56|Isa}} will shelter the believers while {{n:57|the hordes}} pass. {{n:71|What Sinai could not withstand}}, the Codex notes at its final tile, the people of Jannah will be granted at home.

quran.en: When his Lord manifested to the mountain, He leveled it, and Musa fell unconscious.

p-safa-marwah.role: The two hills of Hajar's run
p-safa-marwah.summary: A desperate mother's seven crossings became a pillar of pilgrimage: the only footsteps ritualized forever.
p-safa-marwah.details:
Two low hills flank the valley of {{p:p-kaaba|the House}}, and between them runs the only choreography in worship copied from a woman in crisis. When the water skin emptied and the infant Isma'il writhed, Hajar climbed as-Safa scanning the valley, crossed to al-Marwah, and back, seven times, until {{p:p-zamzam|the answer broke from the ground}} under the angel's strike. The Prophet ﷺ sealed the memory: "may Allah have mercy on the mother of Isma'il" (Bukhari 3364).

Revelation ratified her footsteps into law: "indeed, as-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of Allah" (2:158); every pilgrim's sa'i walks her exact route, and the men jog the stretch where she ran. From as-Safa's top the Prophet later made {{n:30|his first public call}}, asking {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}} if they would believe a raider behind the hill, and receiving the answer his character had already earned: we have never known a lie from you. One hill holds the run of a trusting mother, the other the cry of a trusted son; between them, the religion says, walk.

quran.en: Indeed, as-Safa and al-Marwah are among the symbols of Allah.

p-arafat.role: The Hajj itself · Rehearsal of the Standing
p-arafat.summary: One afternoon a year, one plain, and more emancipations from the Fire than any other day grants.
p-arafat.details:
"The Hajj is Arafah" (Tirmidhi 889, sahih): the Prophet ﷺ reduced the entire pilgrimage to one afternoon of standing on this plain east of {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}}. Here he delivered {{n:45|the Farewell Sermon}} from al-Qaswa's back, here the verse of completion descended on a Friday, and here he taught that the finest thing he and the prophets before him ever said was said on this ground: {{w:w-shahada|la ilaha illallah}}.

The day's gift is mercy beyond measure: "there is no day on which Allah frees more servants from the Fire than the day of Arafah; He draws near and boasts of them to the angels: what do these want?" (Muslim 1348). Fasting the day, for the non-pilgrim, expiates two years (Muslim 1162). And the plain is a rehearsal with the props of the real performance: multitudes in two unstitched cloths, standing exposed under one sun, asking. {{n:66|The Mawqif of the Last Day}} will feel familiar to whoever stood here well; the Codex maps Arafat as the only place on earth where the Hereafter holds a yearly rehearsal.

hadith.text: There is no day on which Allah frees more servants from the Fire than the day of Arafah.

p-mina.role: Valley of the sacrifice · Days of Tashriq
p-mina.summary: Where the knife was stopped and the ram descended; the pilgrims' tent city of dhikr, eating, and stoning the old whisperer.
p-mina.details:
East of {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}}, the valley of Mina holds the oldest completed test in the Codex: here, by the dominant reading, {{n:10|Ibrahim laid his son down}}, and here the ransom descended, "We ransomed him with a great sacrifice" (37:107). Every Eid al-Adha since is this valley's anniversary, wherever the believer's sacrifice is made.

The tradition maps the whisperer onto the geography: at these stations Shaytan appeared to {{n:9|Ibrahim}} urging him to fail the test, and at each the Friend of Allah drove him off with stones; the three Jamarat pillars mark the campaign, and every pilgrim re-enacts the contempt, seven pebbles at a time, takbir with each throw. The Prophet ﷺ spent the days of Tashriq here and defined them: "days of eating, drinking, and remembrance of Allah" (Muslim 1141); from here {{n:45|the sermon of the days of Tashriq}} declared no Arab above a non-Arab except by taqwa. A tent city with no permanent resident, assembled for obedience and folded away: Mina is the Codex's architecture lesson that some places exist purely as verbs.

facts.label: Nature
facts.value: A city that exists as a verb

quran.en: And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice.

p-makkah.role: Mother of cities · Sanctuary since the heavens
p-makkah.summary: “By Allah, you are the best of Allah's earth… had I not been driven out of you, I would not have left.”
p-makkah.details:
An uncultivated valley given a future by one du'a: {{n:11|Ibrahim}} settled his family "in a valley without vegetation, by Your Sacred House," and asked for hearts to incline and fruits to arrive (14:37). Both requests are still being fulfilled daily. Its sanctity is not municipal but cosmic: "this city was made sacred by Allah the day He created the heavens and the earth" (Bukhari 1834), its game unhunted, its trees uncut, its ground the only place on earth where the rules were written before the residents.

It birthed the final Prophet ﷺ, {{n:27|in the Year of the Elephant}}, resisted him for thirteen years, {{n:31|stoned his message}}, {{n:34|exiled him}}, and was conquered by him {{n:42|with almost no blood}} and total amnesty. His feelings on leaving are on record, addressed to the city itself: "by Allah, you are the best of Allah's earth, and the most beloved of Allah's earth to Allah; had I not been driven out of you, I would not have left" (Tirmidhi 3925, sahih). Guarded by angels from {{c:e-dajjal|the Dajjal}}, host of {{p:p-kaaba|the House}}, {{p:p-safa-marwah|the two hills}}, and {{p:p-hira|the cave of light}}: the mother of cities holds a third of the Codex inside her valley.

hadith.text: By Allah, you are the best of Allah's earth and the most beloved of Allah's earth to Allah; had I not been driven out of you, I would not have left.

p-madinah.role: The city that expels its dross
p-madinah.summary: Renamed by heaven, guarded at every pass, and loved with a du'a for double the blessing of Makkah.
p-madinah.details:
Yathrib died as a name the day {{n:37|the emigrant arrived}}; "it is Tabah," he ﷺ said, the good one, a city Allah renamed (Muslim 1385). Its charter of sanctity parallels its elder sister's: sacred between its two lava fields, its game and trees protected (Muslim 1362). Its purifying work never rests: "it is like the bellows, expelling its impurity and brightening its good" (Bukhari 1871), and in {{c:e-dajjal|the Dajjal's}} hour it will shake three times and shake the hypocrites out.

He ﷺ prayed for its increase: "O Allah, place in Madinah double the blessing You placed in {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}}" (Bukhari 1885), and taught the promise of patient residence: whoever endures its hardship, "I will be an intercessor or witness for him on the Day of Rising" (Muslim 1374, 1378). Angels hold its passes so that neither plague nor the Dajjal enters (Bukhari 1880). It received the {{n:34|Hijrah}}, ratified {{n:33|the pledges}}, built {{p:p-madinah-masjid|the mosque}}, buried {{n:46|the Prophet ﷺ}} and most of his companions in al-Baqi, and remains what he made it: the capital city of the sunnah, where dying is itself a du'a he taught {{c:c-umar|Umar}} to make.

hadith.text: Madinah is like the bellows: it expels its impurity and brightens its good.

p-taif.role: The city of stones that became a city of Islam
p-taif.summary: It bloodied the sandals of the best of creation; a generation later its children filled the mosques he hoped for.
p-taif.details:
A garden city on the heights south of {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}}, cool, walled, and proud, Ta'if received {{n:31|the Prophet's ﷺ quietest mission}} and returned the Seerah's cruelest afternoon: chiefs who mocked, and a street of slaves and boys set loose with stones until blood filled his sandals. In the orchard outside its wall he made {{w:w-taif-dua|the complaint of the weak}}, and above it he declined {{c:a-mountains|the Angel of the Mountains'}} offer with the hope that named this city's future: from their loins, worshippers of Allah alone.

The hope compounded fast. Ta'if sent its fighters against {{n:43|Hunayn}} and lost; the Muslims besieged its wall and lifted the siege with the du'a the city never knew it received: "O Allah, guide Thaqif and bring them" (Tirmidhi 3942). Within the year its delegation arrived, negotiated, submitted, and the idol of al-Lat was pulled down by the city's own hands. The boy who carried grapes to the bleeding Prophet in that orchard, Addas, had asked the right question a decade early. The Codex keeps Ta'if as the patron city of long games: nowhere in the Seerah is the distance between a wound and its healing measured so exactly.

facts.label: The return
facts.value: Delegation, within a year of Hunayn

hadith.text: O Allah, guide Thaqif and bring them.

p-jerusalem.role: Land of the prophets · Second of the sanctuaries' story
p-jerusalem.summary: Promised to Musa's people if they entered striving, opened to this ummah by a caliph on foot.
p-jerusalem.details:
The Qur'an calls its region "the land We blessed for the worlds" (21:71): {{n:9|Ibrahim's}} destination out of the fire, {{n:23|Maryam's}} chamber and Zakariya's mihrab, the holy land Musa's generation refused to enter and wandered forty years outside (5:21-26). At its heart stands {{p:p-aqsa|al-Aqsa}}, the second mosque placed on earth.

Its role in this ummah's story is a chain of solemn handovers: first qiblah; terminus of {{n:32|the Isra}}; opened without sack in the caliphate of {{c:c-umar|Umar}}, who entered leading his camel in turn with his servant and cleaned the neglected rock with his own garment; and named by the Prophet ﷺ among the six signs he told {{c:c-hudhayfah|the companions}} to count: "the conquest of Bayt al-Maqdis" (Bukhari 3176). The end of the story returns here as the beginning did: the era of {{n:56|Isa's justice}} runs through this land, and the hadith of the fitan calls it the land of the muster. The Codex holds al-Quds the way the tradition does: not as a prize but as an amanah, a trust whose keeping measures the ummah holding it.

facts.label: Opened
facts.value: By Umar, on foot, no sack

quran.en: We delivered him and Lut to the land We blessed for the worlds.

p-egypt.role: Stage of Yusuf's rise and Musa's exodus
p-egypt.summary: Granary of Yusuf, furnace of Bani Israel, and the estate Allah transferred overnight.
p-egypt.details:
Two of the Qur'an's longest dramas play out on Egypt's stage. {{n:13|Yusuf}} entered it in chains from the caravan, survived its palace and its prison, and rose over "the storehouses of the land" (12:55) to feed the region through seven locked years; his family's migration at his invitation planted Bani Israel by the {{p:p-nile|Nile}}. Generations later the hospitality had become {{n:15|a machinery of infanticide}}: "Pharaoh exalted himself in the land and made its people factions" (28:4).

Egypt then hosted the longest argument between heaven and a throne: nine signs, {{n:23|the duel of the magicians}} in which the professionals prostrated first, the plagues, and the night flight that ended at {{p:p-parted-sea|the sea}}. The estate transfer was recorded with the coldness of a deed: "how many gardens and springs they left behind… thus We caused another people to inherit them" (44:25-28). The Prophet ﷺ later commended Egypt to his ummah by kinship and covenant: be good to its people, "for they have protection (dhimmah) and kinship" (Muslim 2543), Hajar and Maryam's ties running through it. Opened under {{c:c-amr|Amr ibn al-As}}, it became a fortress of the religion, as it had been a fortress against it.

quran.en: Pharaoh called out among his people: O my people, does not the kingdom of Egypt belong to me…?

p-madyan.role: The refuge that hired the fugitive
p-madyan.summary: A well, two sisters, ten years of shepherd's wages: where Musa learned everything Pharaoh's palace never taught.
p-madyan.details:
Northwest Arabia's caravan country, home of {{n:16|the people Shu'ayb warned}} about scales and measures, and later the sanctuary where {{n:16|Musa}} arrived with nothing but the du'a of the emptied: "my Lord, I am, for whatever good You send down to me, in need" (28:24). Its well is the Qur'an's classic scene of strength serving instead of taking: the crowding shepherds, the two held-back sisters, the stranger who watered for them and asked for nothing.

The city's elder, often identified with Shu'ayb in tafsir though the Book leaves him unnamed, weighed the stranger on his daughter's two-word testimony, "the strong, the trustworthy" (26:26), and set the marriage terms as service: eight years, completed as ten. Madyan gave {{n:15|Musa}} what {{p:p-egypt|Egypt}} could not: obscurity, honest labor, a family, and a decade of flocks under open sky, the apprenticeship the Prophet ﷺ said every prophet served: "Allah sent no prophet but that he herded sheep" (Bukhari 2262). From its quiet the road led to {{p:p-tuwa|the burning tree}}. The Codex keeps Madyan as the geography of preparation: some places exist to make you ready for the place after them.

quran.en: My Lord, I am, for whatever good You send down to me, in need.

p-saba.role: Two gardens, one dam, and a queen
p-saba.summary: The kingdom the hoopoe reported, the throne that crossed the world, and the flood that repaid ingratitude.
p-saba.details:
Yemen's Saba was the Qur'an's showcase of engineered abundance: "two gardens, on the right and the left; eat of your Lord's provision and thank Him: a good land, and a forgiving Lord" (34:15). The great dam at Ma'rib watered a civilization; its queen ruled from "a mighty throne," and her people bowed to the sun until {{c:an-hoopoe|a bird}} brought the news that changed the kingdom's religion.

{{n:22|Sulayman's}} letter opened with Bismillah; the queen's counsel chose diplomacy over her generals' appetite; her throne arrived in his court before her, carried by "one with knowledge of the Book" in the return of a glance; and at the glass floor she surrendered her empire's error with the cleanest conversion formula in scripture: "my Lord, I have wronged myself, and I submit with Sulayman to Allah, Lord of the worlds" (27:44). Generations later the gratitude lapsed, and the reckoning came through the dam: "We sent upon them the flood of al-Arim" (34:16), two gardens reduced to thorn and tamarisk, a people scattered into a proverb. Saba's two stories, the queen's rise and the dam's fall, teach one law: kingdoms run on shukr, and fall when they withhold it.

facts.label: The queen
facts.value: Bilqis: converted at the glass floor

quran.en: My Lord, I have wronged myself, and I submit with Sulayman to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

p-babylon.role: City of the two angels' test
p-babylon.summary: Where sorcery was marketed under a prophet's name, and two angels taught with a warning label.
p-babylon.details:
Mesopotamia's ancient capital enters the Qur'an in exactly one verse, attached to exactly one story: "and what was sent down upon the two angels at Babylon, {{c:a-harut-marut|Harut and Marut}}" (2:102). In the generations after {{n:22|Sulayman}}, the shayatin retailed sorcery under his royal brand, claiming the great kingdom had run on magic; revelation cleared the prophet and located the test in this city, where the two angels taught no one without the disclaimer: we are only a fitnah, so do not disbelieve.

Babylon's broader biography in the tradition is the biography of organized bewilderment: the city of confounded tongues in the older scriptures' memory, of ziggurat ambition, of {{n:9|Nimrod's}} debate by the dominant tafsir geography, where a king answered "I give life and cause death" and was silenced by a sunrise. The Codex keeps one municipal lesson from it: every city sells some knowledge that costs the buyer his Hereafter, "and they knew that whoever purchased it has no share in the next life" (2:102). Babylon is merely the one city the verse names; the trade itself never closed.

quran.en: …and what was sent down upon the two angels at Babylon, Harut and Marut.

p-badr.summary: A watering stop on the caravan road where 313 met a thousand, and the angels wore turbans.
p-badr.details:
Badr was nothing before 2 AH: wells, a market season, a stop on the Syria road southwest of {{p:p-madinah|Madinah}}. Then two columns converged on its water, and the place became a word: "the day of the criterion, the day the two forces met" (8:41). At these wells {{n:38|the 313}} camped by the counsel of a companion who asked whether the position was revelation or war-craft, and the rain firmed the sand under their feet.

Here the Prophet ﷺ stretched his hands until his cloak fell, {{c:a-badr|a thousand angels}} arrived "following one another" (8:9), and the chiefs of Quraysh who had tortured the weak of {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}} were laid in one of its dry pits, their Prophet standing over it at night asking whether they had found their Lord's promise true. The men of this field became Islam's aristocracy: "perhaps Allah looked upon the people of Badr and said: do as you wish, for I have forgiven you" (Bukhari 3007), the sentence that saved a man's gravest slip. The Codex marks the site as the Path's proof that geography is made by what obedience does on it: wells, then a criterion.

quran.en: Allah had already given you victory at Badr while you were few.

p-hudaybiyyah.role: The tree of the pledge · The clear victory
p-hudaybiyyah.summary: A dry campsite at the sanctuary's edge where a stalled pilgrimage became the treaty that won the world.
p-hudaybiyyah.details:
On the edge of the Haram west of {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}}, al-Qaswa knelt and would not rise, and the Prophet ﷺ read her: "the One who held back the elephant has held her back" (Bukhari 2731). At this campsite of little water, which his ﷺ arrow-stirred well made abundant, the ummah's hardest diplomatic hour played out: {{n:41|the treaty}} whose clauses read like defeat and computed like conquest.

Under an acacia here, on the rumor of {{c:c-uthman|Uthman's}} death, some 1,400 hands took {{n:41|the Pledge of Ridwan}}, and heaven declared its verdict: "Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree" (48:18), with the seal no court can lift: "none who pledged under the tree will enter the Fire" (Muslim 2496). The campsite's name now titles the whole story: on the road home Surah al-Fath descended, "indeed We have granted you a clear opening" (48:1), dearer to him ﷺ than all the sun rises on. {{c:c-umar|Umar}} later removed the tree's successor from veneration; the pledge was to Allah, not to wood. The Codex keeps Hudaybiyyah as the geography of patience: the site where losing the argument won the era.

facts.label: Al-Qaswa
facts.value: Knelt, read as the elephant's kneeling

facts.label: Named by
facts.value: Surah al-Fath, on the road home

quran.en: Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you under the tree.

p-khaybar.summary: Eight strongholds, a banner given to the one Allah loves, and a gate that became a byword for strength.
p-khaybar.details:
North of {{p:p-madinah|Madinah}}, Khaybar's volcanic ridges carried the strongest fortress chain in the Hijaz, and the wealth that had bankrolled {{n:40|the Confederates}}. In 7 AH, after {{n:41|Hudaybiyyah}} froze the southern front, the Prophet ﷺ marched at dawn and gave the siege its rule of engagement mercy-first: when he heard the morning adhan rise from a settlement he held back the attack.

Fortress by fortress the oasis closed, until the day he announced: "tomorrow I will give the banner to a man who loves Allah and His Messenger, and whom Allah and His Messenger love." The camp barely slept; {{c:c-ali|Ali}} was summoned from an eye ailment, cured by the Prophet's own spittle, and instructed that one man guided through him outweighed red camels (Bukhari 3701, Muslim 2406).
