Khaybar fell, its lands settled by treaty on half-shares, and its aftermath threaded the Seerah: {{c:c-safiyyah|Safiyyah}} became a mother of the believers, the poisoned sheep tested at its table left its long mark, and {{c:c-jafar|Ja'far}} arrived from Abyssinia the same day, doubling one joy with another. The Codex keeps Khaybar as the geography of the banner: the strongholds were bound to fall; the declaration of love was the news.

hadith.text: Tomorrow I will give the banner to a man who loves Allah and His Messenger, and whom Allah and His Messenger love.

p-hunayn.summary: A dawn ambush between rock walls taught the largest Muslim army ever mustered where victory is stored.
p-hunayn.details:
A stony defile on the road from {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}} to {{p:p-taif|Ta'if}}, Hunayn was chosen by Malik ibn Awf precisely for what it does to a column: compresses it, blinds its flanks, and hands the high walls to whoever arrives first. Into it at first light marched {{n:43|twelve thousand}}, the largest force Islam had fielded, carrying the one supply the Qur'an later confiscated: "your great number pleased you, but it availed you nothing, and the earth, vast as it is, narrowed upon you" (9:25).

The arrow-storm broke the vanguard; the valley became a river running backward; and the battle contracted to the width of one mule: the Prophet ﷺ pressing forward alone, announcing himself in verse, {{c:c-abbas|Abbas's}} great voice recalling the men of the tree. The reversal came as reinforcement of the unseen: "then Allah sent down His tranquility upon His Messenger and upon the believers, and sent down soldiers you did not see" (9:26). Hawazin's camp, herds, and captives fell entire, and at Ji'ranah the captives went home free. The Codex maps Hunayn as the humbling of confidence: the one valley where the ummah's largest army met its smallest hour, and learned again where victory is stored.

quran.en: …and on the day of Hunayn, when your great number pleased you, but it availed you nothing.

p-tabuk.role: The far frontier of the hour of hardship
p-tabuk.summary: Six hundred miles of summer for a battle that never happened, and the sorting of every heart that marched or stayed.
p-tabuk.details:
On the Syrian frontier, twenty nights' march north of {{p:p-madinah|Madinah}}, Tabuk was {{n:44|the destination announced openly}} for the only time in the Prophet's ﷺ campaigns: the distance and the season allowed no ambiguity. High summer, ripe orchards left behind, and a Byzantine rumor ahead: the expedition existed, the Qur'an says, to weigh hearts, and it weighed them publicly. {{c:c-uthman|Uthman}} poured out a fortune; weepers were turned away for lack of mounts; the excuse-makers manufactured fatwas about the heat and were answered from heaven: "the fire of Jahannam is more intense in heat" (9:81).

At the wells of Tabuk the army camped twenty days, signed the frontier treaties, and fought no one; the sorting was the campaign. On the road back stood the mosque of harm, demolished by revelation's order, and ahead lay the fifty days of {{c:c-kab|Ka'b's}} silence until forgiveness descended. Passing al-Hijr's ruins the Prophet covered his face and commanded tears or haste. The Codex keeps Tabuk as the geography of cost: the place itself did nothing; the road to it did everything.

quran.en: They said: do not march in the heat. Say: the fire of Jahannam is more intense in heat.

p-zamzam.role: The spring that answered a mother
p-zamzam.summary: Struck open by an angel for a crying infant; still flowing, still drunk for whatever it is drunk for.
p-zamzam.details:
When Hajar's waterskin emptied in the valley with no vegetation, and {{p:p-safa-marwah|her seventh crossing}} ended, the angel struck the ground by the infant {{n:11|Isma'il}}, and water rose where the earth was driest. The Prophet ﷺ replayed the scene with affection and a counterfactual: "may Allah have mercy on the mother of Isma'il; had she left it, Zamzam would have been a flowing spring" (Bukhari 3364). Her practical instinct, walling the water with her hands, contained the spring into a well, and the well built the city: caravans settled by the water, and {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}} exists because a mother trusted and a baby cried.

Its water washed {{n:28|the Prophet's chest}} before the ascent; his grandfather's rediscovery of the buried well restored his house's honor; and his ﷺ standing verdict grades it beyond geology: "it is blessed; it is food that satisfies" (Muslim 2473), with the sunan adding: "and a cure for illness." The ummah drinks it standing or seated, facing the House, asking, on the report that "the water of Zamzam is for whatever it is drunk for" (Ibn Majah 3062, hasan). Four millennia of pilgrims have not emptied a well opened for one child's thirst.

hadith.text: It is blessed; it is food that satisfies.

p-nile.role: The river that carried a basket
p-nile.summary: Pharaoh taxed it as his own; heaven used it as a courier for the infant who would end him.
p-nile.details:
"Does not the kingdom of {{p:p-egypt|Egypt}} belong to me, and these rivers flowing beneath me?" (43:51): Pharaoh's title deed to the Nile was the centerpiece of his theology. The river he claimed was already under contract to the other side. On its current traveled {{n:15|the basket}}, steered past crocodiles and currents into the one dock in Egypt where the state's infanticide could not reach: the tyrant's own bathing steps, into the arms of Asiya.

The Qur'an's staging of the Nile is deliberate irony throughout: the river of the boast becomes the road of the rescue; the water that received murdered infants delivers the avenger of the infants; and when the argument ends, water again gives the verdict, {{p:p-parted-sea|a sea standing in walls}} and closing. The tradition adds the epilogue of ownership: in Umar's caliphate, Egypt's old custom of adorning a bride for the river was answered with a note thrown into the current, addressing the Nile as a servant: if you flowed from yourself, do not flow; if Allah makes you flow, flow. It has flowed since. Rivers, the story concludes, have one Owner, and He lends them to no throne.

quran.en: When you fear for him, cast him into the river, and do not fear and do not grieve.

p-parted-sea.summary: Struck once with a staff: each side a mountain, a nation between them, and the pursuit sealed behind.
p-parted-sea.details:
At the dead end of the exodus, army behind and water ahead, the panicked arithmetic of Bani Israel ("we are surely overtaken") met {{n:18|Musa's}} certainty: {{w:w-inna-maiya|"no indeed; my Lord is with me; He will guide me"}} (26:62). The command was one strike of the staff, and the physics of the planet stepped aside: "it parted, and each portion was like a great towering mountain" (26:63), corridors of seabed walled with standing water.

A nation crossed between the water-walls; the pursuit entered the same corridors and received the other half of the miracle: the walls dismissed. "And We drowned the others" (26:66). {{n:19|Pharaoh's}} last-second faith was refused; his body was kept as a sign. The Prophet ﷺ bound this water into the ummah's calendar on arrival in {{p:p-madinah|Madinah}}: finding Ashura fasted for the deliverance, he said "we have more right to {{n:15|Musa}} than you," fasted it, and commanded it (Bukhari 2004). Every Ashura fast since is this sea's anniversary. The Codex keeps the site unnamed on the map, as the Book left it: the coordinates that matter are "my Lord is with me," reachable from anywhere.

quran.en: It parted, and each portion was like a great towering mountain.

p-tuwa.summary: A nameless mountainside valley, twice called sacred by its Owner, where a shepherd was commissioned against an empire.
p-tuwa.details:
Tuwa is the Qur'an's smallest sanctified geography: a valley by {{p:p-tur|the Mount}}, unknown to any map of pilgrimage, sacred for one reason only: what was said there. "Indeed, I am your Lord, so remove your sandals; you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa" (20:12). The command established the etiquette of holy ground for all scripture: the place where Allah speaks is entered barefoot.

Here {{n:17|Musa}} came for an ember and left with a mission; here the two signs were issued, {{c:an-staff|the staff}} and the white hand; here the assignment "go to Pharaoh, he has transgressed" (20:24) was answered with the du'a of the overwhelmed, {{w:w-rabbishrah|"my Lord, expand for me my chest"}}, and granted in full. The valley is invoked again in Surah an-Nazi'at as the site of the summons (79:16), a double mention for a place with no shrine, no rite, and no address. The Codex maps Tuwa as the theology of place perfected: ground is made sacred by the word spoken on it, and a burning tree in a nameless valley outranks every palace on the planet.

facts.label: Address
facts.value: None; the word is the address

quran.en: Indeed, I am your Lord, so remove your sandals; you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa.

p-tiberias.summary: A chained giant asks sailors about its water level; the hordes will one day drink it dry.
p-tiberias.details:
The freshwater lake of the Jordan valley carries the strangest duty in the Codex's geography: it is the Hereafter's water gauge. In the hadith of {{c:e-jassasa|al-Jassasah}} (Muslim 2942), the shackled colossus on the island questions Tamim's crew sign by sign: tell me about the lake of Tiberias, does it hold water? It does, they said. He said: its water is about to go. {{c:e-dajjal|The chained one}} tracks his release against a shoreline.

The second prophecy drains it entirely: when {{n:57|Yajuj and Majuj}} pour down "from every height," Muslim 2937 records their vanguard passing the lake and drinking it, so that the rearguard arrives and says: there was once water here. A body of water assigned two cameo roles across two hadith, both as a countdown instrument. The Codex keeps Tiberias on the map for the discipline it teaches about signs: the end of time is not scheduled in riddles only; some of its clocks are ordinary places, checkable by anyone, which is precisely why the tradition named them. Water levels, like hearts, are being read.

hadith.text: Their first ranks pass the lake of Tiberias and drink what is in it, and the last of them pass and say: there was once water here.

p-euphrates.role: The river hiding a mountain of gold
p-euphrates.summary: One of the rivers of mercy in the hadith, and the site of the last gold rush, which the wise are ordered to skip.
p-euphrates.details:
Mesopotamia's great river carries two entries in the sound tradition, one gentle and one grim. The gentle: on {{n:32|the Night Journey}} the Prophet ﷺ saw four rivers issuing from the base of the Lote Tree, "two hidden and two apparent," and the two apparent were identified as the {{p:p-nile|Nile}} and the Euphrates (Muslim 164): rivers of this world honored with a heavenly source-marking, which the scholars read as blessing, not plumbing.

The grim entry is a checkable prophecy: "the Hour will not rise until the Euphrates uncovers a mountain of gold, over which the people will fight, and of every hundred, ninety-nine will be killed, each of them saying: perhaps I will be the one who survives" (Bukhari 7119, Muslim 2894). The instruction attached is rare in eschatology, a direct order for the finder: "whoever is present, let him take nothing from it." A retreating river, an exposed treasure, and a fatality rate of ninety-nine percent driven by one sentence of private optimism. {{n:53|The minor signs node}} carries it in sequence; the Codex maps the river itself as the tradition's monument to the last thing the dying world will fight over, and the first thing the believer is told to walk past.

hadith.text: The Hour will not rise until the Euphrates uncovers a mountain of gold over which the people fight… whoever is present, let him take nothing from it.

p-damascus-minaret.role: The landing site of the Descent
p-damascus-minaret.summary: The one address in eschatology named down to the meter: east of Damascus, at dawn, mid-iqamah.
p-damascus-minaret.details:
Prophecy is usually a compass; here it is a street address. "He will descend at the white minaret, east of Damascus, in two saffron garments, his hands resting on the wings of two angels" (Muslim 2937). Sham holds the ummah's end-time capital in the sound corpus: the Prophet ﷺ prayed for its blessing, "O Allah, bless us in our Sham" (Bukhari 1037), called it the land of the muster, and located the final believers' cohesion there: "a party of my ummah will remain manifest upon the truth… and they are in Sham" (Muslim 1924, with Bukhari 3641 unlocated).

The scene the minaret anchors is {{n:56|the Descent}}: Fajr assembled, the iqamah called, {{c:e-mahdi|the imam}} stepping back, and {{c:e-isa-return|the son of Maryam}} declining the mihrab to pray as a follower. From this coordinate the pursuit runs south to {{p:p-ludd|Ludd}}. Damascus's Umayyad mosque has carried a white minaret named for {{n:23|Isa}} for centuries; the Codex, like the careful scholars, pins its certainty to the hadith's words rather than to any current structure: the address is guaranteed; the architecture will be there when needed.

hadith.text: He will descend at the white minaret east of Damascus… his hands on the wings of two angels.

p-ludd.summary: A town gate in Palestine, named fourteen centuries early as the coordinates of the Dajjal's death.
p-ludd.details:
Ludd, ancient Lydda on the Palestinian plain, would be an unremarkable dot on the Codex's map except for one appointment fixed in Sahih Muslim: "the son of Maryam will pursue him and overtake him at the gate of Ludd, and kill him" (Muslim 2937). The longest-running fraud in history, {{c:e-dajjal|the one-eyed claimant}} with his mountains of bread and his inverted paradise, ends at a specific municipal gate.

The staging is deliberate humiliation by geography: the being who claimed divinity over the whole earth is run down at the edge of a small town, dissolving "as salt dissolves in water" at the true {{c:e-isa-return|Masih's}} breath, finished on a spear whose blood is shown to the believers as evidence. The scholars savored the symmetry: the false messiah dies within sight of the land where the true one's story began, in the blessed region his fraud parodied. For the Codex's reader the gate teaches the end-times' deepest comfort in one image: deception was given the address of its death before the deceiver was ever released. Every lie, this map says, is pre-assigned its gate.

hadith.text: The son of Maryam will overtake him at the gate of Ludd and kill him.

p-bayda.role: Where an army enters the earth
p-bayda.summary: A featureless stretch between Makkah and Madinah appointed for one future event: the swallowing of an army.
p-bayda.details:
Al-Bayda is the tradition's name for open, empty ground on the {{p:p-makkah|Makkah}} road, and one future event stands written against it, recorded from {{c:c-umm-salamah|Umm Salamah}} in Sahih Muslim: an army will march against the House to seize {{c:e-mahdi|a man taking refuge}} there, "and when they are at a bayda of the earth, it will swallow their first and their last" (Muslim 2882).

The Prophet's ﷺ questioner asked the enduring legal question: among them are the coerced and the mere traveler who joined the road. The answer wrote the jurisprudence of company forever: "they are swallowed together, then raised on the Day of Rising according to their intentions." The ground makes no exceptions; the resurrection does the sorting. The Codex has met this verb before, under {{n:61|Qarun's house}} and in the three landslides of the Ten, but al-Bayda's entry is the most exact: one plain, one army, one swallowing. As with {{p:p-ludd|Ludd}}, the map's lesson is jurisdictional: the earth is not neutral terrain in the last days; it is deputized. Choose your caravan, the plain advises, as carefully as your creed.

hadith.text: When they are at a bayda of the earth, it will swallow their first and their last… then they are raised according to their intentions.

p-mahshar.role: The white plain of the Standing
p-mahshar.summary: Not any country: a new earth, flat as pressed flour, with no landmark for anyone to claim.
p-mahshar.details:
The last place every human being will stand is a place none has seen. "The Day the earth will be exchanged for another earth, and the heavens" (14:48): the Prophet ﷺ described the replacement surface with a baker's image: "mankind will be gathered on a white plain, tinged with redness, like a pure wheat loaf, with no landmark on it for anyone" (Bukhari 6521, Muslim 2790).

No landmark for anyone: the phrase carries the theology. No hill to rally at, no border to defend, no monument to hide behind, no address to inherit; the geography of privilege abolished by resurfacing. Toward this plain {{n:63|the fire drives}} the last generation, "and Sham is the land of the muster" in the direction-language of this world's map; on it {{n:66|the sun descends to a mile}}, the sweat rises by deeds, and the only elevations are moral: the shade of the Throne, the pulpits of light for the just, the high ground of {{w:w-subhan|remembered words}}. The Codex ends its atlas here deliberately: every place in these five sections was a test or a mercy; the last place is only a floor, and what stands tall on it arrives inside the standing people.

quran.en: The Day the earth will be exchanged for another earth, and the heavens…

hadith.text: Mankind will be gathered on a white plain tinged with redness, like a pure loaf, with no landmark on it for anyone.

w-hasbunallah.meaning: Allah is sufficient for us, and the best Disposer of affairs
w-hasbunallah.summary: Said by Ibrahim flying toward the fire, and by Muhammad ﷺ facing the gathered confederates.
w-hasbunallah.details:
One sentence, two prophets, twenty-five centuries apart. {{c:c-ibnabbas|Ibn Abbas}} certified the chain: "{{n:9|Ibrahim}} said it when he was cast into the fire, and Muhammad ﷺ said it when they said: the people have gathered against you, so fear them; and it only increased them in faith" (Bukhari 4563). It is the believer's response to superior force: not a denial of the odds, but the handing of the whole matter to its best Disposer. The fire was commanded to cool; the confederates were scattered by wind.

The Prophet ﷺ prescribed it forward as well: when {{c:a-israfil|the bearer of the Horn}} was described inclined and waiting, the companions asked what they could possibly say in the face of that; he answered: "say: hasbunallahu wa ni'mal-wakil" (Tirmidhi 2431). The sentence stretches unchanged from a burning pyre to the end of the universe.
whenNow: At any news that outnumbers you: gathered enemies, bad diagnoses, impossible odds
When fear is being marketed to you: the verse's own context (3:173)
Facing the unknown scale of the Last Day, by his ﷺ instruction

quran.en: Those to whom people said: the people have gathered against you, so fear them; but it increased them in faith, and they said: Allah is sufficient for us, and the best Disposer of affairs.

hadith.text: Ibrahim said it when he was thrown into the fire, and Muhammad ﷺ said it when they said: the people have gathered against you.

w-dhunnun.translit: La ilaha illa anta, subhanaka, inni kuntu minaz-zalimin
w-dhunnun.meaning: None has the right to be worshipped but You; glory be to You; I have been of the wrongdoers
w-dhunnun.role: The key that opens from inside the whale
w-dhunnun.summary: Three clauses in triple darkness; the Prophet ﷺ guaranteed the formula for every Muslim who uses it.
w-dhunnun.details:
Inside {{c:an-yunus|the whale}}, in the darkness of night, sea, and belly, {{n:23|Yunus}} built the only exit that existed: tawhid, tanzih, and confession, in that order. None but You; You are perfect; the fault is mine. The Qur'an states the mechanism and generalizes it in the same breath: "so We responded to him and saved him from the distress; and thus do We save the believers" (21:88). Thus: the same way, every time.

The Prophet ﷺ turned the verse's promise into an explicit guarantee: "the supplication of Dhun-Nun when he called in the belly of the whale... no Muslim ever supplicates with it for anything except that Allah answers him" (Tirmidhi 3505, sahih). The scholars noted the engineering: the du'a contains no request at all. It repairs the relationship, and the rescue follows as a consequence. Whoever cannot find words for what he needs can say the three clauses that fit every case unchanged.
whenNow: In any distress, by the explicit guarantee of Tirmidhi 3505
When guilt blocks asking: the formula confesses first and asks nothing
In the personal darknesses: grief, debt, illness, the closed room

quran.en: He called out in the darknesses: none has the right to be worshipped but You; glory be to You; I have been of the wrongdoers. So We responded to him.

hadith.text: No Muslim supplicates with it for anything except that Allah answers him.

w-rabbana-zalamna.translit: Rabbana zalamna anfusana wa il-lam taghfir lana wa tarhamna lanakunanna minal-khasirin
w-rabbana-zalamna.meaning: Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves; if You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will surely be among the losers
w-rabbana-zalamna.summary: The sentence Adam and Hawwa said together at the bottom of the first fall; the template of every tawbah since.
w-rabbana-zalamna.details:
After the slip in the Garden, "{{n:2|Adam}} received from his Lord words, and He accepted his repentance" (2:37): heaven did not only forgive the first sin, it supplied the vocabulary for its confession. The words themselves stand in 7:23, spoken in the dual, by {{n:3|both of them together}}: no blame traded, no whisperer scapegoated, though the whisperer was real.

The anatomy is the permanent template. Ownership first: we wronged ourselves. Dependence second: if You do not forgive us. Realism third: we will surely be among the losers; no plan B is proposed. Compare it, the scholars say, with {{c:j-iblis|Iblis's}} response to his own fall in the same surah: argument, blame, and a request for respite to harm others. Two falls, two scripts, two destinies. Every child of Adam re-enacts one of them after every sin, and the Codex keeps the winning script exactly where a reader in the middle of a bad night can copy it.
whenNow: Immediately after any sin: the first words, before the mood hardens
In sujud and between the adhan and iqamah, the hours of acceptance
Together with a spouse after shared wrong: the original was said in the dual

quran.en: They both said: our Lord, we have wronged ourselves; if You do not forgive us and have mercy on us, we will surely be among the losers.

w-bismillah-majreha.titleEn: The Word that Sailed the Ark
w-bismillah-majreha.meaning: In the name of Allah is its course and its anchorage
w-bismillah-majreha.summary: Nuh's boarding announcement over waves like mountains: journeys run on the Name, not the hull.
w-bismillah-majreha.details:
As the water rose and the animals filed aboard, {{n:6|Nuh}} declared what the ship would sail on: "board it; in the name of Allah is its course and its anchorage" (11:41). Course and anchorage: the going and the stopping, both entrusted to the Name before the first wave hit. The hull was gopher-wood and pitch; the seaworthiness was bismillah. {{n:7|Waves like mountains}} tested exactly that claim and confirmed it.

The ummah inherited the physics. The Prophet ﷺ taught the mount-boarding du'a from the same theology, "glory to Him who subjected this to us, and we could not have subdued it" (43:13), and the tradition kept Nuh's own formula alive for embarkations. The scholars read the verse wide: every project is a vessel, every beginning a boarding. Whoever launches a marriage, a business, a book, or a hijrah needs one flood-tested word, and only one. The Codex sets this word beside its counter-example from the same flood: the son who chose {{n:7|a mountain instead of the Name}}, and the verse's cold arithmetic of that choice.
whenNow: Boarding any vehicle: car, ship, plane; the sunnah's travel dhikr family
Launching any undertaking: the course and the anchorage assigned in advance
Teaching children their first travel word: the ummah's oldest boarding pass

quran.en: He said: board it; in the name of Allah is its course and its anchorage. Indeed my Lord is Forgiving, Merciful.

w-rabbi-inni.translit: Rabbi inni lima anzalta ilayya min khayrin faqir
w-rabbi-inni.meaning: My Lord, I am, for whatever good You send down to me, in need
w-rabbi-inni.summary: Musa at the well of Madyan: no money, no country, no request line, and everything granted within the hour.
w-rabbi-inni.details:
A fugitive with a death warrant behind him and a desert ahead, {{n:16|Musa}} watered two strangers' flock, walked to the shade, and produced the most dignified request for help ever recorded: a description of himself, addressed to his Lord, with the request line left blank (28:24). Whatever good You send: food, work, family, safety; the beggar declines to narrow the field.

The response furnished his whole life within the scene: employment, a household, a decade of training in {{p:p-madyan|Madyan}}, all walking toward him behind one shy woman. The scholars extract the adab: he named his poverty, not his preferences; he asked the Owner, not the crowd; and he had just worked for free, so his ask stood on service, not entitlement. The Codex keeps this word for everyone at the bottom of a move, a loss, or a restart: the Path's proof that heaven reads unfinished sentences, and prefers them.
whenNow: At any restart from nothing: new city, lost job, emptied savings
After serving someone with no wage in sight: the du'a stands on service
When you no longer know what to ask for: leave the field open, as he did

quran.en: My Lord, I am, for whatever good You send down to me, in need.

w-rabbishrah.translit: Rabbi-shrah li sadri, wa yassir li amri, wahlul uqdatan min lisani, yafqahu qawli
w-rabbishrah.meaning: My Lord, expand for me my chest, ease for me my affair, and untie the knot from my tongue, that they may understand my speech
w-rabbishrah.role: The prayer before the impossible task
w-rabbishrah.summary: Assigned to Pharaoh at the burning tree, Musa asked for capacity, ease, clarity, and a partner; all granted in one sentence.
w-rabbishrah.details:
The assignment at {{p:p-tuwa|Tuwa}} was four words: go to Pharaoh (20:24). The response is the believer's template for every oversized task: not refusal, not bravado, but a naming of needs. Breadth: expand my chest. Ease: ease my affair. Clear speech: untie my tongue. A partner: {{n:17|Harun}}, my brother. Heaven's reply compressed all grants into one line: "you have been given your request, O {{n:15|Musa}}" (20:36).

The Prophet ﷺ stood in this du'a's lineage; the expansion Musa asked for, his ummah's founder was given as surgery and as verse: "did We not expand for you your chest?" (94:1). Teachers, khatibs, parents, and anyone walking into a room bigger than their courage have used the four clauses since. The Codex notes the deep adab: Musa did not ask for the task to shrink; he asked for himself to be enlarged. The mission stayed the same size. He grew.
whenNow: Before any speech, class, interview, or hard conversation
On receiving an assignment beyond your size: ask to be enlarged, not excused
When bringing a partner into your work, on Musa's precedent

quran.en: My Lord, expand for me my chest, ease for me my affair, and untie the knot from my tongue, that they may understand my speech.

w-inna-maiya.meaning: No indeed; my Lord is with me; He will guide me
w-inna-maiya.summary: Sea ahead, army behind, a nation panicking: Musa's answer arrived one verse before the road did.
w-inna-maiya.details:
At {{p:p-parted-sea|the water's edge}} the two companies sighted each other, and Bani Israel ran the numbers aloud: "we are surely overtaken" (26:61). {{n:18|Musa's}} reply is the Qur'an's cleanest specimen of iman under pressure: one refusal, one fact, one forecast. Kalla: no indeed, the premise itself rejected. Inna ma'iya rabbi: the fact that redraws every map. Sayahdin: He will guide me, future tense, spoken before any road existed. The next verse issued the road.

The Codex pairs it with its twin from {{n:34|the cave}}: "do not grieve, indeed Allah is with us" (9:40). Two dead ends, two sentences of ma'iyyah, two impossible exits: the sea stood up, and the searchers went blind at the cave mouth. The scholars distinguish the two intimacies: the general withness of knowledge over all creation, and this special withness of help for whoever stands where obedience put him. The word is for the second: whoever is cornered on the road of obedience may say the sentence with its promise intact.
whenNow: At the cornered moment when the numbers are simply true and still not final
Against the crowd's panic arithmetic: kalla is a complete sentence
Waiting for a road that does not exist yet: sayahdin is future tense on purpose

quran.en: He said: no indeed; my Lord is with me; He will guide me.

w-la-tahzan.meaning: Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us
w-la-tahzan.summary: Whispered to one frightened friend under a hundred hunting feet, then bequeathed to every afraid believer since.
w-la-tahzan.details:
In {{p:p-thawr|the cave}}, with the search party's feet visible from the dark, {{c:c-abubakr|Abu Bakr's}} fear was for his companion, not himself. The reassurance he received became scripture: "do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us" (9:40), and in Bukhari's wording a question that ended the mathematics of danger: "what do you think, O Abu Bakr, of two, Allah is their third?"

The grammar rewards attention: la tahzan addresses grief, not the enemy; the danger is not denied, it is outranked. And the basis is not a prediction ("we will escape") but a presence ("Allah is with us"): true even if they had been found, which is why the sentence never expires. The Codex keeps it beside {{w:w-inna-maiya|Musa's kalla}} as the second of the two great ma'iyyah sentences, and notes where else the Book deploys the phrase: to the Prophet at large, "do not grieve over them" (16:127), and to every believer against the whisperer's sorrow-campaigns, "grief is only from shaytan... and in Allah let the believers put their trust" (58:10).
whenNow: To a frightened friend: its first use, comfort handed down with its promise intact
In hiding, waiting, or pursuit of any kind: the third of every two is unchanged
Against engineered sadness: 58:10 names grief as a weapon; this word disarms it

quran.en: When he said to his companion: do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us.

hadith.text: What do you think, O Abu Bakr, of two, Allah is their third?

w-taif-dua.translit: Allahumma ilayka ashku da'fa quwwati, wa qillata hilati, wa hawani 'alan-nas
w-taif-dua.meaning: O Allah, to You I complain of my weakness, my scarcity of means, and my insignificance before people
w-taif-dua.role: The prayer of the worst day
w-taif-dua.summary: Bleeding outside Ta'if's wall, the Prophet ﷺ weighed only one thing: whether his Lord was displeased.
w-taif-dua.details:
After {{n:31|the stoning at Ta'if}}, in Utbah's orchard with blood reaching his sandals, the Prophet ﷺ raised the complaint the sirah has preserved as the ummah's inheritance in catastrophe. Its clauses name the need honestly: weakness, scarcity, insignificance. Its pivot is the question that reorders every disaster: "if You are not angry with me, I do not care." And its refuge is total: "I seek refuge in the light of Your Face... to You belongs all appeal until You are pleased."

The report reaches us through the sirah literature (at-Tabarani; the chain is graded weak by the muhaddithin, and the Codex says so), but its acceptance among the scholars of the heart is ancient, and the day itself is anchored in the Sahih: {{c:c-aisha|Aisha}} asked about the hardest day, and he named {{n:31|the day of Ta'if}}, answered at last by {{c:a-mountains|the Angel of the Mountains}} (Bukhari 3231). Heaven's reply to this complaint is on the record: an angel awaiting orders, and a prophet choosing mercy. Whoever prays these words is in the safest lineage of the broken.
whenNow: On the day people's contempt is the wound: hawani 'alan-nas names it
When strength, means, and status all fail at once: the honest admission
When one question matters more than rescue: are You pleased with me?

facts.label: Day
facts.value: The hardest, by his ﷺ word

facts.label: Pivot
facts.value: “If You are not angry, I do not care”

hadith.text: Aisha asked: was there a day harder than Uhud? He said: I met from your people what I met, and the hardest was the day of Aqabah (Ta'if).

w-sallim.meaning: O Allah, bring them through safely, bring them through
w-sallim.role: The prophets' entire vocabulary at the bridge
w-sallim.summary: On the Sirat, over the Fire, the messengers who split seas will be saying two words on behalf of the crossers.
w-sallim.details:
When {{n:70|the bridge}} is laid over Jahannam's back, sharper than a sword, hooked with sa'dan thorns, crossed at the speed of deeds, the sound tradition records the only speech on it: "none speaks that day but the messengers, and the du'a of the messengers is: Allahumma sallim, sallim" (Bukhari 806, Muslim 182). The men who stood before Pharaoh, cooled in the fire, and fed multitudes from a handful are reduced, at that crossing, to two words, repeated, for others.

The Codex keeps this word for two disciplines. First, proportion: whoever wants to know the Sirat's gravity should weigh what it does to the vocabulary of prophets. Second, direction: even at the rail of the Fire, the prophetic instinct is intercession, sallim for the crossers, not commentary on the falling. The ummah rehearses the word every time it prays for safety in this world's crossings; the full performance is scheduled over the Fire, and the wise pack light for it: light is earned now, "their light running before them" (57:12).
whenNow: At every dangerous crossing of this world: roads, surgeries, verdicts
Praying for others in peril: the prophetic instinct at the rail
Remembering the bridge in comfort: the word keeps the crossing real

hadith.text: None speaks that day but the messengers, and the du'a of the messengers is: O Allah, bring through, bring through.

w-subhan.meaning: Glory to Allah and praise Him; glory to Allah the Magnificent
w-subhan.summary: Light on the tongue, heavy on the Scale, beloved to the Most Merciful: the closing hadith of Sahih al-Bukhari.
w-subhan.details:
Imam al-Bukhari sealed his entire Sahih, seven thousand hadith of law, war, and revelation, with this one: "two words, light on the tongue, heavy on the Scale, beloved to the Most Merciful: subhanallahi wa bihamdih, subhanallahil-azim" (Bukhari 7563, Muslim 2694). The scholars read the placement as the muhaddith's last word on what a life is for.

At {{n:69|the Mizan}}, where a mustard seed is admissible evidence, density matters more than volume, and these clauses are the tradition's densest alloy: tanzih (He is beyond flaw) fused with hamd (He is owed praise), twice, in different registers. The rewards around them are published: whoever says subhanallahi wa bihamdih a hundred times a day has his sins removed though they be like the sea's foam (Bukhari 6405); a palm is planted in Jannah for each saying (Tirmidhi 3464). The Codex keeps this word where the reader can reach it in traffic: the heaviest weight on the Scale costs four seconds of the tongue.
whenNow: A hundred times a day: sea-foam clause (Bukhari 6405)
In the dead minutes: queues, traffic, kettle-time; the deed fits anywhere
As a settled morning-evening anchor with the other adhkar

hadith.text: Two words, light on the tongue, heavy on the Scale, beloved to the Most Merciful: subhanallahi wa bihamdih, subhanallahil-azim.

w-shahada.meaning: None has the right to be worshipped but Allah; Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah
w-shahada.summary: The best thing said by him ﷺ and the prophets before him; the card that outweighs ninety-nine scrolls.
w-shahada.details:
Every node of the Path is this sentence in costume. It is what {{n:9|Ibrahim}} argued from the stars, what {{n:30|Iqra's}} garment-wrapped man rose to announce, what {{n:42|the Opening}} installed over the emptied idols, and what {{c:c-bilal|Bilal}} compressed under the boulder into Ahad, Ahad. The Prophet ﷺ ranked it at {{p:p-arafat|Arafat}}: "the best of what I and the prophets before me have said is: la ilaha illallah, alone, without partner" (Muwatta; Tirmidhi 3585).

Its performance at {{n:69|the Scale}} is documented in the bitaqa hadith: ninety-nine scrolls of sin against one card bearing the two testimonies, "and the scrolls fly up, and the card outweighs; nothing outweighs the name of Allah" (Tirmidhi 2639, sahih). Its performance at the deathbed is commissioned in advance: "whoever's last words are la ilaha illallah enters Jannah" (Abu {{n:21|Dawud}} 3116). The Codex's whole architecture, sixty-four tiles and every seal, is commentary; this word is the text.
whenNow: Renewing iman in the ordinary afternoon: the best dhikr outright
Teaching it as the first sentence and praying it as the last
One hundred times daily in the tahlil formula: Muslim 2691's fortress

hadith.text: The scrolls fly up and the card outweighs; nothing outweighs the name of Allah.

w-adhan-dua.translit: Allahumma rabba hadhihid-da'watit-tammah... ab'ath-hu maqamam-mahmudan alladhi wa'adtah
w-adhan-dua.meaning: O Allah, Lord of this perfect call... raise him to the praised station You promised him
w-adhan-dua.role: A daily ballot for the Great Intercession
w-adhan-dua.summary: Thirty seconds after every adhan, the ummah nominates its Prophet for the station he will hold on the Day.
w-adhan-dua.details:
Five times daily the call ends, and the sunnah opens a thirty-second window with an eternal payout: "whoever says, when he hears the call: O Allah, Lord of this perfect call and the established prayer, give Muhammad the wasilah and the excellence, and raise him to the praised station You promised him; my intercession becomes lawful for him on the Day of Rising" (Bukhari 614).

The praised station is {{n:67|al-Maqam al-Mahmud}} of 17:79: the Great Intercession, when mankind's plea passes from prophet to prophet and stops at "I am for it." The du'a's mechanism moves in two directions at once: the sayer asks elevation for the Prophet ﷺ, and the Prophet's intercession is secured for the sayer. The wasilah itself, he explained, is a rank in Jannah fitting only one servant, "and I hope that I am he" (Muslim 384): even at the summit, the grammar of hope. The Codex keeps this word as its most practical link: one tile of the Nihaya, joined to a habit five minutes from now.
whenNow: After every adhan: the window is short and the clause is explicit
Adding the salawat first, as Muslim 384 sequences it
Teaching children the meaning: they are voting daily for their Prophet

hadith.text: Whoever says it when he hears the call, my intercession becomes lawful for him on the Day of Rising.

w-sayyid-istighfar.translit: Allahumma anta rabbi, la ilaha illa ant, khalaqtani wa ana abduk...
w-sayyid-istighfar.meaning: O Allah, You are my Lord; none has the right to be worshipped but You; You created me and I am Your servant...
w-sayyid-istighfar.summary: Covenant renewed, blessing acknowledged, sin confessed: said with certainty, it prices a day at Jannah.
w-sayyid-istighfar.details:
The Prophet ﷺ titled one du'a himself: sayyid al-istighfar, the master of seeking forgiveness. Its clauses move like the renewal of a covenant: identity (You are my Lord, I am Your servant), pledge (I am upon Your promise and pledge as I am able), refuge (from the evil of what I have made), confession (I acknowledge Your blessing upon me, and I acknowledge my sin), and the closing that names the only Forgiver: "forgive me, for none forgives sins but You" (Bukhari 6306).

The guarantee attached is timed to the two halves of the day: whoever says it in the day with certainty and dies before evening is of the people of Jannah, and whoever says it at night with certainty and dies before morning, the same. Certainty is the active ingredient; the words are its carrier. The scholars loved its balance: no despair (blessing acknowledged first) and no delusion (sin acknowledged next). The Codex sets it beside {{w:w-rabbana-zalamna|Adam's words}} as the matured form of the same species: mankind's first confession, grown into a daily covenant.
whenNow: Morning and evening, with certainty: the shift-schedule guarantee
As the day's reset after the confession: blessing, then sin, in order
Memorized once, owned for life: the master key stays cut

hadith.text: Whoever says it during the day, certain of it, and dies that day before evening, he is of the people of Jannah.

w-hawqala.titleEn: La Hawla wa la Quwwata illa Billah
w-hawqala.translit: La hawla wa la quwwata illa billah
w-hawqala.meaning: There is no power to change and no strength except by Allah
w-hawqala.role: A treasure from the treasures of Jannah
w-hawqala.summary: The Prophet ﷺ stopped Abu Musa on the road to hand him this sentence and name its vault.
w-hawqala.details:
On a journey, as the companions' takbir rose loud on the climbs, the Prophet ﷺ first taught volume ("you are not calling upon someone deaf or absent"), then pulled Abu {{n:15|Musa}} al-Ash'ari close for a private transfer: "shall I not point you to a treasure from the treasures of Jannah? La hawla wa la quwwata illa billah" (Bukhari 4205, Muslim 2704).

The sentence covers causality completely: no shifting of any state and no force to sustain one, except by Him. The scholars unpack its uses along that line: said at the muadhdhin's "hayya alas-salah" because even walking to prayer needs His power; said at overwhelming tasks because it disclaims self-sufficiency before asking; said at helplessness because it relocates the levers. A treasure of Jannah, Ibn Hajar notes, means a reward stored where nothing spoils. The Codex sets it beside {{w:w-subhan|the two light-heavy words}}: treasures of the tradition, open to any tongue, in any traffic, costing nothing and stored where nothing spoils.
whenNow: Answering the muadhdhin at the two hayya clauses
At the too-heavy task and at the immovable circumstance
As stored treasure: said now, banked where nothing spoils

hadith.text: Shall I not point you to a treasure from the treasures of Jannah? La hawla wa la quwwata illa billah.

w-salawat.translit: Allahumma salli 'ala Muhammadin wa 'ala ali Muhammad, kama sallayta 'ala Ibrahim...
w-salawat.meaning: O Allah, send Your salat upon Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You sent it upon Ibrahim...
w-salawat.role: The bridge between the two Friends
w-salawat.summary: Every tashahhud joins the final Prophet to the first Khalil; one saying returns ten from Allah.
w-salawat.details:
When the companions asked how to send salat upon him ﷺ, the answer he taught wove {{n:9|Ibrahim}} into every prayer of this ummah until the end of time (Bukhari 3370): the Friend who built {{p:p-kaaba|the House}} and asked for {{n:11|a messenger from his descendants}}, invoked in the very worship of the community that answered his du'a. The Codex reads the salawat as the Path folded into a sentence: from Khalil to Habib, one line of light.

The exchange is published: "whoever sends salat upon me once, Allah sends salat upon him ten times" (Muslim 408). The nearest people to him on the Day are those who said it most (Tirmidhi 484); Fridays carry a standing order for increase; and du'a itself is taught to travel wrapped in it. One meeting of the tradition weighs the whole practice: a man offered his entire du'a time as salawat, and was told: "then your concern will be sufficed and your sin forgiven" (Tirmidhi 2457, hasan). The Codex keeps this word as its own signature: the reader who finishes any tile has one obvious next deed.
whenNow: In every tashahhud: the appointed place
Fridays, abundantly: the day of increase
Wrapping any du'a: it travels accepted company

hadith.text: Whoever sends salat upon me once, Allah sends salat upon him ten times.

w-rabbana-atina.translit: Rabbana atina fid-dunya hasanah, wa fil-akhirati hasanah, wa qina 'adhaban-nar
w-rabbana-atina.meaning: Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire
w-rabbana-atina.role: The Prophet's ﷺ most frequent du'a
w-rabbana-atina.summary: Both worlds in one breath, revealed among the rites of Hajj as the correction of one-world asking.
w-rabbana-atina.details:
The verse arrived as a correction of scope: among the pilgrims of {{n:45|the Hajj}} were those who asked only, "our Lord, give us in this world," and the Book recorded what remained to them: "and he has no share in the Hereafter" (2:200). The believers' formula follows in the next verse, and Anas testified to its rank in the Prophet's ﷺ own usage: "the most frequent supplication of the Prophet was: our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire" (Bukhari 6389, Muslim 2690).

Its genius is its refusal to itemize: hasanah in this world covers health, spouse, provision, and every unnamed need, the mufassirun say, and hasanah in the next covers everything from the grave to {{n:71|the Vision}}. He ﷺ used it as the pilgrims' litany between the Corner and the Corner, and as the summary when a wasted man asked for his punishment early (Muslim 2688): do not ask for the load, ask for the balance. The Codex closes its Words section on this one because the Path itself is its shape: a dunya walked well, an akhirah reached safe, and the Fire skipped.
whenNow: As the backbone du'a of every sitting: his ﷺ most frequent
Between the Yemeni Corner and the Black Stone, its tawaf station
Whenever asking feels too complicated: two goods and one protection

quran.en: Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter, and protect us from the punishment of the Fire.

w-inna-lillah.translit: Inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un
w-inna-lillah.meaning: Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we return
w-inna-lillah.role: Ownership, stated at the moment of loss
w-inna-lillah.summary: Umm Salamah said it over her husband's death, added the taught du'a, and was compensated with the Prophet ﷺ himself.
w-inna-lillah.details:
The Qur'an assigns these words to one moment: "who, when calamity strikes them, say: indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we return" (2:156), and names their reward in the next verse: salawat from their Lord, and mercy, "and it is they who are guided." The sentence is not resignation; it is a title deed read aloud: the lost thing was never owned, and the destination was never in doubt.

{{c:c-umm-salamah|Umm Salamah}} put the words to the hardest of tests. Her husband, wounded at {{n:39|Uhud}}, died; she said the istirja and the addition the Prophet ﷺ had taught: "O Allah, reward me in my calamity and replace it for me with better." She admitted her own doubt in the narration: who could be better than Abu Salamah? "Then Allah replaced him for me with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ" (Muslim 918). The Codex keeps her story bound to the formula permanently: the words work above the sayer's imagination, and the promise of replacement is signed by the One who owns both what left and what arrives.
whenNow: At every loss, large or small: the deed is read aloud, then the heart follows
With the addition: “reward me in it and replace it with better” (Muslim 918)
Teaching it before the losses come: the sentence is learned in calm

quran.en: Who, when calamity strikes them, say: indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we return.

hadith.text: O Allah, reward me in my calamity and replace it for me with better. Then Allah replaced him for me with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.
